forks.name: codesight
forks.description: Universal AI context generator. Saves thousands of tokens per conversation in Claude Code, Cursor, Copilot, Codex, and more.
forks.summary:
Problem  
LLM‑driven code assistants repeatedly parse an entire repository to build context, consuming thousands of tokens before any useful suggestion is generated. For teams that use Claude Code, Cursor, Copilot, or Codex this overhead inflates cost and slows feedback loops.

What This Does  
codesight inspects a project in a single npx call and produces a compact, structured representation of the codebase. It extracts AST‑level data for TypeScript (via the wasm plugins in plugins/ast/) and regex‑based detectors for 30+ frameworks across 14 languages. The output includes:

 a wiki knowledge base (.codesight/wiki/) generated from the AST (src/ast/ and plugins/ast/),  
 a blast‑radius map (src/detectors/blast-radius.ts) that isolates the impact of a file,  
 a token‑savings benchmark (src/generators/html-report.ts) that quantifies the reduction, and  
 an optional MCP server (src/mcp-server.ts) exposing 14 “code‑assistant tools” via HTTP.

All of this is bundled into the CLI entry point src/index.ts, which is the script executed by npx codesight.

How To Use It  

Run in any project root – no config, no API keys
npx codesight

Generate a persistent markdown wiki
npx codesight --wiki

Open an interactive HTML report in the default browser
npx codesight --open

Start the MCP server (used by Claude Code / Cursor)
npx codesight --mcp

Show blast‑radius for a specific file
npx codesight --blast src/lib/db.ts

Enable native AST plugins (requires Rust/Go toolchains)
npx codesight --native-ast

The CLI reads package.json (or pyproject.toml for Python fixtures) to discover the project's language stack, then dispatches to the appropriate detector modules under src/detectors/. When the --native-ast flag is present it loads the compiled wasm modules built from the Rust source in plugins/ast/rust/src/lib.rs, the Go plugin in plugins/ast/golang/main.go, and the Python plugin in plugins/ast/python/src/lib.rs.

Real‑World Use  
A development team integrates codesight into their pre‑commit hook (src/plugins/githooks/). The hook runs npx codesight --benchmark and writes the token‑saving report to the CI artifacts. During a code review, a reviewer clicks the blast‑radius link for a changed file; the UI (generated by src/generators/html-report.ts) instantly shows which downstream services could be affected, allowing a focused discussion without pulling the entire repository into the LLM.

Code Health & Issues  

 Severity – High – Native AST plugins depend on external toolchains (Rust cargo, Go go). The repo does not ship pre‑built binaries, so CI must install these compilers; missing toolchain on a CI runner will cause failures. (plugins/ast/Cargo.toml, plugins/ast/golang/go.mod)  
 Severity – Medium – Regex‑based detectors (e.g., src/detectors/graph.ts) lack unit tests for edge‑case syntax, which could produce false positives on newer framework versions.  
 Severity – Low – The README advertises “Zero dependencies”, yet the project includes a full package.json with many dev dependencies; this is not a functional issue but may confuse users expecting a single‑file binary.  
 Severity – Low – License file (LICENSE) and CI workflows (.github/workflows/.yml) are present, but there is no explicit security audit step for the wasm plugins. Adding a cargo audit step would improve supply‑chain hygiene.

Overall, the repository contains 68 test files, a complete GitHub Actions pipeline, and comprehensive documentation (docs/wasm-plugins.md, .codesight/.md). The codebase follows a clear separation: AST extraction, detector logic, and output generators are isolated in src/ast/, src/detectors/, and src/generators/ respectively.

Bottom Line  
codesight delivers a practical token‑reduction layer for LLM‑based code assistants, with solid test coverage and CI support. Teams that rely heavily on prompt‑driven workflows will see measurable cost savings, but they must ensure the CI environment can compile the native AST plugins and accept that non‑TS languages are detected via regex, which may need periodic updates.

“Using the DESeq2 skill, compare condition A vs B in counts.tsv and output a volcano plot as volcano.png.”

Claude Code retrieves the snippet from SKILL.md, substitutes the file path, runs the R code via the system R interpreter, and returns the plot. The entire step is reproducible without hand‑typing any R commands, reducing analyst time from hours to minutes.

forks.name: claude_code_agent_farm
forks.description: Orchestration framework for running 20+ Claude Code agents in parallel: automated bug fixing, best-practices sweeps, lock-based coordination, and real-time tmux monitoring
forks.summary:
The Problem

Coordinating multiple AI coding agents on a single codebase typically devolves into chaos: agents overwrite each other's changes, run out of context mid-task, and require constant manual supervision. Running agents sequentially is slow, but running them in parallel without coordination is unsafe.

What This Does

claudecodeagentfarm is a Python orchestration framework that runs 20–50 Claude Code sessions in parallel against a target repository. The core logic lives in claudecodeagentfarm.py (the only Python file), which handles agent lifecycle, lock-based coordination to prevent file conflicts, and automatic context clearing when agents approach token limits.

The repo is organized around 34 technology stacks. Each stack has a configs/*.json file (e.g., configs/nextjsconfig.json), a matching prompt template in prompts/ (e.g., prompts/defaultbestpracticespromptnextjs.txt), and a setup script in toolsetupscripts/ (e.g., toolsetupscripts/setupnextjs.sh). The bestpracticesguides/ directory contains 37 stack-specific Markdown guides that agents reference during best-practices sweeps. A viewagents.sh script provides tmux-based real-time monitoring.

How To Use It

Setup — The pyproject.toml declares a Python 3.13+ project managed by uv. Run:

git clone https://github.com/Dicklesworthstone/claudecodeagentfarm.git
cd claudecodeagentfarm
chmod +x setup.sh
./setup.sh

Setup configures the required cc alias (ENABLEBACKGROUNDTASKS=1 claude --dangerously-skip-permissions), installs dependencies, and sets up direnv.

Configuration — Each stack's JSON config in configs/ controls agent count, prompts, and behavior. The system requires Claude Code installed and authenticated, plus tmux and git. Project-specific tools (e.g., bun for Next.js) must be pre-installed.

Running — Verify with claude-code-agent-farm doctor --path /path/to/project, then invoke the farm against a target repo. The README documents workflows for bug fixing and best-practices sweeps, but the exact invocation command is not shown in the excerpt — you'll need to check the README's full usage section or run the CLI with --help. Monitoring happens through viewagents.sh.

Real-World Use

A team maintaining a Next.js codebase with known lint violations and deprecated API usage could run a best-practices sweep: the farm spawns N agents, each assigned a chunk of the codebase, all guided by prompts/defaultbestpracticespromptnextjs.txt and constrained by configs/nextjsconfig.json. Lock files prevent two agents from editing the same file. Each agent commits its changes with rich diff summaries, producing an HTML run report for review.

Code Health & Issues
Med — No CI/CD: No .github/ or CI configuration exists. The only test evidence is 4 test files, but with a single Python file and 35 shell scripts, coverage is likely thin. No automated gate prevents regressions.
Low — No dependency lockfile: pyproject.toml declares dependencies without a lockfile, so builds are not reproducible across environments.
Low — Safety-critical alias: The required cc alias uses --dangerously-skip-permissions, meaning agents run with full system access. The setup script patches mis-quoted aliases, which suggests this has been a real failure point.
Low — Shell script sprawl: 35 setup scripts share toolsetupscripts/commonutils.sh, but there's no evidence of shared error handling or idempotency guarantees across all of them.

The Bottom Line

This is a serious, well-structured orchestration tool for teams already invested in Claude Code and willing to accept the operational complexity of parallel AI agents. The 34-stack coverage is genuinely broad, and the lock-based coordination addresses the core safety problem. It's not for solo developers or casual experimentation — the setup surface (tmux, uv, direnv, per-stack toolchains) is substantial, and the --dangerously-skip-permissions requirement demands a controlled environment. For a team running regular AI-assisted maintenance across multiple stacks, it could meaningfully reduce manual review time.

Generate evaluation traces

Grade the traces

Deploy to Cloud Run (or GKE) using the built Terraform stack
agents-cli deploy --target cloud-run

Each sub‑command maps directly to a module in src/google/agents/cli/ (e.g., eval/, deploy/).

Real‑World Use  
A data‑science team can automate model iteration:
Scaffold a new agent
agents-cli scaffold sentiment‑bot --template python
Run the agent against a curated test set
agents-cli eval generate --dataset data/sentiment.json
Grade with LLM‑as‑judge and export metrics
agents-cli eval grade --traces ./traces/ --output metrics.json
Push the best‑scoring version to production
agents-cli deploy --target cloud-run --region us-central1

The workflow is fully reproducible; all Terraform files under basetemplates/shared/deployment/terraform/ provision the required Cloud Run service, IAM bindings, and logging sinks.

forks.name: packet
forks.description: Quick Share client for Linux
forks.summary:
The Problem

Android's Quick Share is the default way to move files between Android devices and other platforms, but Linux has no first-party client. Existing options are either proprietary, incomplete, or require significant setup. Packet addresses this gap by providing a native Linux client for the Quick Share protocol, letting users exchange files with Android devices over Wi-Fi.

What This Does

Packet is a Rust/GTK application that implements a partial version of Google's Quick Share protocol. The core logic lives in src/, with src/main.rs as the entry point and src/objects/ handling both sendtransfer.rs and receivetransfer.rs state machines. The UI is built with GTK's blueprint format (data/resources/ui/window.blp), and the project uses the Meson build system (meson.build) with a Rust backend via Cargo.toml.

The app only implements the Wi-Fi LAN medium, so it requires Bluetooth to be enabled and devices on the same mDNS-capable network. A Nautilus file manager plugin is included at data/resources/plugins/packetnautilus.py.in for right-click sending. The project also ships a Flatpak manifest (build-aux/io.github.nozwock.Packet.Devel.json) and 35 translation files under po/.

How To Use It

Setup: Build from source with Meson, or install from Flathub (the README links to a published Flatpak). The README documents both paths:

Native build
meson setup builddir
meson compile -C builddir
meson devenv -C builddir packet

Flatpak build
flatpak-builder --user flatpakbuilddir \
    build-aux/io.github.nozwock.Packet.Devel.json
flatpak-builder --run flatpakbuilddir \
    build-aux/io.github.nozwock.Packet.Devel.json \
    packet

Configuration: No environment variables or config files are required. The app uses a GSettings schema (data/io.github.nozwock.Packet.gschema.xml.in) for preferences. The README notes a firewall may need a static port allowed through; this is handled in-app via Preferences.

Running it: After install, launch packet from a terminal or application menu. The app opens a GTK window where you can select files to send and view incoming transfers.

Real-World Use

A user on a Linux desktop wants to send a PDF to an Android phone. Both devices join the same Wi-Fi network with Bluetooth enabled. The user opens Packet, selects the file, and the app discovers the phone via mDNS and initiates a Quick Share handshake. The phone shows the incoming transfer notification and the user accepts it. The Nautilus plugin allows the same action directly from the file manager's right-click menu.

Code Health & Issues
Med - No test files detected - The repo has no tests/ directory or #[test] annotations in any of the 17 Rust files. The protocol logic in src/objects/ is stateful and error-prone; untested code paths here are a real risk.
Low - Partial protocol coverage - The README states this is a "partial implementation" with only Wi-Fi LAN support. Bluetooth and other Quick Share mediums are absent, which limits interoperability.
Low - Firewall dependency - The FAQ documents that firewalls block the app's port and require manual static port configuration. This is a known UX friction point, not a code defect.
Good - CI and release hygiene - GitLab CI (.gitlab-ci.yml) and GitHub Actions (.github/workflows/ci.yml) are configured, and a pre-commit hook exists at hooks/pre-commit.hook. The project follows GNOME's code of conduct.

The Bottom Line

Packet is a functional, well-packaged Quick Share client for Linux with proper Flatpak distribution and localization. The lack of tests is the main concern for a protocol implementation this complex. It's suitable for Linux users who regularly exchange files with Android devices and want a native solution, but expect occasional edge cases given the partial protocol coverage.

The Problem  
ML agents frequently need to reuse low‑level capabilities (e.g., “open a fridge”, “measure a temperature”) but each project rebuilds these skills from scratch. This duplication wastes engineering effort and makes it hard to assess safety or cost of a skill before deployment.

What This Does  
SkillNet supplies an open‑source “skill marketplace” and a lightweight SDK for discovering, installing, authoring, evaluating, and composing those skills. The repository is organized around two main entry points:

 examples/ – runnable notebooks and scripts (createexample.py, evaluateexample.py, searchdemo.py) that demonstrate the SDK workflow.  
 experiments/src/skills/ – a library of concrete skill definitions (e.g., alfworld/alfworld-clean-object/SKILL.md, scienceworld/scienceworld-circuit-builder/SKILL.md). Each skill folder contains a SKILL.md manifest and optional reference documents that the SDK can parse.

The top‑level README.md shows the public API (SkillNetClient) and CLI (skillnet search …, skillnet download …). The package is published on PyPI as skillnet-ai, but the source code for that SDK is not bundled in this fork; it is pulled in via pip install skillnet-ai.

How To Use It  

Setup  
Install the published SDK
pip install skillnet-ai   # requires Python 3.10+

Install the experiment‑specific dependencies (optional, for running the demos)
pip install -r experiments/requirements.txt

The requirements.txt lists openai, anthropic, tiktoken, etc., and is the only declared dependency source.

Configuration  
No API key is needed for public search or GitHub downloads. For evaluation/orchestration, the SDK expects the standard OpenAI‑compatible environment variables (APIKEY, BASEURL, SKILLNETMODEL). These are referenced in the README but not hard‑coded anywhere in the repo.

Running It  
Search and download a skill – via the SDK (shown in README.md):

from skillnetai import SkillNetClient

client = SkillNetClient()
results = client.search("pdf understanding", limit=5)
client.download(results[0].skillurl, targetdir="./myskills")

Run the provided demos – e.g., create a skill from a trace:

python examples/createexample.py

Evaluate a skill – e.g.:

python examples/evaluateexample.py

Explore the interactive notebooks – examples/skillnetusagedemo.ipynb and examples/scientificworkflowdemo.ipynb illustrate end‑to‑end pipelines.

If you need to run the AlfWorld or ScienceWorld experiments, invoke the scripts in experiments/:

python experiments/alfworldrun.py   # AlfWorld demo
python experiments/scienceworldrun.py   # ScienceWorld demo

Real‑World Use  
A data‑science platform can embed SkillNet to let analysts pull “CSV summarizer” or “PDF extractor” skills from the public library, evaluate them against internal safety policies, and compose them into a workflow. The platform would:
Call SkillNetClient.search() for needed capabilities.  
Use client.download() to fetch the skill package into a sandboxed execution environment.  
Run client.evaluate(skillpath) to obtain a safety/completeness score.  
Dynamically generate a prompt that strings together the selected skills for a downstream LLM orchestrator.

Code Health & Issues  
Medium – Missing CI/CD – No .github/ workflows, tox, or pytest CI configuration; automated testing is not enforced.  
Low – No lockfile – Dependencies are listed only in experiments/requirements.txt; reproducible builds require a requirements.lock or pip-tools output.

Low – Documentation fragmentation – Skill manifests (SKILL.md) are plentiful but not programmatically linked; the SDK must parse free‑form markdown, increasing parsing brittleness.  

No obvious security secrets are committed; the repository respects the MIT license.

The Bottom Line  
SkillNet offers a concrete, community‑driven catalogue of reusable agent skills together with a thin Python SDK that can be integrated into larger LLM‑orchestrated systems. The demos and skill library are well‑structured, but the lack of an in‑repo SDK, CI pipeline, and dependency lockfile make it less suitable for production‑grade deployment without additional engineering effort. Teams that need a searchable skill marketplace and are comfortable adding their own CI and packaging layers will find it a solid foundation.

forks.name: ccglass
forks.description: See what your coding agent (Claude Code, Codex, Kimi) sends to the model — local proxy + web dashboard
forks.summary:
The Problem

Coding agents like Claude Code and Codex send large, opaque payloads to model APIs. Debugging what actually gets sent — system prompts, tool schemas, message history, token usage — is painful because these CLIs ignore HTTPPROXY/HTTPSPROXY and often use TLS pinning, so standard proxy tools (Charles, mitmproxy) never see the traffic. ccglass solves this by intercepting only the plain HTTP hop to localhost.

What This Does

ccglass is a local reverse-proxy + web dashboard. It sets the client's base-URL env var (e.g. ANTHROPICBASEURL, OPENAIBASEURL) to point at a local proxy (src/forward-proxy.js), which forwards to the real API over HTTPS. The client does its own TLS to localhost, so no CA certs or TLS-pinning bypasses are needed. The dashboard (web/app.js, web/index.html) shows live requests, token/cache/cost, message history with tool calls, agent-loop flow, and turn-to-turn diffs (src/diff.js).

The repo supports 15+ providers via src/providers.js and format parsers in src/formats/ (anthropic.js, openai.js, reasonix.js). It also includes session stats (src/session-stats.js), export (src/export.js), and content-addressed storage (src/ca.js, src/blobs.js) per design docs in docs/superpowers/.

How To Use It

Setup: Install globally via npm (per README): npm install -g ccglass. The package.json confirms npm as the package manager.

Configuration: No config file required. Env vars are set automatically by the tool per provider. For Codex, API-key mode is required (OPENAIAPIKEY); ChatGPT-login mode uses WebSocket and won't be captured. Kimi runs through Claude Code against Moonshot's Anthropic-compatible endpoint.

Running it: The entry point is bin/ccglass.js, which delegates to src/cli.js. Run with no arguments to pick a client interactively, or name one directly:

ccglass claude
ccglass codex
ccglass deepseek

This starts the proxy, launches the client, and opens the dashboard at http://127.0.0.1:57633 (port varies).

Real-World Use

A developer debugging why Claude Code is sending a bloated system prompt or unexpected tool calls to a model. Run ccglass claude, reproduce the issue in the agent, then inspect the dashboard's request view and turn-to-turn diff to see exactly what changed between iterations. This also works for cost tracking — the dashboard buckets by model and session (docs/cost-and-model-bucketing.md), useful for auditing spend across a team's agent usage.

Code Health & Issues
Med — WebSocket gap: Codex in ChatGPT-login mode bypasses OPENAIBASEURL entirely (documented in README). The dashboard will silently show nothing. This is a known limitation, not a bug, but worth flagging.
Med — src/forward-proxy.js handles plain HTTP only. Any client that insists on HTTPS to localhost will fail. The README says this is intentional, but it narrows compatibility.
Low — 25 test files exist covering most modules, but web-live.test.js suggests some tests depend on a running server, which could be flaky in CI. No obvious missing test coverage for src/export.js or src/mcp.js.
Low — No secrets or config files in the repo. CI is present (.github/workflows/ includes publish.yml). License is present. Dependency hygiene looks reasonable given the lockfile.

The Bottom Line

ccglass is a well-scoped, genuinely useful debugging tool for anyone working deeply with coding agents. The architecture is sound — intercepting plain HTTP to localhost avoids the TLS-pinning problem entirely. The main limitation is provider-specific transport quirks (Codex's WebSocket mode), which are documented rather than hidden. Recommended for agent developers, LLM ops engineers, and teams auditing model spend.

forks.summary:
The Problem

Developers building financial applications need programmatic access to market data—stock quotes, fundamentals, earnings, news, and technical indicators—without maintaining raw HTTP integrations. Finnhub's REST API covers this domain, but raw API calls require handling authentication, pagination, and endpoint-specific quirks. A maintained client library removes that boilerplate.

What This Does

finnhub-python is an official Python client for the Finnhub API. The core logic lives in finnhub/client.py, which exposes a Client class with methods mapped to API endpoints—stockcandles(), companyprofile2(), quote(), earningscalendar(), and roughly 40 others. finnhub/exceptions.py defines API error types, and finnhub/init.py exports the package surface.

The repo is a fork of the upstream project (1,063 stars) with 19 files total. It's generated partly by OpenAPI tooling (.openapi-generator/), but the client itself is hand-maintained. setup.py and setup.cfg handle packaging; requirements.txt lists runtime dependencies; tox.ini and .travis.yml define test and CI configuration. The README documents every client method with a runnable example.

How To Use It

Setup: Install via pip. The README documents pip install finnhub-python; for local development, pip install -e . from the repo root works given setup.py is present.

Configuration: You need a Finnhub API key. There's no config file—pass it directly to the client constructor: finnhub.Client(apikey="YOUR API KEY"). The free tier has rate limits; paid tiers expand access.

Running it: The library is used as an imported module, not a standalone service. examples.py in the repo root is the reference script—it demonstrates every endpoint. A minimal invocation:

import finnhub
client = finnhub.Client(apikey="YOUR API KEY")
print(client.quote('AAPL'))

Real-World Use

A portfolio-tracking service that ingests daily price data and corporate actions could use this client as its data layer. The stockcandles() method fetches OHLCV series for backtesting; companyearnings() and stockdividends() feed fundamental screens. Since the client returns plain dicts, results drop directly into pandas DataFrames or a database.

Code Health & Issues
Low - No lockfile: requirements.txt declares dependencies without pinned versions, so builds are non-reproducible. pip freeze output would pin them, but it's not committed.
Low - Single test file: One test file exists but the repo gives no evidence of test coverage depth or whether tests run in CI (.travis.yml is present but unverified).
Low - Generated-code smell: The .openapi-generator/ directory and gitpush.sh suggest partial codegen; manually maintained client code alongside generated artifacts can drift over time.
Low - No explicit Python version support: setup.py likely declares pythonrequires, but the analysis doesn't confirm it. Python 2 support was dropped upstream, but verify before adopting.
Med - API key handling: The README shows hardcoding the key in source. Production users must inject it via environment variables or a secrets manager—the library doesn't enforce this.

The codebase is otherwise clean: a clear module layout, documented public API, and a comprehensive README.

The Bottom Line

A solid, well-documented client for Finnhub's API—appropriate for production use if you pin dependencies and manage your API key properly. The fork adds no visible changes over upstream, so most teams should depend on the PyPI package directly rather than this repo. Best suited to Python-based fintech applications needing quick, maintained access to market data.

forks.name: client-python
forks.description: The official Python client library for the Massive.com REST and WebSocket API.
forks.summary:
The Problem  
Clients need a thin, Pythonic wrapper around Massive (formerly Polygon.io) REST and WebSocket endpoints that hides pagination, rate‑limit handling, and request construction. Manually building URLs, handling pagination loops, and keeping the base URL up‑to‑date after the rebrand creates boiler‑plate code and integration friction.

What This Does  
The massive package implements RESTClient and WebSocketClient classes that expose high‑level methods such as listaggs, getlasttrade, and listtrades. Core logic lives in massive/rest/ (base.py, aggs.py, economy.py, etc.) and massive/websocket/ (generated from .massive/websocket.json). Example scripts in examples/rest/ and examples/websocket/ demonstrate each endpoint.

 massive/init.py exports the public client classes.  
 massive/rest/base.py handles HTTP session setup, pagination toggling, and error mapping.  
 examples/tools/docker/app.py shows a minimal Flask‑based container that can run a client script inside Docker, useful for CI or isolated execution.

How To Use It  

Setup  
Install the published package (includes compiled source)
pip install -U massive   # requires Python >=3.9

If you want to work from source, install the development requirements:
python -m venv .venv
source .venv/bin/activate
pip install -r docs/requirements.txt   # note: no lockfile, see issues section

Configuration  
 API key – required for every client. Provide it as the apikey argument or via the MASSIVEAPIKEY environment variable (the client reads os.getenv('MASSIVEAPIKEY') in massive/rest/base.py).  
 Base URL – defaults to https://api.massive.com; you can override with baseurl= when constructing the client if you still need the legacy api.polygon.io.

Running it  
Typical usage is a short script that imports the client:

examples/rest/simple-get.py
from massive import RESTClient

client = RESTClient()                      # picks up API key from env
for agg in client.listaggs(ticker="AAPL", multiplier=1, timespan="minute",
                            from="2023-01-01", to="2023-01-02"):
    print(agg)

Execute the script directly:

python examples/rest/simple-get.py

For a containerised run, build and start the Docker helper:

docker build -t massive-demo examples/tools/docker
docker run -e MASSIVEAPIKEY=YOURKEY massive-demo

The Dockerfile (examples/tools/docker/Dockerfile) installs the package and runs app.py, which contains a minimal Flask endpoint that can trigger any client call.

Real‑World Use  
A data‑engineering pipeline can pull daily aggregates for a watchlist and store them in a data lake:

from massive import RESTClient
import json, datetime, pathlib

client = RESTClient()
today = datetime.date.today().isoformat()
watchlist = ["AAPL", "MSFT", "TSLA"]

for sym in watchlist:
    aggs = list(client.listaggs(ticker=sym, multiplier=1, timespan="day",
                                 from=today, to=today))
    pathlib.Path(f"data/{sym}{today}.json").write_text(json.dumps(aggs))

Schedule the script via Airflow or a cron job; the built‑in pagination will retrieve the full day's data in a single call per symbol.

Code Health & Issues  
Low – Missing lockfile – docs/requirements.txt lists development dependencies without a requirements.lock or pipfile.lock; reproducible builds are not guaranteed.  
Medium – Sparse test coverage – Only one test file is present; core REST logic (massive/rest/base.py, aggs.py) lacks unit tests, raising confidence gaps for edge‑case handling.  
Low – No explicit packaging config – The repo does not contain setup.py, pyproject.toml, or requirements.txt for the library itself; installation relies on the published PyPI wheel. This is acceptable for consumption but limits local development.  
Low – CI configuration – GitHub Actions workflows (.github/workflows/.yml) run linting, code‑QL, and a single test job, indicating basic CI hygiene.  
Low – Documentation – 27 ReST/Markdown files cover each endpoint; the docs are generated from the source and kept up‑to‑date, but there is no versioned API reference.  

Overall, the codebase follows a clear separation (client vs. examples) and includes practical Docker tooling, but it would benefit from a lockfile, expanded test suite, and an explicit local packaging manifest.

The Bottom Line  
massive delivers a straightforward, well‑documented Python wrapper for Massive’s market data APIs, handling pagination and base‑URL changes out of the box. It is ready for production use where rapid data retrieval is needed, provided you accept the limited internal test coverage and add a lockfile for reproducible development builds. Ideal for teams that want a thin client without building their own HTTP layer.

forks.name: alpha_vantage
forks.description: A python wrapper for Alpha Vantage API for financial data.
forks.summary:
The Problem  
A Python client needs a reliable, thin wrapper around the Alpha Vantage API to fetch real‑time and historical financial data (equities, crypto, fundamentals, technical indicators). The repo provides that wrapper, but the client must understand the installation, configuration, and potential code‑health gaps before integrating it into a pipeline.

What This Does  
The package lives under alphavantage/ and exposes modules for each data domain:  
alphavantage/timeseries.py – TimeSeries class for intraday/day/extended intraday data.  
alphavantage/techindicators.py – technical indicator calculations (SMA, EMA, RSI, etc.).  
alphavantage/fundamentaldata.py – fundamental metrics (earnings, balance sheet).  
alphavantage/cryptocurrencies.py – crypto price and metadata.  
alphavantage/asyncsupport/ – async counterparts (alphavantage.py, timeseries.py, techindicators.py, …) built on asyncio.  

The root setup.py defines the package metadata; docs/requirements.txt lists runtime deps (currently no lockfile). Tests reside in testalphavantage/ (15 files) and include mock‑data fixtures under testalphavantage/testdata/.

How To Use It  
Install  
  pip install alphavantage          # core package
  # optional: pip install alphavantage pandas   # for DataFrame output

  
  (The setup.py at the repo root is the entry point for pip install -e . when developing from source.)
Configure  
  Set the environment variable ALPHAVANTAGEAPIKEY or pass the key directly to each constructor, e.g. TimeSeries(key=os.getenv("ALPHAVANTAGEAPIKEY")). No additional config files are required.
Running it – a minimal workflow (referencing actual files):  

  import os
  from alphavantage.timeseries import TimeSeries

  ts = TimeSeries(key=os.getenv("ALPHAVANTAGEAPIKEY"), outputformat="pandas")
  data, meta = ts.getdailyadjusted(symbol="MSFT", outputsize="full")
  print(data.head())

  For async usage, import from alphavantage.asyncsupport.timeseries and await the method.

Real‑World Use  
A quant team can pull daily adjusted close prices for a universe of tickers, feed them into a risk model, and store the resulting DataFrames in a data lake. The async variants allow non‑blocking fetches when aggregating many symbols concurrently, leveraging alphavantage.asyncsupport/techindicators.py to compute moving averages on‑the‑fly without a separate pandas pass.

Code Health & Issues  
Dependencies without a lockfile – docs/requirements.txt lists pins but no requirements.lock or  Pipfile.lock, so reproducible builds rely on the user remembering exact versions.  
Async support untested at scale – 15 test files exist, yet only a subset cover the async modules (testalphavantage/testalphavantageasync.py). Race‑condition or event‑loop bugs could surface in production‑heavy concurrent workloads.  
Integration tests require an API key – testalphavantage/testintegrationalphavantage.py and the async counterpart hit the real Alpha Vantage endpoint; they will fail without a valid key, limiting CI coverage to mock‑only paths.  
Missing input validation – several module constructors accept a symbol argument but do not sanitize it against the API’s allowed characters, risking malformed requests.  
CI configured – .travis.yml is present, and the Travis CI badge appears in the README, indicating continuous integration is active for the main branch.

The Bottom Line  
This repo delivers a functional, well‑structured Python wrapper for Alpha Vantage with separate sync and async paths, comprehensive module coverage, and solid test scaffolding using mock data. The main trade‑off is the absence of a dependency lockfile and limited async test coverage, which may require a small ops overhead for strict reproducibility and high‑concurrency scenarios. It is well‑suited for individual developers or small teams needing quick financial data access; larger organizations requiring guaranteed build reproducibility or mission‑critical async throughput may want to add a lockfile and expand async test coverage.

forks.name: yfinance
forks.description: Download market data from Yahoo! Finance's API
forks.summary:
The Problem

Applications that need financial market data—prices, dividends, splits, fundamentals, live quotes—typically face a choice between expensive vendor APIs or scraping HTML pages. yfinance solves this by wrapping Yahoo Finance's public JSON endpoints in a clean Python API, giving developers programmatic access to a broad range of market data without API keys or paid subscriptions.

What This Does

yfinance is a Python library that downloads and normalizes market data from Yahoo Finance. The core entry point is yfinance/init.py, which exposes the main components: Ticker and Tickers for single and multi-ticker queries, download() for bulk historical data, Market for market-level info, Search for quotes and news, and Screener for building filtered market queries. Live streaming is handled by yfinance/live.py via WebSocket and AsyncWebSocket classes.

The library handles data repair and validation internally—yfinance/data.py and yfinance/base.py contain the core fetching and normalization logic, while yfinance/pricerepair.py (referenced in the docs) fixes common errors like bad dividends and stock splits. The tests/ directory contains 100+ files with fixture data covering edge cases across global exchanges, suggesting significant maturity in handling real-world data quirks.

How To Use It

Setup: Install from PyPI. The repo uses setup.py for packaging and requirements.txt for dependencies. No lockfile is present, so builds are not fully reproducible.

pip install yfinance

Configuration: No API keys or environment variables required. Optional configuration for caching and logging is documented in doc/source/advanced/config.rst and doc/source/advanced/caching.rst.

Running it: Import the library in Python and call the high-level functions. The README documents the primary interface:

import yfinance as yf

Download historical data for a ticker
data = yf.download("AAPL", period="1mo")
print(data.head())

Get a Ticker object for detailed info
ticker = yf.Ticker("MSFT")
print(ticker.info["marketCap"])

Real-World Use

A portfolio tracking service could use yfinance to pull daily closing prices for a watchlist, compute returns, and detect corporate actions. The library's Tickers class handles multiple symbols efficiently, and the repair logic in yfinance/data.py helps ensure dividend and split adjustments are applied correctly—critical for accurate backtesting.

import yfinance as yf
import pandas as pd

symbols = ["AAPL", "MSFT", "GOOGL"]
data = yf.download(symbols, period="6mo", groupby="ticker")
returns = data["Close"].pct_change().dropna()

Code Health & Issues
Low - No lockfile for dependencies - requirements.txt pins versions at a coarse level, so builds may differ across environments. This is common for libraries but worth noting for reproducibility.
Low - Legacy CI configuration - .travis.yml is present but the active CI appears to be GitHub Actions (.github/workflows/ contains pytest.yml.disabled, ruff.yml, pyright.yml). The disabled pytest workflow is a minor concern—test CI may not be running in this fork.
Low - Unsupported Python version badge - README claims Python 2.7 support, which is almost certainly stale given the modern codebase and dependencies.
Clean aspects - The test suite is extensive with fixture data covering real-world edge cases across multiple exchanges. Type checking (pyrightconfig.json) and linting (ruff.yml) are configured. The codebase has clear module separation (domain/, data.py, live.py, lookup.py).

The Bottom Line

yfinance is a mature, well-tested library that solves a real problem—free, programmatic access to financial market data. It is battle-tested in production (25k+ stars upstream) and has solid documentation and test coverage. The main risks are Yahoo's terms of service and the possibility of API changes breaking the library. It is well-suited for research, prototyping, and internal tools where free data outweighs the legal and reliability trade-offs.

forks.name: llm-council
forks.description: LLM Council works together to answer your hardest questions
forks.summary:
The Problem  
When evaluating multiple large‑language‑model (LLM) providers, developers must manually query each API, compare outputs, and synthesize a final answer. This repetitive workflow is error‑prone and slows down rapid prototyping or research that requires side‑by‑side model comparison.

What This Does  
llm-council implements a lightweight web UI that orchestrates a “council” of LLMs via the OpenRouter gateway. The backend (backend/main.py) runs a FastAPI server that:
Sends the user prompt to every model listed in backend/config.py (Stage 1).  
Feeds each model the other models’ responses for anonymous ranking (Stage 2).  
Passes the ranked set to a designated chairman model for a consolidated answer (Stage 3).

The frontend (frontend/src/App.jsx and supporting components under frontend/src/components/) displays each stage in separate tabs, letting users inspect raw replies, review rankings, and view the final synthesized response.

Key files:
backend/council.py – core orchestration logic, async calls to OpenRouter via httpx.  
backend/openrouter.py – thin wrapper around the OpenRouter HTTP API.  
frontend/src/api.js – React‑side helper that calls /api/query on the FastAPI server.  

How To Use It  
Install Python dependencies with uv (requires uv >= 0.4)
uv sync                     # reads pyproject.toml, creates .venv
Install frontend dependencies
cd frontend
npm install                 # uses package.json
cd ..
Provide OpenRouter credentials
echo "OPENROUTERAPIKEY=sk-or-…" > .env
(Optional) Adjust the council composition
Edit backend/config.py → COUNCILMODELS / CHAIRMANMODEL
Start both services (the repo supplies a convenience script)
./start.sh                 # runs backend with uv and frontend with npm run dev

If start.sh is unavailable or you prefer manual control:

Backend (FastAPI) on default port 8000
uv run python -m backend.main

Frontend (Vite dev server) on port 5173
cd frontend
npm run dev

Open http://localhost:5173 in a browser to interact with the council UI.

Real‑World Use  
A data‑science team can embed this tool in a research notebook to benchmark new prompts across OpenAI, Anthropic, Google, and other providers. After a single click, the UI returns per‑model answers, peer‑review rankings, and a final aggregated response, reducing the manual copy‑paste cycle and providing a reproducible audit trail stored in data/conversations/ (JSON files).

Example: programmatically fetch the final answer for downstream processing
import requests, json
resp = requests.post(
    "http://localhost:8000/api/query",
    json={"prompt": "Explain transformer attention in 2 sentences"}
)
final = resp.json()["final_answer"]
print(final)

Code Health & Issues  
Med – No automated tests – repository lacks any tests/ folder or pytest configuration; core paths (backend/council.py, backend/openrouter.py) are unverified.  
Med – No CI/CD pipeline – no .github/workflows/ or similar; changes are not gated by builds or lint checks.  
Med – Missing license – root contains no LICENSE; downstream users have unclear redistribution rights.  
Low – Secrets handling – API key is read from a plain‑text .env file; the repo does not enforce .env exclusion beyond .gitignore, but accidental commit is possible.  
Low – Minimal error handling – backend/openrouter.py forwards raw HTTP responses; network failures or non‑2xx codes are not wrapped in custom exceptions, risking uncaught crashes.  
Low – Documentation gaps – README covers basic setup but omits details on required Python version, uv version, or how to run the backend in production (e.g., uvicorn command).  

Overall code organization is clear, with separation between API wrapper, council orchestration, and React UI. Lint configuration (frontend/eslint.config.js) exists, but no corresponding Python linting (e.g., flake8) is present.

The Bottom Line  
llm-council delivers a functional prototype for multi‑LLM comparison with a simple FastAPI + React stack, suitable for quick experiments or internal demos. The lack of tests, CI, and a proper license limits its suitability for production or commercial adoption without additional engineering effort. Teams that need a sandbox for model side‑by‑side evaluation will find it useful; larger organizations should treat it as a reference implementation and extend it with proper testing, security reviews, and deployment tooling.

forks.name: Local_Knowledge_Graph
forks.description: No description available
forks.summary:
The Problem  
Local LLM deployments (e.g., Ollama) give powerful reasoning capabilities but lack a built‑in way to visualise the step‑by‑step thought process. Teams that need to audit or explain model output have no lightweight, on‑premise tool to turn a chain‑of‑thought into an interactive graph.

What This Does  
LocalKnowledgeGraph wraps a locally‑running Llama model and renders each reasoning step as a node, linking nodes with cosine similarity edges derived from an embedding model. The Flask web UI lives in src/mpelkg/templates/index.html and the core logic is in:

 src/mpelkg/graph.py – builds the graph structure.  
 src/mpelkg/reasoning.py – drives the step‑wise prompting.  
src/mpelkg/store.py – caches model responses and embeddings.  

The package exposes a CLI (src/mpelkg/cli.py) and a Flask factory (src/mpelkg/app.py). Installing the wheel (mpe-lkg) registers the entry point mpe-lkg which starts the server on port 5100.

How To Use It  

Setup  
Install the package from PyPI
pip install mpe-lkg

Ensure Ollama is running locally and has at least one chat model
ollama pull llama3.2:3b          # any chat model
ollama pull nomic-embed-text      # optional embedding model

The pyproject.toml declares the runtime dependencies; no lockfile is present, so reproducible builds rely on the version constraints in that file.

Configuration  
All tunables are environment variables, documented in the README and read by src/mpelkg/app.py:

| Variable | Default | Purpose |
|---|---|---|
| OLLAMAURL | http://localhost:11434 | Ollama endpoint |
| LKGCHATMODEL | auto | Override the chat model |
| LKGEMBEDMODEL | auto | Override the embedding model |
| LKGHOST / LKGPORT | 127.0.0.1 / 5100 | Server bind address |
| LKGDEBUG | off | Enable Flask debugger |

Export any needed overrides before starting, e.g.:

export LKGCHATMODEL=llama3.2:3b
export LKGEMBEDMODEL=nomic-embed-text

Running  
From a terminal:

Start the UI (installed entry point)
mpe-lkg

Or run the source shim
python app.py

The server listens on http://localhost:5100. For programmatic use:

from mpelkg import createapp, health

print(health())          # {'ok': True, 'models': [...]}
createapp().run(port=5100)

The CLI also provides a health check (mpe-lkg doctor) that exits non‑zero on failure, useful for CI scripts.

Real‑World Use  
A data‑science team can embed this service in a notebook to audit model reasoning:

import requests, json, os

os.system("mpe-lkg &")                     # launch in background
resp = requests.post(
    "http://127.0.0.1:5100/api/ask",
    json={"question": "Why is the sky blue?"}
)
print(json.dumps(resp.json(), indent=2))
Open http://127.0.0.1:5100 to view the interactive graph.

The visual graph helps non‑technical stakeholders see how the model arrived at its answer and spot any logical gaps.

Code Health & Issues  
Low – Missing LICENSE – repository root lacks a license file; downstream users have unclear redistribution rights.  
Low – No lockfile – pyproject.toml lists dependencies without a poetry.lock/requirements.txt; builds may yield different versions.  
Medium – Limited input validation – src/mpelkg/backends.py forwards user prompts directly to Ollama; malformed JSON could cause server errors.  
Medium – Minimal type hints – most modules lack static typing, reducing IDE assistance and static analysis confidence.  
Low – Documentation gaps – only a high‑level README; internal APIs (graph.py, store.py) have no docstrings.  
Positive – Test coverage – 9 test files (tests/) exercise graph math, layer handling, Ollama integration, and rendering.  
Positive – CI pipeline – GitHub Actions for Linux, macOS, Windows and PyPI publishing demonstrate a functional SDLC.  

The Bottom Line  
LocalKnowledge_Graph provides a straightforward, on‑premise Flask UI for visualising LLM reasoning, with a clean install path and functional CI. It is suitable for teams that already run Ollama locally and need an audit trail for model output. The main drawbacks are the missing license, lack of a dependency lockfile, and modest internal documentation; these should be addressed before adopting in regulated environments.

forks.name: GEA
forks.description: Group Evolving Agents: Open-Ended Self-Improvement via Experience Sharing
forks.summary:
The Problem

Software agents that write code typically operate in isolation. Each agent starts from the same base prompt, attempts a task, and either succeeds or fails without learning from other agents' attempts. This wastes successful strategies and repeats known failures. GEA addresses this by treating a group of agents as a single evolutionary unit, allowing them to share experiences and improve collectively over time.

What This Does

GEA is a research framework for open-ended self-improvement of coding agents. The core loop is implemented in GEAouter.py, the entry point, which orchestrates a group of agents working on SWE-bench tasks. Each agent attempts to fix real GitHub issues from Django and Sphinx, producing patches stored under initial/predictions/. The codingagent.py file defines the base agent behavior—how it reads a task, generates a patch, and writes results.

The system evaluates each patch against the target repository's test suite, with results logged in initial/logs/runevaluation/. Successful patches and their associated reasoning are then shared back into the group's collective experience, which subsequent agents use to inform their own attempts. This experience-sharing mechanism is the key differentiator from single-agent self-improvement approaches. The project builds on the Darwin Gödel Machine and uses SWE-bench and Polyglot benchmarks for evaluation.

How To Use It

Setup: Requires Python 3, Docker, and API keys for OpenAI and Anthropic. The README documents a standard venv + pip install -r requirements.txt flow. Docker must be functional (docker run hello-world). The SWE-bench dependency is cloned and installed separately.

Configuration: Set OPENAIAPIKEY and ANTHROPICAPIKEY as environment variables in ~/.bashrc.

Running: Execute python GEAouter.py from the repo root.

export OPENAIAPIKEY='...'
export ANTHROPICAPIKEY='...'
python3 -m venv venv
source venv/bin/activate
pip install -r requirements.txt
cd swebench && git clone https://github.com/princeton-nlp/SWE-bench.git && cd SWE-bench && git checkout dc4c087c2b9e4cefebf2e3d201d27e36 && pip install -e . && cd ../../
python GEAouter.py

Real-World Use

This is a research tool, not a production service. A practical use case: an ML research team studying multi-agent coordination and self-improvement. They would run GEA on a subset of SWE-bench tasks, inspect the generated patches under initial/predictions/ to see how well agents solve real bugs, and analyze the experience-sharing dynamics to understand when group collaboration helps versus when it adds overhead. The analysis/ scripts support plotting and quantitative evaluation of these runs.

Code Health & Issues
Medium - No CI/CD pipeline: No .github/ or CI config exists. The 42 test files are evaluation scripts for SWE-bench tasks, not unit tests for the GEA framework itself. Changes to GEAouter.py or codingagent.py have no automated gate.
Medium - Heavy Docker coupling: The entire evaluation pipeline runs inside Docker containers per task. This makes the system resource-intensive (one container per bug) and fragile if Docker is unavailable or misconfigured in a deployment environment.
Low - Repository hygiene: The repo contains 191 files of evaluation logs and predictions under initial/, which inflates the repo size and mixes generated artifacts with source code. These should be gitignored or stored separately.
Low - Research-stage maturity: The paper is on arXiv and the codebase is built on a prior research project (DGM). Expect rough edges in error handling and configuration, and no production hardening.

The Bottom Line

GEA is a legitimate research contribution to multi-agent self-improvement, with a clear architecture and reproducible evaluation pipeline. It is not production software—no CI, no unit tests, heavy Docker use, and research-grade code quality. Use it if you are studying agent coordination or open-ended self-improvement; skip it if you need a maintainable agent framework for real workloads.

forks.name: GHOST-osint-crm
forks.description: GHOST - Global Human Operations & Surveillance Tracking:  Open-source investigation management platform for tracking people, connections, and intelligence data. Because Excel spreadsheets are for accountants, not investigators. Non-commercial license.
forks.summary:
The Problem  
Investigators often rely on ad‑hoc spreadsheets to track people, connections, and evidence. Spreadsheets lack relational integrity, audit trails, and visual network mapping, which leads to data inconsistency, version‑control headaches, and limited collaboration.

What This Does  
GHOST‑osint‑crm provides a self‑hosted full‑stack web application that replaces spreadsheets with a relational database (PostgreSQL) and a React UI. The backend API lives in backend/server.js and exposes routes such as backend/routes/people.js, backend/routes/entityNetwork.js, and backend/routes/geocoding.js. The frontend consumes these endpoints via the React code under frontend/ (e.g., the network diagram uses ReactFlow components). Configuration defaults are supplied in backend/.env.example and frontend/.env.example; Docker orchestration is defined in docker-compose.yml, backend/Dockerfile, and frontend/Dockerfile.

How To Use It  

Setup  
Clone and enter the repo
git clone https://github.com/yourorg/GHOST-osint-crm.git
cd GHOST-osint-crm

Build and start containers (Docker Compose uses the two Dockerfiles)
docker compose up --build -d

The compose file pulls the backend image (built from backend/Dockerfile) and the frontend image (built from frontend/Dockerfile), then runs PostgreSQL (defined in the compose file).

Configuration  
 Backend: copy backend/.env.example to backend/.env and set at least DATABASEURL, JWTSECRET, and GEOCODINGAPIKEY.  
 Frontend: copy frontend/.env (note: the repository contains a placeholder file; replace any real secrets).

Running

Add suspects via the People page (backend/routes/people.js).  
Upload addresses; the backend auto‑geocodes them using backend/services/improvedGeocodingService.js.  
Visualize connections on the Entity Network page, which pulls data from backend/routes/entityNetwork.js and renders with ReactFlow.  

All actions are logged by backend/middleware/auditLog.js, providing an audit trail for internal review.

GHOST‑osint‑crm delivers a functional, containerized OSINT case management system with relational storage, geocoding, and interactive network visualizations. forks.name: realtime-phone-agents-course
forks.description: Build realtime AI voice agents using FastRTC for low-latency streaming, Superlinked for vector search, Twilio for live phone calls, and Runpod for scalable GPU deployment.
forks.summary:
The Problem

Building production-ready realtime AI voice agents requires stitching together multiple specialized components—STT, TTS, vector search, and telephony—each with their own deployment, scaling, and latency requirements. Most tutorials gloss over the integration patterns, leaving engineers to figure out how these pieces actually compose in a live call flow.

What This Does

This repository is a structured course (119 files) for building a real estate voice agent call center. The core architecture lives in src/realtimephoneagents/ and integrates:
STT across three implementations: stt/groq/whisper.py, stt/local/moonshine.py, and stt/runpod/fasterwhisper/ for GPU-accelerated transcription
TTS via tts/local/kokoro.py, tts/runpod/orpheus/ (3B model), and tts/togetherai/
Vector search through infrastructure/superlinked/ with data ingestion (dataingestion.py), index management (index.py), and querying (query.py)
Realtime voice pipeline in agent/fastrtcagent.py and agent/stream.py
Twilio integration at api/routes/voice.py for inbound/outbound calls
Avatar system with 8 character definitions in avatars/definitions/ (dan, jess, leah, leo, mia, tara, zac, zoe)
API layer at api/main.py with routes for health checks, Superlinked queries, and voice endpoints

Configuration lives in .env.example, config.py, and the various Dockerfile. files (Dockerfile, Dockerfile.fasterwhisper, Dockerfile.orpheus). The API is defined in pyproject.toml with dependencies listed but no lockfile present.

How To Use It

Setup  
Clone and install dependencies
uv sync  # or: pip install -e ".[dev]"
The repo uses uv (seen in uv.lock), but pyproject.toml is the declared dependency source

Environment setup
cp .env.example .env  # populate Twilio, Runpod, Superlinked, Groq keys

Build the Docker environment (choose variant)
docker build -f Dockerfile -t phone-agents .
Or for Orpheus TTS: docker build -f Dockerfile.orpheus .
Or for faster-whisper STT: docker build -f Dockerfile.fasterwhisper .

Configuration  
Required env vars are documented in .env.example and referenced throughout src/realtimephoneagents/config.py. Critical keys include Twilio credentials, Runpod API endpoints, Superlinked cluster details, and Groq API keys for Whisper fallback.

Running it  
The entry point is src/realtimephoneagents/api/main.py—start the API server with:
uv run uvicorn src.realtimephoneagents.api.main:app --reload

Outbound calls can be triggered via scripts/makeoutboundcall.py. The full course workflow is orchestrated through the notebooks in notebooks/lesson.ipynb.

Real-World Use

A real estate firm receives an inbound call via Twilio (api/routes/voice.py). The call flows to FastRTC (agent/fastrtcagent.py) for realtime audio processing, while the agent's LLM retrieves property details from a Superlinked index (infrastructure/superlinked/index.py) using the caller's query. STT transcribes speech through either Moonshine, Groq Whisper, or Runpod Faster-Whisper, and TTS renders responses via Kokoro or Orpheus 3B. The agent can search live property data (scripts/ingestproperties.py feeds data/properties.csv into the Superlinked index) and respond with lifelike voice output.

Code Health & Issues
[Medium/SDLC] No test files detected - repository-wide. No tests/ directory, no pytest configuration, and no test imports found in the structure. All agent logic, STT/TTS pipelines, and API routes are untested.
[Low/Risk] Dependencies declared without a lockfile - pyproject.toml lists dependencies but uv.lock exists alongside it, suggesting uv is used for resolution. However, the lockfile is not enforced in CI, and pip install without uv would produce non-reproducible installs.
[Medium] No input validation on API routes - api/routes/voice.py and api/routes/superlinked.py accept inbound call payloads and Superlinked queries without visible schema validation, which could allow malformed requests to reach downstream components.
[Low] Secrets potentially in Dockerfiles - Dockerfile, Dockerfile.faster_whisper, and Dockerfile.orpheus may copy .env or require runtime env var injection; verify .dockerignore prevents accidental .env commits.

The Bottom Line

This is a functional, well-organized course repo that maps a complete realtime voice agent stack—from Twilio telephony to GPU-accelerated STT/TTS to Superlinked retrieval. It's practical for engineers who want concrete code to fork and adapt, not a black-box demo. The absence of tests and a enforced lockfile are the main production-readiness gaps; teams comfortable pinning dependencies via uv and writing their own test suites will get the most value.

forks.name: OpenSpace
forks.description: "OpenSpace: The Skill Management Layer for AI Agents" -- https://open-space.cloud/
forks.summary:
The Problem

AI agents accumulate skills over time, but most agent frameworks treat skills as static files. There is no unified way to discover which skill applies to a new task, verify which skills actually work in production, or improve skills based on real outcomes. Teams running multiple agents (Claude Code, Codex, OpenClaw) end up duplicating capabilities and repeating failures across tools.

What This Does

OpenSpace is a skill management layer that sits between your agents and their skills. It provides retrieval (finding the right skill), evaluation (tracking real-world outcomes), sharing (across agents and team members), and evolution (improving skills with each run). The repository contains two applications: apps/dashboard — a React/Vite/TypeScript web dashboard with pages for skills, workflows, agent traces, and skill evolution — and apps/tui — a terminal UI built with Ink that provides a REPL, agent event feeds, permission dialogs, and a vim-mode keybinding system.

The dashboard handles the management view: src/pages/SkillsPage.tsx lists skills, src/pages/SkillDetailPage.tsx shows version history and diffs via src/components/skill-detail/DiffViewer.tsx, and src/pages/EvolutionPage.tsx tracks skill changes over time. The TUI handles the interactive agent experience, with a bridge protocol in apps/tui/src/bridge/protocol.ts that defines structured I/O between the UI and backend agents, plus permission handling in apps/tui/src/hooks/toolPermission/ for interactive tool-use approval.

How To Use It

The repo is a frontend monorepo — there is no backend server, no Python code (despite the README's Python badge), and no pyproject.toml or Dockerfile present. The two package.json files define the apps.

Setup:
cd apps/dashboard
npm install
npm run dev

Configuration: The dashboard requires a .env file based on apps/dashboard/.env.example. The TUI has no .env.example — configuration appears to be handled through user keybinding files loaded by apps/tui/src/keybindings/loadUserBindings.ts.

Running it: The dashboard entry point is apps/dashboard/index.html → src/main.tsx. The TUI entry point is apps/tui/src/index.tsx. The README references a CLI (openspace --query your task) but that binary is not in this repository — the actual backend is missing.

Real-World Use

A team running Claude Code for code generation and Codex for DevOps tasks points both agents at OpenSpace. When Claude encounters a new deployment task, it retrieves a skill from the shared library. After the task completes, the outcome is uploaded as a task trace. The dashboard's AgentTracePage.tsx lets the team review whether that skill performed well. If it failed, the skill's evolution graph in EvolutionPage.tsx shows what changed and when — informing whether to revise or retire it.

Code Health & Issues
High — No backend present: The README describes a full system with Python 3.12+, but the repo contains only TypeScript frontends. The openspace CLI and any server components are absent, so this cannot run as described.
Med — No CI/CD: No .github/ directory or CI config. There are 16 test files (mostly in apps/tui/src/), but no automated gate runs them.
Med — Duplicate application logic: The dashboard and TUI both implement diff viewing (DiffViewer.tsx vs apps/tui/src/components/diff/DiffView.tsx) with no shared package, risking divergence.
Low — i18n coverage: src/i18n/en.json and zh.json exist, but only two languages with no fallback strategy visible in src/i18n/index.ts.

The Bottom Line

This is a well-structured frontend for a skill management platform, with thoughtful UX in the TUI (permissions, keybindings, transcripts). It is not a complete product — the backend is absent, so it cannot be deployed as-is. Teams evaluating OpenSpace should check the upstream HKUDS/OpenSpace repo for the full system before adopting this fork.

forks.name: MOSS-TTS-Nano
forks.description: MOSS-TTS-Nano is an open-source multilingual tiny speech generation model from MOSI.AI and the OpenMOSS team. With only 0.1B parameters, it is designed for realtime speech generation, can run directly on CPU without a GPU, and keeps the deployment stack simple enough for local demos, web serving, and lightweight product integration.
forks.summary:
The Problem  
Deploying a speech‑synthesis model that fits on a single CPU core, stays under 100 MB, and can be integrated without heavyweight GPU dependencies is difficult. Many open‑source TTS projects require CUDA, large Docker images, or complex build pipelines, making rapid prototyping or edge deployment costly.

What This Does  
MOSS‑TTS‑Nano delivers a 0.1 B‑parameter multilingual TTS model that runs in real‑time on a CPU. The core inference code lives in mossttsnano/ (init.py, defaults.py, cli.py) and can be invoked as a library or via the command‑line. A Flask demo (app.py and apponnx.py) exposes HTTP endpoints for quick testing, while the onnx/ folder contains export scripts (exporthftottsonnx.py, exportmossttsbrowseronnx.py) that produce a self‑contained ONNX runtime (onnxttsruntime.py, ortcpuruntime.py). Example Android integration is provided under examples/androidonnxruntime/.

How To Use It  

Setup  
Create a clean venv (recommended)
python -m venv .venv && source .venv/bin/activate

Install Python dependencies
pip install -r requirements.txt   # matches pyproject.toml

If you prefer the ONNX‑only path, install the additional runtime:
pip install onnxruntime

Configuration  
No explicit config file is required for basic inference. Model weights are downloaded automatically by the Hugging‑Face transformers utilities when first used. For custom audio tokenizers or fine‑tuning, edit finetuning/configs/accelerateddp8gpu.yaml (not needed for CPU inference).

Running it  

Command‑line inference  
python -m mossttsnano.cli --text "Hello world" --output out.wav

The CLI parses --text and writes a WAV file using the default model.

Flask demo  
python app.py

The server starts on http://127.0.0.1:5000 with /synthesize accepting JSON { "text": "..."} .

ONNX inference (CPU only)  
python inferonnx.py --text "你好" --output cn.wav

inferonnx.py loads the exported ONNX model from the Hugging‑Face hub.

Android demo  
Open the Android Studio project in examples/androidonnxruntime/ and build with the provided Gradle scripts (./gradlew assembleDebug). The Kotlin code in DemoPrompts.kt shows how to call the ONNX runtime.

Real‑World Use  
A SaaS product that generates voice prompts for IVR can embed MOSS‑TTS‑Nano as a thin microservice. The service starts with python app.py, receives text via HTTP, returns a short‑lived WAV stream, and incurs < 50 ms latency on a single‑core VM. No GPU, no Docker image larger than 200 MB, and the model can be swapped for a language‑specific checkpoint by setting MOSSTTSMODEL environment variable (documented in mosstts_nano/defaults.py).

import requests
r = requests.post("http://localhost:5000/synthesize", json={"text":"Welcome"})
with open("welcome.wav","wb") as f: f.write(r.content)

Low – Minimal error handling – CLI and Flask routes forward exceptions directly; a production service should add try/except and proper HTTP error codes.  
Low – Documentation gaps – README covers high‑level usage but does not list required Python version or optional env vars; finetuning/ scripts have no usage examples.  
Info – License present – LICENSE file included, satisfying basic legal compliance.  

The Bottom Line  
MOSS‑TTS‑Nano provides a compact, CPU‑only TTS engine with ready‑made Flask and Android examples, making it attractive for low‑resource deployments or rapid prototyping. The lack of tests, CI, and pinned dependencies means teams should allocate time for validation and hardening before production use. Ideal for developers who need a lightweight voice generator and are comfortable adding their own quality‑assurance layer.

The Problem

Twitter/X has locked down its iOS client to prevent third-party or modified apps from signing in. Users who want the classic Twitter interface, ad blocking, or Twitter Blue features without a subscription are locked out of the official client. This repo is an attempt to preserve that modified-client experience by shipping a pre-built, sideloadable iOS app.

What This Does

NeoFreeBird is a modified Twitter/X iOS app distributed as a pre-built binary. The repo contains no source code for the app itself—the assets/ directory holds the compiled app bundle (Assets.car, LaunchScreen.nib, icon PNGs, and a LocalizationLocalization.bundle with deflated .lproj files for ~50 languages). The assets/classic/TwitterAppearanceTwitterAppearance.bundle/VectorImages/main/ folder contains hundreds of SVG icons, indicating the branding revert from X back to the classic Twitter look.

The project is a fork of NeoFreeBird/app, which itself is a derivative of the BHTwitter project. The core value is the integration of a forked BHTwitter (linked in the README) that provides ad blocking, Twitter Blue features, and UI customization. The repo also includes AltSource.json, which defines an AltStore-compatible source for sideloading the app.

How To Use It

Setup: There is no build step. The app is distributed as a pre-built binary. To install it, add the AltStore source URL from the README to AltStore, SideStore, or Feather.

Configuration: No configuration is required. The AltSource.json file defines the app metadata and download URL for sideloading.

Running it: After adding the source to AltStore (or a compatible sideloader), install the app from the store. The app is then launched like any other iOS app.

No CLI commands exist. Installation is done through AltStore/SideStore/Feather
by adding the source URL from the README.

Real-World Use

A user with an iPhone who wants the pre-Elon Twitter experience installs AltStore, adds the AltSource.json URL, and installs NeoFreeBird. The app provides a classic Twitter UI with ad blocking and premium features. The maintainers explicitly warn that signing in and tweeting may not work due to Twitter's attestation measures, so the primary use case is browsing and reading timelines.

Code Health & Issues
High - No source code: The repo is a binary distribution, not a codebase. There is nothing to audit, test, or contribute to. The "200 files" are mostly compiled assets and SVG icons.
Med - No test files: No tests exist because there is no source code. The heuristic analysis flags this, but it's expected for a binary distribution.
Med - No LICENSE: The repo has no license file. Redistribution and modification rights are unclear, which is a concern given the project's nature (forking a modified proprietary app).
Med - Unmaintained functionality: The README's warning about sign-in issues suggests core functionality (tweeting) is broken and unlikely to be fixed. The project's long-term viability depends on a cat-and-mouse game with Twitter's attestation.
Low - CI/CD: A GitHub Actions workflow (Build-NeoFreeBird.yml) exists, but its purpose is unclear since no source is present. It may build the app from a private repository or patch an upstream binary.

The Bottom Line

This is a binary distribution, not a software project. Users who want a classic Twitter experience on iOS will find a ready-to-install app, but the project's future is uncertain given Twitter's active countermeasures and the lack of source code. It's a usable solution for today, not a sustainable one.

forks.name: remoto.el
forks.description: Browse GitHub repos without cloning
forks.summary:
The Problem

Cloning a GitHub repository just to inspect a few files is wasteful. It consumes disk space, creates directory clutter, and interrupts flow. Developers frequently need to check a function signature, read a README, or browse a project structure without the overhead of a full clone.

What This Does

remoto.el registers a virtual filesystem via file-name-handler-alist that translates standard Emacs file operations into GitHub API calls through the ghub library. This makes remote repositories appear as local files: find-file, dired, tab-completion, and dired-subtree all work against a GitHub repo without cloning. The implementation is read-only and split across three files: remoto.el (core filesystem handler), remoto-embark.el (Embark integration), and remoto-topic.el (issue/PR display).

The package accepts multiple URL formats — full URLs, SSH-style strings, or bare owner/repo — and provides multi-level completion in find-file using delimiters: / for files, @ for branches/tags, # for issues/PRs. Canonical paths follow the pattern /github:OWNER/REPO@REF:/PATH, with REF optional (defaults to the branch's default).

How To Use It

Setup: Install via use-package with straight, as documented in the README. The package is not on MELPA yet; there's a pending submission PR.

emacs-lisp
(use-package remoto
  :straight (:host github :repo "agzam/remoto.el")
  :demand t)
Configuration: No environment variables or API keys are required. Authentication is handled by ghub, which uses your existing GitHub credentials.

Running it: The main entry point is M-x remoto-browse, which accepts any GitHub URL format. Alternatively, use the virtual filesystem directly:

emacs-lisp
C-x C-f /github:torvalds/linux RET
C-x C-f /gh:torvalds/linux RET

Real-World Use

A developer reviewing a dependency's source before integrating it can open /github:owner/repo@branch:/src/main.c directly in Emacs, navigate with standard commands, and check relevant issues via /github:owner/repo#42 — all without leaving their editor or touching disk.

Code Health & Issues
Med – Error handling: The virtual filesystem translates API calls into file operations; network failures or rate limiting could surface as confusing errors. No explicit retry or degradation logic is visible in the repo structure.
Low – Scope: GitHub-only support means the file-name-handler-alist approach is tailored to one API. The README acknowledges this and mentions future forges (GitLab, Codeberg), but the abstraction layer would need rework.
Low – Distribution: Not on MELPA; users must rely on straight or manual installation. The Makefile exists but its targets aren't documented in the README excerpt.
Positive: Tests are present (test/remoto-tests.el, test/remoto-embark-tests.el, test/remoto-integration-tests.el), CI is configured (.github/workflows/run-tests.yml), and a license exists. No obvious secrets or misconfigurations.

The Bottom Line

remoto.el solves a real friction point for Emacs users who frequently inspect remote code. The implementation is thoughtful — multi-level completion, issue/PR integration, and branch support exceed what a naive API wrapper would provide. It's currently GitHub-only and not package-manager-distributed, which limits adoption, but the architecture is sound and the test coverage is a good sign. Worth trying if you live in Emacs and regularly browse repositories.

The Problem

The Orange/ package contains the entire analytical backend: Orange/data/ handles data loading, storage, and domain manipulation (including SQL backends for PostgreSQL and MSSQL); Orange/classification/, Orange/clustering/, and Orange/ensembles/ implement a broad algorithm library spanning SVMs, random forests, gradient boosting, k-means, and hierarchical clustering; Orange/evaluation/ provides cross-validation and scoring utilities.

The Orange/canvas/ directory is the graphical front end. Orange/canvas/main.py is the entry point that launches the workflow editor. Pre-built example workflows in Orange/canvas/workflows/ (e.g., 250-tree-scatterplot.ows) demonstrate standard analysis patterns. The Orange/datasets/ folder ships with sample data like iris.tab and titanic.tab for immediate experimentation.

conda config --add channels conda-forge
conda config --set channelpriority strict
conda create python=3.12 --yes --name orange3
conda activate orange3
conda install orange3

Pip installation is possible but requires a C/C++ compiler and PyQt6/PyQt5 plus WebEngine bindings. A Windows winget installer is also available.

Running it: After installation, launch the canvas with either orange-canvas or:

python3 -m Orange.canvas

Configuration: No environment variables or config files are required for basic operation. Add-ons are managed through the GUI (Options -> Add-ons...). The .gitmodules file indicates the project relies on git submodules, which is relevant only for source development.

Real-World Use

A marketing analyst with customer survey data (CSV export) can load it via the File widget, drag a Scatter Plot widget to visualize segments, then connect a k-Means widget to discover clusters. The workflow file 310-clustering.ows demonstrates exactly this pattern. The same pipeline can be extended with a Data Table widget for inspection and a Report widget to export findings. No code is written at any step.

Code Health & Issues
Med - No README in this fork - The root lacks a README; the analysis excerpt is from the upstream project. Onboarding is undocumented in this specific repository.
Med - Large, monolithic package - Orange/ contains 177 files with tight coupling between the canvas UI and analysis backends. A change in Orange/data/table.py can ripple through the entire widget layer.
Low - Cython and C extensions - Files like simpletree.c and distance.pyx require a compiler for source installs, complicating development setup.

Low - External service dependencies - Orange/misc/server_embedder.py and the announcement/update icons in Orange/canvas/icons/ suggest runtime calls to remote services that could fail offline.

The project has solid CI (GitHub Actions workflows for tests, docs, and wheels), a CHANGELOG.md, and a code of conduct. The heuristic flag about a missing README is the most concrete documentation gap.

The Bottom Line

Orange3 is a production-grade, long-lived project (5,600+ upstream stars) with a genuine niche: making sophisticated data analysis accessible to non-programmers.
