forks.name: sqlit
forks.description: A user friendly TUI for SQL databases. Written in python. Supports SQL server, Mysql, PostreSQL, SQLite, Turso and more.
forks.summary:
The Problem  
Developers often need to run ad‑hoc SQL against many different back‑ends, but launching a full‑featured GUI (SSMS, DBeaver, VS Code extensions) is heavyweight for quick queries. Switching between CLI tools, driver installations, and connection strings adds friction, especially when working across cloud providers or Docker containers.

What This Does  
sqlit provides an ncurses‑style TUI that discovers local Docker containers, reads cloud‑CLI credentials (AWS, Azure, GCP), and presents a modal editor with Vim‑style keybindings. The core entry point is sqlit/cli.py, which boots the Textual UI and wires the connection manager (sqlit/core/connectionmanager.py). Provider implementations live under sqlit/domains/connections/providers/ (e.g., postgresql, mysql, duckdb, aws/athena). The discovery layer in sqlit/domains/connections/discovery/cloud/ parses the respective cloud CLIs to build connection profiles. Themes and keymaps are defined in sqlit/core/keymap.py and docs/screenshots/.

How To Use It  

Setup  
The project uses a standard pyproject.toml. Installation is documented in the README:

pipx install sqlit-tui          # recommended, isolates the tool
or, from source
python -m pip install .         # run from the repository root

Configuration  
Default settings are stored in config/sqlit-config/settings.json. Users can copy the template config/settings.template.json and edit fields such as defaulttheme, keymappath, or keyringbackend. Credentials are stored securely via the OS keyring; no clear‑text passwords are committed.

Running  
Launch the TUI with the installed entry point:

sqlit                           # invokes sqlit/cli.py
or, for a direct run from source
python -m sqlit.cli

The UI presents a connection picker, which draws from:
 Docker discovery (sqlit/domains/connections/discovery/dockerdetector.py)  
 Cloud discovery (.../cloud/aws/provider.py, .../azure/provider.py, .../gcp/provider.py)  
Saved profiles (sqlit/core/connectionmanager.py)

From there, users can edit queries, run them, and explore results with built‑in filters (sqlit/core/actionvalidation.py).

Real‑World Use  
A data‑engineer on a Linux workstation needs to query a PostgreSQL instance running in a Docker compose stack and a Snowflake warehouse accessed via the AWS CLI. After installing sqlit:

sqlit                 # pick the Docker‑detected PostgreSQL container
run quick SELECTs, copy results
sqlit                 # switch to the Snowflake profile auto‑populated from AWS credentials

The engineer never leaves the terminal, avoids driver installation hassles (the “dependency wizard” in sqlit/domains/connections/app/installstrategy.py), and can filter millions of rows instantly.

Code Health & Issues  
Low – Missing lockfile – Dependencies declared only in pyproject.toml; no poetry.lock or uv.lock → builds are not reproducible.  
Low – Test coverage – Only one test file detected; CI runs but does not enforce extensive testing (.github/workflows/ci.yml exists).  
Medium – Cloud provider error handling – Cloud discovery modules (aws/provider.py, azure/provider.py) assume CLI tools are present; missing fallback could raise FileNotFoundError.  
Low – License present – MIT license is included, no violation.  
Low – Secrets exposure – No secret keys are hard‑coded; credentials are stored via OS keyring.  
Medium – Tight coupling to Textual – UI logic (sqlit/cli.py) is intertwined with core connection handling, making headless usage harder without additional wrappers.  

Overall, the repository follows a clear package layout, includes CI pipelines, and documents usage in the README. The primary gaps are reproducible dependency management and limited automated testing.

The Bottom Line  
sqlit delivers a functional, terminal‑first experience for managing and querying a wide range of databases with minimal setup. It is well‑structured and documented, making it suitable for solo developers or small teams that prefer CLI workflows. The main drawbacks are the lack of a lockfile and thin test coverage, which should be addressed before adopting it in environments where reproducible builds and high reliability are required.

Configuration is handled through YAML files—cli/app/fixtures/testConfig.yaml shows the expected format. The export command (cli/app/exportcmd.go) generates deployable configurations. forks.name: vps-audit
forks.description: lightweight, dependency-free bash script for security, performance auditing and infrastructure monitoring of Linux servers.
forks.summary:
The Problem  
System administrators need a quick, repeatable way to surface common security and performance gaps on newly‑provisioned or unmanaged VPS instances. Manual checklist execution is error‑prone and time‑consuming, especially when the same baseline must be applied across dozens of servers.

What This Does  
The repository contains a single Bash script, vps-audit.sh, that runs a series of checks covering SSH configuration, firewall status, fail2ban, update level, running services, open ports, sudo logging, password policies, SUID binaries, and basic resource utilization (disk, memory, CPU, network connections).  

Results are printed to the console with colour‑coded symbols (🟢 PASS, 🟡 WARN, 🔴 FAIL) and simultaneously written to a timestamped report file (vps-audit-report-<TS>.txt). The script is self‑contained; there are no external library dependencies beyond standard Linux utilities (e.g., grep, awk, netstat, ufw). Documentation lives in README.md, and licensing is declared in LICENSE.

How To Use It  
Download the script (the only executable artifact)  
   wget https://raw.githubusercontent.com/vernu/vps-audit/main/vps-audit.sh
   # or
   curl -O https://raw.githubusercontent.com/vernu/vps-audit/main/vps-audit.sh
Make it executable  
   chmod +x vps-audit.sh
Run with root or sudo (the script checks for privileged execution early)  
   sudo ./vps-audit.sh

  

The script will perform all checks, display coloured output, and create a report file in the current directory. No additional configuration files are required; thresholds are hard‑coded near the top of vps-audit.sh and can be edited directly if custom limits are needed.

Real‑World Use  
A DevOps engineer managing a fleet of Ubuntu 22.04 droplets can embed the command in a cron job (e.g., weekly at 02:00) to generate vps-audit-report-$(date +%F).txt and ship it to a central log aggregation system. The report provides immediate visibility into drift from baseline hardening policies and flags resource saturation before it impacts service availability.

Code Health & Issues  
Medium – No automated tests – repository lacks any *_test.sh or CI‑run test suite; code paths are unverified.  
Medium – No CI/CD pipeline – .github/ only contains FUNDING.yml; there is no workflow file to lint, test, or validate the script on push.  
Low – Limited error handling – many commands assume the presence of utilities (ufw, netstat) and do not check exit codes; failures could produce misleading PASS results.  
Low – Hard‑coded thresholds – thresholds are embedded as scalar variables; no external config means changes require editing the script, increasing the risk of accidental modification.  
Low – Debian/Ubuntu scope – the script explicitly checks for apt‑based tools and UFW; it will fail or produce false negatives on other distributions without adaptation.  
Low – No versioning inside script – no internal version string or self‑update mechanism, making downstream users reliant on manual pulls.  

No obvious security secrets are present; the script only reads system files and does not transmit data.

The Bottom Line  
vps-audit.sh offers a lightweight, zero‑dependency way to obtain a baseline security and performance snapshot on Debian/Ubuntu VPS instances. It is suitable for small‑to‑medium environments where rapid, ad‑hoc auditing is needed, but the lack of tests, CI, and flexible configuration limits its reliability for large‑scale, automated compliance pipelines. Consider augmenting with external validation or integrating into a broader monitoring framework before adopting as a production‑grade compliance tool.

forks.name: gpu-hot
forks.description: 🔥 Real-time NVIDIA GPU dashboard
forks.summary:
The Problem  
Operators of compute nodes need live visibility into GPU utilization, temperature, power draw, and per‑process usage. Existing tools (nvidia‑smi, proprietary dashboards) either require manual polling, lack a web UI, or cannot aggregate multiple hosts without custom glue.

What This Does  
gpu-hot runs a lightweight web server that polls the NVIDIA Management Library (NVML) or falls back to nvidia‑smi and pushes JSON snapshots over a Socket.IO connection to a React front‑end. The back‑end lives in app.py (FastAPI + Socket.IO) and delegates GPU collection to core/monitor.py, which uses the NVML wrapper in core/metrics/collector.py. Multi‑node aggregation is handled by core/hub.py and its WebSocket handlers in core/hubhandlers.py. The UI assets (static/js/.js, templates/index.html) render real‑time charts and a process table.

How To Use It  

Setup – Build and run the provided Docker image (the repo supplies a Dockerfile and docker‑compose.yml).  
git clone https://github.com/psalias2006/gpu-hot
cd gpu-hot
docker compose up --build   # builds the image defined in Dockerfile

For a single‑machine deployment, the README’s Docker command is also valid:  
docker run -d --gpus all -p 1312:1312 ghcr.io/psalias2006/gpu-hot:latest

Configuration – All runtime knobs are environment variables read in core/config.py. Typical settings:  

| Variable | Purpose | Default |
|----------|---------|---------|
| NVIDIAVISIBLEDEVICES | Comma‑list of GPUs to expose | all |
| NVIDIASMI | Force nvidia‑smi fallback (older cards) | false |
| GPUHOTMODE | hub to run aggregation node | single |
| NODENAME | Human‑readable identifier (fallback: hostname) | hostname |
| NODEURLS | Comma‑separated URLs of peer nodes (required for hub mode) | – |
| UPDATEINTERVAL | NVML poll interval (seconds) | 0.5 |
| NVIDIASMIINTERVAL | Fallback poll interval (seconds) | 2.0 |

Set them when launching the container, e.g.:  
docker run -d --gpus all -p 1312:1312 \
  -e GPUHOTMODE=hub \
  -e NODENAME=gpu‑server-1 \
  -e NODEURLS=http://server1:1312,http://server2:1312 \
  ghcr.io/psalias2006/gpu-hot:latest

Running – The container starts uvicorn app:app (see app.py). For local development without Docker:  

python -m venv .venv && source .venv/bin/activate
pip install -r requirements.txt
uvicorn app:app --host 0.0.0.0 --port 1312

Open http://localhost:1312 to view the dashboard.

Real‑World Use  
A research cluster can deploy one hub container on a non‑GPU node and a “worker” container on each GPU server. The hub aggregates per‑node streams and presents a single pane of glass. Example orchestration (Kubernetes) would mount the same image, set GPUHOTMODE=hub on the hub pod, and GPUHOTMODE=single on workers, relying on the NODEURLS list for discovery.

worker pod spec excerpt
env:
name: GPUHOTMODE
    value: "single"
name: NODE_NAME
    valueFrom:
      fieldRef:
        fieldPath: metadata.name

Code Health & Issues  
Low – Missing lockfile – requirements.txt is present but no requirements.lock or pipfile.lock; reproducible builds depend on exact package versions.  
Low – Docker build cache – Dockerfile does not pin base image tags (uses python:3.10-slim implicitly), potentially pulling newer layers unintentionally.  
Low – Limited CI coverage – GitHub Actions workflow (.github/workflows/publish.yml) builds and pushes the image but does not run the unit test suite; test failures could go unnoticed.  
Low – No secret management – Environment variables are injected directly; no guidance for handling credentials if future extensions need them.  
Low – Minimal type safety – Python code lacks type hints; static analysis tools would be less effective.  
Low – Front‑end test scope – Front‑end tests exist (tests/frontend/.test.js) but no linting or coverage enforcement is configured.  

No critical bugs are evident; the repository includes 30 test files covering backend units (tests/unit/*.py) and front‑end components, and the Docker images run successfully in the provided examples.

The Bottom Line  
gpu-hot delivers a functional, containerized real‑time GPU dashboard with multi‑node aggregation, backed by a modest test suite. It is ready for small‑to‑medium clusters where quick visibility outweighs the need for hardened CI pipelines or pinned dependencies. Teams should add a lockfile, tighten CI to include tests, and consider adding type hints before adopting it for production‑critical monitoring.

forks.name: quant-mind
forks.description: QuantMind is an agent-native knowledge extraction and retrieval framework for quantitative finance.
forks.summary:
The Problem

Quantitative finance teams need to transform unstructured financial data—papers, news, filings—into structured, citable knowledge that downstream systems can query and trust. Existing pipelines typically stitch together ad hoc scrapers, format converters, and retrieval systems without deterministic preprocessing, making provenance and time-based queries difficult to maintain. This repo attempts to solve that with a framework designed for agent-driven pipeline construction, but the implementation details matter for adoption.

What This Does

QuantMind provides a framework for converting any financial information source into typed knowledge artifacts (Paper, News, Earnings, Factor, Thesis) that carry their own text, asof timestamp, and source reference. The repository is organized around three core layers: preprocess handles fetch/parse/format/clean in a deterministic, model-out-of-the-loop manner; knowledge defines the typed structures; and library/rag/mind provide retrieval variants (local BM25/similarity, persistent search, agentic reasoning). Agent-oriented design is emphasized—coding agents can construct pipelines against the repo's contracts, skills, and deterministic verification within the checkout.

The directory structure shows quantmind/preprocess/ with fetch modules (http, arxiv, doi, rss, local, rss), format converters (html, pdf), and cleaning utilities. The quantmind/knowledge/ directory contains the typed artifact definitions. Retrieval variants live in quantmind/rag/, quantmind/library/, and quantmind/mind/. Configuration is driven by pyproject.toml and per-flow configs under quantmind/configs/ (paper.py, news.py, earnings.py, retrieval.py, structure.py).

How To Use It

Setup: The repository uses pyproject.toml for dependencies with no lockfile present (a reproducibility risk noted in the heuristic analysis). Install with:

pip install -e .

or

uv pip install -e .

The .env.example file at the root provides the template for required environment variables—copy it to .env and populate keys such as API credentials for fetch modules. The pyproject.toml also defines the project metadata and dependency specifications.

Configuration: Required environment variables and config files are named in .env.example. Per-flow immutable build configs live under quantmind/configs/ (e.g., quantmind/configs/paper.py, quantmind/configs/news.py). These bind a PaperFlow(cfg).build(input) contract once and apply it per input, eliminating boilerplate asyncio.gather patterns.

Running it: The collectnews example in examples/flows/ demonstrates news collection against a replayable source window. Entry points include the flow scripts under quantmind/flows/ (news.py, batch.py, paper/). The quantmind/magic.py file likely provides convenience utilities, and the scripts/ directory contains verification scripts (verifypdfrage2e.py, verifystructuree2e.py, verifynewse2e.py) that can be invoked to validate pipeline outputs.

Real-World Use

A quantitative research team needs to ingest recent earnings call transcripts, extract structured factor data, and make it available for semantic search and agentic reasoning. They would:
Define a PaperFlow config in quantmind/configs/earnings.py specifying the PDF fetch path, format conversion, and cleaning rules.
Run collectnews or batchrun across the transcript directory, producing News or Factor typed knowledge cards with asof timestamps and source references.
Index the output via quantmind/library/local.py for persistent local search or through quantmind/rag/ for similarity-based retrieval.
Query via quantmind/mind/retrieval.py for agentic, reasoning-based access.

This replaces a custom scraper + PDF parser + ChromaDB pipeline with a deterministic, config-driven flow that preserves provenance and enables time-queries standalone.

Code Health & Issues
Low/Risk - Dependencies declared without a lockfile: pyproject.toml lists dependencies but no uv.lock, requirements.txt, or Pipfile.lock is present in the root. This creates non-reproducible builds across environments—pip install -e . may resolve different dependency versions over time. [pyproject.toml]
Tests present and CI configured: 58 test files exist across knowledge, library, flows, contexts, and hooks modules. GitHub Actions workflows (ci.yml, e2e.yml, pr-title.yml, stale.yml) are defined under .github/workflows/, and pre-commit configuration is at .pre-commit-config.yaml. This suggests the project maintains a functional SDLC despite the lockfile gap.
No lockfile for reproducibility: As noted, the absence of a lockfile is the primary dependency hygiene issue. Without it, pip install -e . may pull different transitive dependency versions across fresh environments.

The Bottom Line

QuantMind is a well-structured, agent-native framework for financial knowledge engineering that replaces ad hoc pipelines with deterministic, config-driven flows and typed knowledge artifacts. It’s best suited for teams building or extending quantitative finance AI systems where provenance, timestamped citations, and replayable pipelines are required. The lack of a dependency lockfile is a moderate risk for reproducibility, but the presence of 58 tests and full CI coverage mitigates other SDLC concerns. Teams already invested in LangChain-based RAG or agentic workflows will find the least friction adopting this; solo practitioners or teams needing quick, one-off financial data ingestion may prefer building custom pipelines given the initial config overhead.

forks.summary:
The Problem  
Managing a Traefik reverse‑proxy by hand means editing multiple YAML files, restarting services, and tracking changes across homelab nodes. A mistake can take a service offline at night, and keeping backups or syncing configs between machines is tedious.

What This Does

Functions such as core/traefik.py query the Traefik API, while core/backups.py handles timestamped local backups and optional Git pushes. The Go agent provides a thin proxy for remote Traefik instances, exposing the same API over HTTP (agent/handlers.go).  

All components are containerised; the top‑level Dockerfile builds the UI + Python server, and agent/Dockerfile builds the Go binary.

How To Use It  

Setup  

Clone the repo
git clone https://github.com/chr0nzz/traefik-manager.git
cd traefik-manager

Build and start with Docker Compose (uses the provided compose file)
docker compose up -d

Evidence: docker-compose.yml defines two services – the manager container (exposes port 5000) and an optional agent service. The repository also ships a Makefile with a make docker-build target that runs docker build -t traefik-manager ., confirming the intended build path.

Configuration  
Copy the example env file and edit as needed:

cp .env.example .env
Edit .env – at minimum set COOKIESECURE, TRAEFIKURL, and optional GIT credentials

Key variables referenced in core/config.py include TRAFFIKURL, APIKEY, and BACKUPPATH. The agent reads its own .env.example (agent/.env.example) for AGENTPORT and the shared secret used to authenticate the manager.
Mount persistent volumes as shown in the README snippet:

volumes:
/path/to/traefik/dynamic.yml:/app/config/dynamic.yml
/path/to/traefik-manager/config:/app/config
/path/to/traefik-manager/backups:/app/backups

Running  

The manager runs automatically when the container starts (entrypoint defined in Dockerfile). For a native run without Docker:

Install Python deps (requirements.txt is inferred from imports)
pip install -r requirements.txt   # not explicit but typical for Flask/Django mix
python app.py

The Go agent can be run directly for debugging:

cd agent
go run main.go

Once the container is up, open http://<host>:5000 and follow the web‑based setup wizard.

Real‑World Use  
A homelab with three Raspberry‑Pi nodes runs Traefik on each. Deploy the Go agent on every node (via its own Docker image) and point a single Traefik‑Manager instance to the agents’ URLs. The UI then presents a unified dashboard where the admin can add a new subdomain, assign it to a service on node 2, and enable a rate‑limit middleware—all with one click, while the manager automatically commits the change to a Git backup repository.

Example agent definition in docker-compose.yml
agent:
  image: ghcr.io/chr0nzz/traefik-agent:latest
  environment:
AGENTSECRET=supersecret
TRAEFIKURL=http://traefik-node2:8080

Code Health & Issues  
Bugs / Risks  
Medium – core/crypto.py handles secret storage but lacks explicit zero‑ing of memory; in a high‑security environment this could retain keys in RAM.  
Low – UI component ComposeUpgrader.vue imports a remote image URL without fallback, which may break in offline setups.
SDLC & Code Violations  
Low – No requirements.txt or pyproject.toml is present, so Python dependency management is implicit; this can hinder reproducible builds.  
Low – Tests exist for the Go agent (_test.go), but the Python/ Vue layers have no automated test suite. CI runs the Go tests but not UI or Python linting.  
None – License (GPL‑3.0) is included, CI workflows are defined (.github/workflows/.yml), and Dockerfiles are present, indicating a reasonable release process.

Overall the repository shows a coherent structure, clear entry points, and functional CI for the compiled component. The missing Python dependency file and lack of frontend tests are the most notable gaps.

The Bottom Line  
traefik-manager delivers a practical UI plus a Go agent for centralized Traefik control, making homelab routing far less error‑prone. It is production‑ready for single‑node or small‑cluster setups, provided you accept the limited automated testing of the Python/Vue layers and add your own dependency lock file. Teams that need rapid UI‑driven configuration without building a custom front end will find it immediately useful.

What This Does  
TREK delivers a single self‑hosted web app that combines real‑time collaboration, interactive mapping, budgeting, packing lists, and a journal. The front‑end lives under client/ (the bulk of the repo, 160 files) and is built with React + TypeScript. Core UI components such as the drag‑and‑drop planner (client/src/components/Planner/...) and the collaborative chat (client/src/components/Collab/CollabChat.tsx) are shipped as reusable TSX modules. Backend services are packaged in the same Docker image defined by the top‑level Dockerfile, allowing the whole stack to run behind a single container.

How To Use It  

Setup  
Clone the repo
git clone https://github.com/liketrek/TREK.git
cd TREK

Build the Docker image (the Dockerfile copies the client build)
docker build -t trek .

The Dockerfile pulls Node, runs npm ci (note: no lockfile, see Issues), builds the React app, and serves it with a lightweight web server.

Configuration  
 API endpoint and authentication details are read from client/src/api/client.ts. Adjust the BASEURL constant or inject environment variables at container start (e.g., APIURL).  
 Optional SSO settings are stored in the Helm chart under charts/trek/values.yaml; the chart creates ConfigMaps and Secrets (templates/configmap.yaml, templates/secret.yaml).  

Running  
Run the container, exposing the web UI on port 3000
docker run -d -p 3000:3000 --name trek trek

The entry point is the built client/index.html, which loads the bundled SPA (client/src/App.tsx). Access the UI at http://localhost:3000.

For development without Docker, inspect client/package.json for the standard scripts (npm install, npm run dev) and run them from the client/ directory.

Real‑World Use  
A small travel agency can deploy TREK on an internal server, point the BASE_URL to its own authentication provider, and let clients collaboratively edit itineraries. Changes appear instantly in the planner and map view, while the budget panel (client/src/components/Budget/BudgetPanel.tsx) automatically recalculates cost splits for each participant.

Code Health & Issues  
Low – Missing lockfile – client/package.json declares dependencies but no package-lock.json or yarn.lock; reproducible builds depend on the npm registry state.  
Low – Limited secret handling – No encrypted secret management in the repo; any API keys must be supplied via environment variables or Helm secrets (charts/trek/templates/secret.yaml).  
Medium – Potential runtime errors – Several WebSocket utilities (client/src/api/websocket.ts) lack explicit reconnection logic; edge‑case disconnections could crash the UI.  
Low – Test coverage – 37 test files (e.g., client/src/components/Budget/BudgetPanel.test.tsx) indicate decent unit coverage, and CI runs them via the test.yml workflow.  
Low – CI/CD – GitHub Actions include linting (lint-prettier.yml), Docker builds (docker.yml), and security scans (security.yml), showing an active pipeline.  
Low – Documentation – Core README provides feature overview and Docker badge, but lacks explicit env‑var docs; the README.md does not list required configuration keys.  

Overall the codebase follows modern TypeScript practices, component separation is clear, and the presence of Helm charts (charts/trek/) suggests ready‑to‑deploy Kubernetes support.

The Bottom Line  
TREK offers a well‑structured, feature‑rich travel‑planning SPA that can be self‑hosted via a single Docker image, making it suitable for teams that need collaborative itinerary management on‑premise. The primary drawbacks are the missing lockfile (affecting deterministic builds) and sparse runtime documentation; these are straightforward to address. Deployers comfortable with Docker/Kubernetes will find the project ready for production use.

forks.name: FileSync
forks.description: Send files from one device to many in real-time.
forks.summary:
The Problem
Organizations and individuals need reliable real-time file sharing across distributed devices without compromising privacy or requiring third-party infrastructure. Traditional solutions either centralize data on corporate servers, impose size limits, or require client software installation—barriers that hinder spontaneous collaboration across diverse network environments.

What This Does
FileSync is a peer-to-peer file sharing system that operates entirely in the browser. The web frontend (web/index.html with modular code in web/js/modules/) implements WebRTC data channels for direct browser-to-browser transfer. The backend (api/main.py and api/signaling.py) handles only the initial handshake and TURN relay negotiation; it never processes file contents. Docker configuration (deploy/docker-compose.yml, deploy/docker-compose-ssl.yml) provides a single-image self-hosted deployment model. The system streams received files straight to disk via blob.stream(), enabling multi-gigabyte transfers with minimal memory footprint—a key differentiator from solutions that buffer entire files in RAM.

How To Use It
Setup: Clone the repository and install dependencies. The API runs on Python (api/requirements.txt lists aiohttp, aiohttp-cors, websockets), while the frontend uses npm-managed React dependencies (e2e/package.json confirms the build toolchain).

Configuration: Generate a secret key for TURN credential signing:
python3 -c "import secrets, base64; print(base64.b64encode(secrets.tokenbytes(32)).decode())"

Replace both <SECRETKEY> placeholders in deploy/docker-compose.yml with your generated value.

Running it:
HTTP (local network / quick start)
docker compose up -d
Opens at http://localhost

HTTPS (public domain, recommended)
Caddy obtains and renews TLS certificates automatically
docker compose -f deploy/docker-compose-ssl.yml up -d

Real-World Use
A distributed product team needs to share a 2GB design assets folder across five workstations on different networks. One team member self-hosts FileSync via the HTTPS Docker Compose configuration, shares the generated room link, and colleagues access it instantly from their browsers—no VPN, no account creation, no upload queue. The TURN relay fallback in api/signaling.py ensures connectivity through restrictive corporate firewalls where direct WebRTC peer connections would otherwise fail.

Code Health & Issues
SDLC & code violations: CI is configured (.github/workflows/ contains check, dependabot, and release workflows). License (MIT) and lockfile (e2e/package-lock.json) are present. However, the secret key generation command and both placeholder values appear in deploy/docker-compose.yml — committing generated secrets to version control is a medium-severity risk.
Bugs / risks: No client-side input validation beyond basic HTML5 file API; large file transfers over plain HTTP (>500 MB) are noted as unreliable in the README. The WebRTC data channel has no progress event handling for transfer resumption if a connection drops mid-transfer.
Evidence supporting quality: End-to-end tests exist (e2e/run.mjs), GitHub Actions CI runs on every push, and the codebase has clear structural separation between signaling (api/signaling.py), WebRTC modules, and frontend UI.

The Bottom Line
FileSync delivers on its core promise: private, limitless, one-to-many file sharing entirely in-browser with straightforward self-hosting. It's well-suited for teams that need occasional large-file transfers without third-party infrastructure, provided the secret key is managed externally and deployments use HTTPS. Organizations requiring transfer resumption, fine-grained access controls, or audit logging should look elsewhere.

forks.name: knowledge-Api
forks.description: The world's largest API knowledge base, built for agents.
forks.summary:
The Problem

API documentation is fragmented across vendor portals, PDFs, and developer dashboards, and it goes stale quickly. AI agents that rely on this documentation often guess at parameters, mis-handle authentication flows, and fail silently on edge cases. There is no single, structured, machine-readable source of truth for API knowledge at scale.

What This Does

knowledge-Api is a fork of withoneai/knowledge — a public-facing repository that documents the One Knowledge API. The actual knowledge base (80,000+ tools across 500+ platforms) is hosted at api.withone.ai; this repo is the front door: it explains the API, links to the hosted knowledge, and provides issue templates for community contributions.

The repository contains only documentation and metadata files. The root has README.md (the full API reference and quick-start guide), LICENSE (OKCL-1.0), and .gitignore. The .github/ISSUETEMPLATE/ directory holds two YAML templates: report-outdated-knowledge.yml and request-new-platform.yml. There is no application code, no build system, and no test suite — this is a documentation and community-intake repo, not a service implementation.

How To Use It

There is nothing to build or run locally. The repo serves two purposes:
As a user: Read the README.md for the API contract. All endpoints use https://api.withone.ai as the base URL and require an x-one-secret header with a free API key from the One Dashboard.
As a contributor: Use the issue templates in .github/ISSUETEMPLATE/ to report outdated knowledge or request a new platform. No code contribution workflow exists.

The README documents the CLI setup:

npm install -g @withone/cli
one init

That CLI is a separate repository (withoneai/cli), not part of this repo. The API endpoints are documented in the README's table, including GET /open/knowledge/:platform and GET /open/knowledge/:platform/actions.

Real-World Use

An agent developer integrating Airtable support would call the knowledge API to fetch structured action definitions rather than scraping Airtable's docs:

curl 'https://api.withone.ai/open/knowledge/airtable/actions' \
  --header 'x-one-secret: YOURONEAPI_KEY'

The response would feed directly into an agent's tool-calling layer, giving it method, URL, headers, and parameter schemas without manual curation. The issue templates let users flag gaps — e.g., a new platform or a changed auth flow — so the hosted knowledge stays current.

Code Health & Issues
Med — No test files: The repo has no tests, but there is no application code to test. This is a documentation repo; the absence is expected, not a defect.
Med — No CI/CD pipeline: No GitHub Actions or CI config exists. Again, with no code to build or deploy, this is acceptable for the current scope.
Low — Single-maintainer risk: The repo is a fork with 0 stars and no visible contribution history. The knowledge base itself is hosted externally, so this repo's value depends entirely on the upstream service staying available.
Low — License clarity: The LICENSE file uses OKCL-1.0, which is not a standard OSI-approved license. Verify it meets your organization's open-source policy before relying on it.

The Bottom Line

This is a thin documentation and community-intake layer for a hosted API knowledge service. It is useful as a reference for the One Knowledge API and as a channel for requesting platform coverage, but it contains no code to evaluate or deploy. Teams building agent tooling may find the hosted API valuable; the repo itself is not a dependency.

forks.name: build-your-own-openclaw
forks.description: A step-by-step guide to build your own AI agent.
forks.summary:
The Problem  
Developers who want a hands‑on, incremental guide to building an autonomous LLM‑powered agent often struggle to locate a single, coherent codebase that demonstrates each architectural layer (chat loop, tool use, persistence, web access, event‑driven design, etc.). Without a step‑by‑step scaffold, integration effort and debugging time increase dramatically.

What This Does  
The repository is a linear tutorial split into 18 folders, each representing a progressive stage of an OpenClaw‑style agent. Every stage contains a self‑contained Python package with its own pyproject.toml, a minimal CLI (src/mybot/cli/main.py), and supporting modules under src/mybot/core, src/mybot/tools, and src/mybot/provider.  
00‑chat‑loop delivers the bare‑bones REPL (mybot.cli.chat.ChatCLI) and the core agent (mybot.core.agent.Agent).  
01‑tools adds a pluggable tool registry (mybot.tools.registry) and built‑in tools (builtintools.py).  
02‑skills introduces a skill loader (mybot.core.skillloader) that parses SKILL.md files.  
03‑persistence adds mybot.core.history and a simple file‑based storage layer.  
04‑slash‑commands implements a command‑registry (mybot.core.commands) for user‑driven session control.  
05‑compaction adds history compression (mybot.core.contextguard).  
06‑web-tools brings two web providers (webread, websearch) and corresponding CLI tools.  
07‑event-driven refactors the agent around an eventbus and events module, exposing the same CLI entry point but now ready for external consumers.

Each folder can be built and run independently, letting a learner focus on one concern at a time while reusing the same code layout.

How To Use It  
Clone the repo
git clone https://github.com/yourorg/build-your-own-openclaw.git
cd build-your-own-openclaw
Install a step (example: step 06 – web tools)
cd 06-web-tools
pip install -e .   # pyproject.toml defines the package; editable install keeps changes in sync
Prepare API keys
cp defaultworkspace/config.example.yaml defaultworkspace/config.user.yaml
edit defaultworkspace/config.user.yaml with your LLM and web‑search keys (see README)
Run the CLI for that step
python -m mybot.cli.main   # invokes src/mybot/cli/main.py

Replace 06-web-tools with any other step folder (00-chat-loop, 01-tools, …) to execute that stage. The pyproject.toml files list required dependencies (e.g., litellm, crawl4ai, httpx). No additional build scripts are present; a standard pip install -e . suffices.

Real‑World Use  
A SaaS platform that wants a lightweight “assistant‑as‑a‑service” could adopt step 07 as a library:

from mybot.core.agentloader import loadagent
from mybot.core.eventbus import EventBus

bus = EventBus()
agent = loadagent("06-web-tools")   # loads the fully featured agent
bus.subscribe("usermessage", agent.handle)
bus.publish("user_message", {"text": "What’s the weather in Tokyo?"})

The event‑driven core lets the platform route messages from HTTP, Slack, or mobile SDKs without rewriting the agent logic.

Code Health & Issues  
Medium – Test coverage – No tests/ directory; all code paths are untested.  
Medium – CI/CD – No .github/workflows or other pipeline definitions; builds are manual.  
Medium – License – Repository lacks a LICENSE file; downstream usage is legally ambiguous.  
Low – Lockfile – pyproject.toml declares dependencies but no poetry.lock/uv.lock; reproducible installs depend on PyPI state.  
Low – Duplicate packages – Each step repeats the same core modules (mybot.core., mybot.tools.). While intentional for the tutorial, it inflates the repo and can cause version drift if a bug is fixed in one step but not propagated.  
Low – Minimal error handling – Core classes (e.g., mybot.provider.llm.base.LLMBase) assume successful API calls; no retries or explicit exception mapping observed.

No obvious security secrets are committed; API keys are expected only in the user‑provided YAML file.

The Bottom Line  
The repo delivers a clear, incremental learning path for building an LLM agent, with concrete, runnable code at each stage. It is best suited for individual developers or small teams that need a pedagogical reference rather than a production‑ready library. The main drawbacks are the absence of tests, CI, and a license, which limit confidence for enterprise adoption without additional engineering effort.

forks.name: obsidian-pm
forks.description: Project management natively in your Obsidian vault. Table, Gantt, and Kanban views with subtasks, dependencies, time tracking, and custom fields — all stored as plain Markdown. No external services.
forks.summary:
The Problem  
Managing projects inside Obsidian currently requires manual markdown tables or external tools, which breaks the “everything‑in‑one‑vault” workflow and forces users to keep data in separate, non‑searchable formats.

What This Does  
obsidian-pm stores every project and task as a regular .md file with YAML front‑matter, then renders three native views—Table, Gantt, and Kanban—directly inside the Obsidian UI. Core logic lives in src/store/ (e.g., ProjectStore.ts, TaskTreeOps.ts) and UI components in src/ui/ and src/views/. The plugin entry point is src/main.ts, which registers commands and view types using the Obsidian API defined in manifest.json.

Setup  
Install dependencies with the lockfile present
pnpm install

Build the plugin (the CI uses pnpm run build and scripts/build-styles.mjs)
pnpm run build

  
The build outputs a main.js and styles.css that Obsidian loads from the plugin folder.

Configuration  
All user‑adjustable options are defined in src/settings.ts and surfaced through Obsidian’s Settings UI; no external config files or environment variables are required.

Running  
Copy the compiled plugin folder (containing main.js, manifest.json, styles.css) into <vault>/.obsidian/plugins/project-manager.  
Enable “Project Manager” in Obsidian → Settings → Community plugins.  
Open any markdown file with a project front‑matter or use the command palette to create a new project (ProjectModal). The views appear via src/views/ProjectView.ts and src/views/KanbanView.ts.

Real‑World Use  
A product team stores a sprint backlog as sprint-2024-09.md with tasks defined in YAML. Opening the file shows the Table view, allowing bulk status changes. Dragging a bar in the Gantt view (src/views/gantt/GanttView.ts) automatically updates dependent tasks’ dates via Scheduler.ts, keeping the schedule consistent without leaving the vault.

forks.name: Prediction-Markets-Trading-Bot-Toolkits
forks.description: Production-grade Rust trading bots for prediction markets — Polymarket, Kalshi, Limitless. 10 strategies on one execution core. Predict.fun & 20+ venues on the roadmap.
forks.summary:
The Problem

Prediction-market trading spans multiple venues—Polymarket, Kalshi, Limitless—each with different APIs, order-book formats, and execution semantics. Teams building trading bots typically write separate implementations per venue, duplicating strategy logic, risk checks, and order execution. That duplication makes adding a new venue expensive and makes consistent risk management across venues nearly impossible.

What This Does

This repo is a venue-agnostic trading engine written in Rust. A single execution core (src/service/orderexecutor.rs, src/service/riskguard.rs) runs ten strategy bots—arbitrage, copy-trading, market making, orderbook imbalance, resolution sniping, spread farming, and more, all under src/bot/. Each venue is a thin adapter in src/service/clob.rs and src/service/onchain.rs, so adding a market means writing one adapter, not a new bot.

The codebase is organized into clear layers: src/models.rs for data types, src/service/ for execution and risk, src/bot/ for strategies, and src/ui/ for the terminal dashboard. Configuration lives in config.yaml.example, and the entry point is src/main.rs. The pages/index.html file is a static landing page, not part of the runtime.

How To Use It

The README documents a workflow that clones a per-venue repo (e.g., HarrierOnChain/Polymarket), not this monorepo directly. The core commands:

git clone https://github.com/HarrierOnChain/Polymarket
cd Polymarket
cp config.example.yaml config.yaml
cargo run --release -- run copy-trading

Configuration requires editing config.yaml—the example file is present in this repo. Every bot defaults to enabletrading: false, so the first run is a dry-run with no real orders. There is no Cargo.lock in this repo, so builds are not reproducible; the per-venue repos may include one.

Real-World Use

A trading desk wants to run the same market-making strategy on Polymarket and Kalshi. They write one strategy in src/bot/marketmaker.rs, configure both venue adapters in config.yaml, and the engine handles order routing, position monitoring (src/service/positionmonitor.rs), and risk limits (src/service/riskguard.rs) uniformly. The dashboard in src/ui/ gives a live view of positions and PnL across both venues.

Code Health & Issues
Medium – No test files detected. With 29 Rust source files covering execution, risk, and ten strategies, the absence of any #[test] module or tests/ directory means untested code paths. This is a significant risk for a system that moves real money.
Low – No Cargo.lock. Dependencies are declared in Cargo.toml but not pinned, so builds are not reproducible. This is acceptable for a library but risky for a production trading binary.
Low – No license file. LICENSE is present in the file list, so this is likely fine, but the README's MIT badge should be verified against the actual file.
Low – README overstates venue coverage. The badge claims 7 live venues, but this repo contains adapters for Polymarket, Kalshi, and Limitless only. The other venues live in separate repos.
Low – CI is configured (.github/workflows/rust.yml), which is good, but without tests it only verifies compilation.

The Bottom Line

This is a well-structured Rust codebase with a sensible separation between strategy, execution, and risk layers. The venue-agnostic adapter pattern is the right call for multi-market trading. The lack of tests is the main concern for production use—this is a tool for teams that can add their own test coverage, not for someone expecting a drop-in, battle-tested binary.

forks.name: FUXA
forks.description: Web-based Process Visualization (SCADA/HMI/Dashboard) software
forks.summary:
The Problem  
Industrial operators need a web‑based interface that can display live sensor data, historic trends, and control actions without installing heavyweight SCADA clients on every workstation. Existing solutions often require proprietary runtimes or complex server setups, making rapid deployment on edge devices difficult.

What This Does  
FUXA delivers a full‑stack SCADA/HMI platform built on Node.js (backend) and Angular (frontend). The backend lives under app/electron/ with the entry point app/electron/main.js, while the compiled UI assets are in client/dist/. Docker support is baked in (Dockerfile, compose.yml) so the whole stack can be started with a single container. Protocol adapters for Modbus, OPC‑UA, MQTT, Siemens S7, etc., are bundled as Node modules referenced from app/electron/package.json.

How To Use It  

Setup (Docker – recommended)  
Pull the official image
docker pull frangoteam/fuxa:latest

Run with default ports
docker run -d -p 1881:1881 frangoteam/fuxa:latest

Persist data, history, logs and images
docker run -d -p 1881:1881 \
  -v fuxaappdata:/usr/src/app/FUXA/server/appdata \
  -v fuxadb:/usr/src/app/FUXA/server/db \
  -v fuxalogs:/usr/src/app/FUXA/server/logs \
  -v fuxaimages:/usr/src/app/FUXA/server/images \
  frangoteam/fuxa:latest

Or use the provided compose file:
wget https://raw.githubusercontent.com/frangoteam/FUXA/master/compose.yml
docker compose up -d

Setup (Source)  
Install Node 18 LTS (required – older versions are explicitly unsupported).  
From the repository root, install backend dependencies:  
   cd app/electron
   npm ci            # uses package-lock.json
Build the Angular UI:  
   cd ../../client
   npm ci
   npm run build    # defined in client/package.json → populates client/dist/
Start the Electron server:  
   cd ../../app/electron
   npm start         # runs node main.js

Configuration  
Persistent storage paths are hard‑coded in the Dockerfile and Electron scripts (appdata, db, logs, images). No .env.example is present, so any required secrets (e.g., database passwords) must be added to the runtime environment manually. Documentation of environment variables lives in the online docs, not in the repo.

Running it  
Docker: open http://localhost:1881 in Chrome.  
Source: after npm start, the same URL is served by the local Node process.

Real‑World Use  
A manufacturing line can deploy FUXA on a Raspberry Pi. The Pi runs the Docker container, mounting a local directory for db to store InfluxDB‑style tag history. Sensors publish MQTT messages to the container; the built‑in MQTT driver stores values, and the web UI displays live gauges (client/dist/assets/lib/gauge/gauge.min.js). Operators interact via a browser on any workstation, no additional client software required.

Example Docker compose snippet for edge deployment
services:
  fuxa:
    image: frangoteam/fuxa:latest
    ports: ["1881:1881"]
    volumes:
./appdata:/usr/src/app/FUXA/server/appdata
./db:/usr/src/app/FUXA/server/_db

Code Health & Issues  
Low – Limited test coverage – only one test file detected; critical paths (protocol adapters, historian) lack automated verification.  
Medium – Missing runtime configuration docs – no .env.example or schema in repo; operators must infer required env vars from external documentation, increasing deployment risk.  
Low – Large static asset bundle – client/dist/ contains thousands of pre‑compiled fonts, icons, and SVGs; this inflates the Docker image but does not affect functionality.  
Low – Electron packaging scripts – app/electron/package.json defines build scripts, but no CI step validates the packaged binaries; manual verification required for cross‑platform releases.  
None – License & CI – MIT license present, CI workflows for Docker builds and linting (.github/workflows/*.yml) are configured, indicating a basic release process.

The Bottom Line  
FUXA offers a ready‑to‑run Dockerized SCADA/HMI stack with support for common industrial protocols and a web‑based editor. It is suitable for teams that can accept modest test coverage and handle configuration manually. Deploying via Docker is straightforward; source builds require typical Node tooling. If you need a fully audited, test‑rich platform, additional effort will be required.

forks.name: explore-claude-code
forks.description: Learn Claude Code by exploring it as it was designed - interactive IDE-style docs for commands, MCP, skills, CLAUDE.md and more.
forks.summary:
The Problem

Teams adopting Claude Code often struggle to understand the full configuration surface area — .claude/settings.json, .claude/commands/, .claude/skills/, and MCP integrations — without digging through official documentation or trial-and-error. This project exists to flatten that learning curve by presenting every concept as a live, inspectable file.

What This Does

The site renders a navigable tree of Claude Code's configuration surface. Everything under .claude/ represents project-level config you create and commit: settings.json for permissions and guardrails, rules/ for file-type-scoped conventions, commands/ for custom slash commands, agents/ for delegated sub-tasks, skills/ for autonomous knowledge folders, and hooks/ for lifecycle shell scripts. The built-in/ section covers features shipping with Claude Code out of the box — /simplify, /batch, /debug, /loop, /claude-api — requiring no setup. A visual separator divides project config from built-in features. The manifest.json under site/data/ drives the entire UI, mapping every file and badge. The content-loader.js handles custom markdown parsing and rendering, while app.js serves as the main controller for routing and keyboard navigation. The live demo at exploreclaudecode.com requires no install; locally, any static server pointed at site/ works — the README documents npx serve site or python -m http.server -d site 8080.

How To Use It

Clone the repo and serve the site/ directory. No build step, no framework installation:

git clone https://github.com/LukeRenton/explore-claude-code.git
cd explore-claude-code
npx serve site
or
python -m http.server -d site 8080

Open the browser at the displayed address. Click the sidebar to explore .claude/ and built-in/ sections, read annotated config files, and copy scaffolding into your own projects. The content is sourced real — each markdown file is a genuine Claude Code config example, not a description of one.

Real-World Use

A new hire joining a team can clone the repo, click through .claude/settings.json to understand permission boundaries, review .claude/commands/ to see saved workflows, and examine .claude/skills/ to learn what autonomous skills the team's Claude instances load. Instead of reading theory, they inspect live config they'll commit to their own repo. Meanwhile, a staff engineer can use the built-in/bundled-skills/code-review.md as a reference when designing a custom review skill, copying the pattern into their project's .claude/skills/ directory.

Code Health & Issues
No CI/CD pipeline — the .github/ directory contains only FUNDING.yml; there is no automated build, test, or lint gate. Any contributor can push config changes without validation.
No test files — the heuristic detects exactly two test files; the repo contains none. Changes to the JavaScript logic (app.js, content-loader.js) have no automated regression guard.
Static site, no framework — the zero dependencies badge is accurate; the UI is vanilla HTML/CSS/JS with no bundler. This reduces attack surface but means no code splitting or build-time checks.
License present — LICENSE file is included, which is a minimum expectation for code redistribution.

The Bottom Line

This is a well-executed learning tool that successfully demystifies Claude Code's configuration surface. It's ideal for teams onboarding to Claude Code or wanting to audit their existing .claude/ setup. The request/response schema is defined in fastflights/pb/flights.proto, with generated Python bindings in flightspb2.py.

The API is clean and ergonomic. FlightQuery in fastflights/types.py accepts per-leg filters (max stops, airlines, departure/arrival windows, layover times, emissions preference), while createquery() handles search-wide options like currency, baggage, and price caps. The package ships with two optional integrations in fastflights/integrations/: BrightData for IP rotation and SearchApi for richer response data. The getflights() entry point returns a typed FlightsResult model defined in fastflights/model.py.

Setup: Install via pip. The pyproject.toml specifies the package metadata and dependencies.

pip install fast-flights

Configuration: No environment variables or API keys required for the base scraper. The BrightData integration needs a zone name; SearchApi needs an API key set via environment variable (per its integration module).

Running it: The primary entry point is getflights() from fastflights/init.py. Use createquery() to build a FlightQuery and pass it to getflights().

from fastflights import FlightQuery, Passengers, createquery, getflights

query = createquery(
    flights=[FlightQuery(date="2025-06-15", fromairport="MYJ", toairport="TPE")],
    seat="economy",
    trip="one-way",
    passengers=Passengers(adults=1),
)
res = getflights(query)

A fare-alert service that polls getflights() on a schedule, filters results for price thresholds, and notifies users when prices drop. The domain system (kgb/domains/) ships with default and legal domains, each containing extraction prompts (promptopen.md, promptconstrained.md), augmentation strategies, and examples.

A notable feature is triple origin tracking: every extracted triple is tagged explicit, while augmented triples that bridge disconnected components are tagged contextual. The visualization step (kgb/visualization/graphviz.py) produces interactive Cytoscape.js HTML output with color-coded nodes by origin.

Running it: The entry point is kgb/main.py. Basic usage:

Interactive REPL
kgb

One-shot extraction
kgb extract --input data.jsonl --domain legal --client gemini

Full pipeline via YAML config
kgb run-pipeline --config kgb/pipeline/configs/legalollama.yaml

Full pipeline via flags
kgb run-pipeline --input data.jsonl --domain legal --client ollama \
  --extract --augment --convert --visualize

Individual steps work as documented: kgb augment connectivity, kgb convert, kgb visualize network, and kgb visualize extraction.

KGB is a well-structured, genuinely useful tool for teams that need domain-customizable knowledge graph extraction with local LLM support. Media type support – documents, videos, photos, stickers, and even Telegraph pages.  The bot’s handlers live in client/bot/handlers/: media.go, mediagroup.go, telegraph.go, and save.go process incoming updates.  
Bypass “restrict saving content” – logic in client/bot/handlers/utils/ruleutil/rule.go and client/bot/handlers/utils/filters/url.go evaluates and overrides Telegram’s saving restrictions.  
yt‑dlp integration – download from 1 000+ websites.  Tasks and format definitions reside in core/tasks/ytdlp/.  A Go wrapper (common/utils/tgutil/media.go) forwards URLs to the yt‑dlp binary.  
Aria2 download engine – core/tasks/aria2dl/ executes metalink/magnet downloads and streams them to storage.  
Storage back‑ends – configured via config/storage/ (local.go, s3.go, alist.go, webdav.go, rclone.go, minio.go).  A factory in config/storage/factory.go selects the appropriate backend at runtime.  
Watch & filter – client/bot/handlers/watch.go and client/bot/handlers/config.go let users monitor specific chats with custom rules.  
Transfer between storages – core/tasks/transfer/ moves files from one backend to another without client‑side re‑download.  
Multi‑user isolation – config/user.go defines per‑user storage whitelists/blacklists; the middleware client/middleware/default.go enforces these limits.  

How To Use It  
Install – The repo ships three minimal Dockerfiles (Dockerfile, Dockerfile.micro, Dockerfile.pico) and a full docker-compose.yml.  Pull the image:  

   docker pull ghcr.io/krau/saveany-bot:latest
Configuration – Create config.toml at the project root (the README provides a minimal example).  Essential sections:

   lang = "en"
   [telegram]
   token = ""                # from @BotFather
   [telegram.proxy]
   enable = false
   url = "socks5://127.0.0.1:7890"

   [[storages]]
   name = "Local Disk"
   type = "local"
   enable = true
   basepath = "./downloads"

   [[users]]
   id = 114514
   storages = []
   blacklist = true

   The file is read by config/viper.go and validated against config/storage/types.go.  
Run – Using Docker (as documented):

   docker run -d --name saveany-bot \
       -v ./config.toml:/app/config.toml \
       -v ./downloads:/app/downloads \
       ghcr.io/krau/saveany-bot:latest

   Alternatively, build from source with go build ./cmd/run.go (the entry point is cmd/run.go) or use docker-compose up -d for local dev stack.
Interaction – Send any Telegram file to the bot; it will store it according to the user’s storage config.  Use /help (handler help.go) for command list, and /config (handler config.go) to adjust per‑user rules.

Real‑World Use  
A marketing team wants to archive every video posted in a public channel to an S3 bucket for later analysis.  They set type = "s3" in config.toml, provide AWS keys via environment variables (AWSACCESSKEYID, AWSSECRETACCESSKEY), and add the storage entry:

[[storages]]
name = "S3 Archive"
type = "s3"
enable = true
bucket = "my‑archive"
region = "us-east-1"

When a new video arrives, the yt‑dlp task (core/tasks/ytdlp/execute.go) downloads the source if the URL is from a supported site, then core/tasks/transfer/execute.go streams the file directly to the S3 bucket, avoiding local disk overhead.  The watch handler ensures only videos from the target channel are processed.

Code Health & Issues  
Tests & CI – 11 test files exist (e.g., api/handlerstest.go, core/tasks/ytdlp/tasktest.go).  GitHub Actions workflows (build-release.yml, build-docker.yml, docs.yml) run on every push, providing baseline coverage.  
License – LICENSE is present and MIT‑compatible.  
Dependency hygiene – The project uses Go modules (go.mod/go.sum are present); no obvious vulnerable third‑party binaries are embedded, though the yt‑dlp and aria2 binaries must be available on the host/container (not vendored).  
Potential risk – Storage credentials are read from env‑vars or the TOML file; if committed to version control they become exposed.  The repo does not ship a .env

forks.name: Learn-Prompt-Hacking
forks.description: This is The most comprehensive prompt hacking course available, which record our progress on a prompt engineering and prompt hacking course.
forks.summary:
The Problem

LLM applications introduce a new attack surface that traditional security tooling does not cover. Prompt injection, jailbreaks, and prompt leakage can bypass application guardrails and expose underlying system instructions or data. Most development teams lack a structured way to learn these attack classes and the corresponding defenses.

What This Does

This repository is a structured curriculum for prompt engineering and prompt hacking. It is a fork of TrustAI-laboratory/Learn-Prompt-Hacking (357 stars upstream) and contains 60 files organized into seven numbered course modules plus reference collections.

The core learning material lives in Jupyter notebooks: 1Basics/ covers prompt engineering fundamentals, 3PromptingHacking/ contains offensive and defensive techniques including 04PromptLeakageAttack.ipynb and 05BypassAIFirewall.ipynb, and 4RedTeamLLM/ covers red teaming at scale. The 5BlueTeamDefence/ notebooks demonstrate practical defenses using Meta's Llama Guard and Prompt Guard.

Reference material is substantial: PaperCollections/ has 20 markdown files organizing academic papers by topic (jailbreaks, prompt injection, model theft), and HackResourceCollections/ contains ready-to-use datasets including jailbreakprompts1.csv, jailbreakprompts2.csv, and injectionprompt.csv.

How To Use It

Setup: The repository is notebook-based. There is no requirements.txt, pyproject.toml, or environment configuration file. You need a Python environment with Jupyter and an LLM API client installed manually.

Configuration: No environment variables or config files are documented. The notebooks reference LLM APIs (OpenAI, Meta models) but the exact keys and setup steps are not specified in the README.

Running it: Open any .ipynb file in Jupyter Notebook or JupyterLab and execute cells sequentially. Start with 1Basics/02PromptEngineering.ipynb if you are new to the material, or go directly to 3PromptingHacking/01PromptHackingExamples.ipynb for attack demonstrations.

git clone https://github.com/TrustAI-laboratory/Learn-Prompt-Hacking
cd Learn-Prompt-Hacking
jupyter notebook

Real-World Use

A security consultant evaluating a client's LLM application would work through 3PromptingHacking/ to reproduce common attack classes, then apply the defenses in 5BlueTeamDefence/. The HackResourceCollections/*.csv files provide test payloads for automated scanning. A red team engineer could use 4RedTeamLLM/01Redteamingatscale.ipynb and 02RedteamingLLMswithLLMs.ipynb to build an automated attack pipeline against an internal LLM endpoint.

Code Health & Issues
Med - No CI/CD pipeline - no .github/ directory or CI config exists, so there is no automated test or lint gate. This is a documentation/education repo, so the impact is low, but it means notebook quality is unverified.
Med - No dependency manifest - the absence of requirements.txt or similar means the notebooks' library versions are unmanaged. Notebooks that worked at authoring time may break as APIs and packages change.
Low - No license file - the root contains only README.md and LICENSE is listed in the file structure, so licensing appears present. The README references upstream badges but the fork's own metadata is sparse.
Low - No evaluation harness - the 7Evaluationand_BenchmarksTesting/ notebooks use third-party tools (Inspect, Mindgard, garak) but there is no wrapper or script to run them as a repeatable suite.

The Bottom Line

This is a solid educational resource for anyone needing to understand LLM attack and defense patterns quickly. The notebook format and curated paper lists make it practical for self-study or internal training. It is not a tool or library—there is nothing to install or integrate. Teams looking for automated LLM security scanning should look at garak or Mindgard directly; teams needing to build awareness and skill should start here.

forks.name: Neo3dEngine
forks.description: A minimalist CPU-based 3D console engine in C# (.NET 8) built from scratch. Features Raycasting/Raytracing, dynamic lighting & shadows, .obj loader, and custom TCP-based multiplayer with real-time chat. No external graphics APIs.
forks.summary:
The Problem  
Developers who need a quick, visual proof‑of‑concept for 3‑D algorithms often must set up heavyweight graphics pipelines (OpenGL, DirectX, Vulkan) and deal with platform‑specific dependencies. This adds friction when the goal is to experiment with ray‑casting, lighting math, or simple multiplayer networking in a controlled, console‑only environment.

What This Does  
Neo3dEngine implements a complete 3‑D renderer that runs inside a system console, using only CPU calculations. Core rendering logic lives in 3dEngine/Structure/ (e.g., Vector3.cs, Ray.cs, RenderData.cs) and 3dEngine/Shape/ (Sphere.cs, Triangle.cs). The engine drives pixel generation via Parallel.For in 3dEngine/Implementation/DisplayManagerAsync.cs, mapping brightness to a character gradient.  

Networking is provided by the custom TCP stack in 3dEngine/Network/ (NetworkManager.cs, PacketManager.cs) and demonstrated in the sample game (SampleGame/NetworkPackets/ChatPacket.cs, TransformPacket.cs). Input abstraction (IInputProvider.cs and concrete providers) lets the engine poll keyboards on Windows (User32InputProvider.cs) and Linux (LibX11InputProvider.cs). The sample scene (SampleGame/Scenes/PreviewScene.cs) loads an OBJ model using 3dEngine/StaticClass/ObjLoader.cs and renders it with the ray‑tracer.

How To Use It  
Prerequisites – .NET 8 SDK must be installed. No external graphics libraries are required.  
Build – From the repository root run:  

   dotnet restore          # restores NuGet packages
   dotnet build 3dEngine.sln -c Release

  

   The solution compiles both the engine library and the SampleGame console app.  
Run the demo – Execute the sample project:  

   dotnet run --project SampleGame/SampleGame.csproj

  

   The program opens a console window, detects its dimensions, and renders the OBJ model (SampleGame/monkey.obj).  
Network test – The sample automatically starts a TCP server and client on localhost (ports are hard‑coded in NetworkManager.cs). Running two instances of the command will display a simple chat UI (UI/UIText.cs).  

Configuration: No external config files are present; all parameters (e.g., console size, network port) are defined in code. Adjust them by editing the relevant constants in NetworkManager.cs or ConsoleScreen.cs.

Real‑World Use  
A teaching assistant could use the engine to illustrate ray‑triangle intersection and shadow ray casting without installing a GPU driver. For instance, a unit test could instantiate Camera, feed a synthetic Scene containing a few Sphere objects, and verify that RenderData contains the expected character gradient values. The same code base can be extended to prototype low‑latency multiplayer mechanics for a text‑based RPG, leveraging the existing packet serialization (INetworkPacket.cs) and event subscription model.

Code Health & Issues  
Medium – No automated tests – repository contains zero *.Tests projects; core math (Vector3.cs, Ray.cs) and networking code are unverified.  
Medium – Missing CI/CD – .github/ only holds contribution templates; no workflow YAML defines build or lint steps.  
Low – Hard‑coded network parameters – NetworkManager.cs uses fixed ports; changing them requires source modification, limiting deployment flexibility.  
Low – Platform‑specific input fallback – DotNetInputProvider.cs is labelled “inefficient” and lacks robust handling of modifier keys, which could cause missed input in fast‑paced games.  
Low – Limited error handling – Several file‑IO operations (e.g., OBJ loading in ObjLoader.cs) do not catch exceptions, risking ungraceful termination on malformed assets.  

No obvious security secrets are present, and the GPL‑3.0 license is correctly included.

The Bottom Line  
Neo3dEngine delivers a self‑contained, CPU‑only 3‑D console renderer with built‑in networking, suitable for educational demos, algorithm prototyping, or ultra‑lightweight multiplayer sketches. The codebase is functional but lacks tests, CI, and flexible configuration, so production use would require adding validation, automated builds, and more robust input/network handling.

forks.name: httptap
forks.description: Rich-powered CLI that breaks each HTTP request into DNS, connect, TLS, wait, and transfer phases with waterfall timelines, compact summaries, or metrics-only output.
forks.summary:
The Problem

Diagnosing slow HTTP requests is usually guesswork. Standard tools like curl report total time but hide where the time goes—DNS resolution, TCP connect, TLS handshake, server processing, or body transfer. Teams debugging latency regressions or tuning performance baselines need phase-level visibility without building custom instrumentation.

What This Does

httptap is a Python CLI that breaks an HTTP request into five phases—DNS, connect, TLS, wait, and transfer—and renders them as a waterfall timeline, compact summary, or metrics-only output. Core logic lives in httptap/analyzer.py (phase decomposition), httptap/implementations/ (per-phase timing via dns.py, tls.py, timing.py), and httptap/render.py (the Rich-powered display). The CLI entry point is httptap/cli.py, with formatting and export handled by httptap/formatters.py and httptap/exporter.py.

Output modes include a full waterfall table, a compact one-line summary, and a metrics-only format for scripting. JSON export is supported for regression analysis. An SLO threshold checker (httptap/slo.py) flags requests that exceed defined latency budgets, and exit codes reflect pass/fail state for CI integration.

How To Use It

Setup: Install via pip install httptap or uv tool install httptap. The repo uses uv as its build tool (uv.lock present) and pyproject.toml for packaging. A Dockerfile exists for containerized use. Homebrew installation is also documented.

Configuration: No required environment variables. SLO thresholds are passed as CLI flags, not read from a config file. The httptap/slo.py module defines the threshold-checking logic.

Running it:
httptap https://example.com
httptap https://example.com --format compact
httptap https://example.com --format metrics
httptap https://example.com --json > output.json
httptap https://example.com --slo-dns 100ms --slo-tls 500ms

Real-World Use

A backend team debugging a slow API endpoint runs httptap https://api.internal/v1/orders --format waterfall and sees DNS at 5ms, connect at 20ms, TLS at 15ms, but wait at 850ms. That isolates the problem to server-side processing, not network infrastructure. The same team pipes --format metrics into a CI job that fails if the wait phase exceeds 1s, catching regressions before deployment.

Code Health & Issues
Med – No lockfile for dependencies (pyproject.toml only). Non-reproducible builds across environments. uv.lock exists, which mitigates this if the team standardizes on uv.
Low – 102 files but only 21 test files. Coverage is configured (codecov.yml) and CI runs tests, but the test-to-source ratio is thin for a tool with this many modules.
Low – The repo carries heavy governance overhead (CODEOWNERS, GOVERNANCE.md, SECURITY.md, assurance-case.md) for a 0-star fork. Some of this is inherited from the upstream project and may be boilerplate.
Positive – CI is well-configured: GitHub Actions workflows for CI, CodeQL, CodSpeed, dependency updates, pre-commit, and release. OpenSSF Scorecard and Best Practices badges indicate security hygiene was taken seriously.

The Bottom Line

httptap is a focused, well-engineered tool for phase-level HTTP latency analysis. It solves a real debugging problem cleanly and supports scripting and CI integration. The heavy governance and docs suggest a mature upstream project, but the missing lockfile and thin test coverage are minor concerns. Teams doing regular HTTP performance work will find it immediately useful.

forks.name: floci-ui
forks.description: Any Cloud. Locally. - The local cloud console for Floci, an AWS-Console-style UI for your local multi-cloud runtime.
forks.summary:
The Problem  
Developers running local multi‑cloud runtimes need a single UI that mirrors the look‑and‑feel of a cloud console while showing only real resources. Maintaining separate dashboards or hand‑crafting mock data quickly becomes a maintenance burden and obscures the true state of the local emulators.

What This Does  
floci-ui delivers a browser‑based console that aggregates services from the API (packages/api/src/index.ts) and presents them in a unified explorer (packages/frontend/src/App.tsx). The service catalog lives in packages/api/src/cloud-spi/serviceCatalog.ts; adapters for AWS, Azure, and GCP are under packages/api/src/adapter‑. The frontend pulls data via the generated client in packages/frontend/src/api/cloudProxyClient.ts. Dockerfiles (docker/Dockerfile, packages/api/Dockerfile, packages/frontend/Dockerfile.dev) enable containerised builds, and the monorepo is managed with pnpm (pnpm-workspace.yaml).

How To Use It  
Clone and install dependencies
git clone https://github.com/floci-io/floci-ui.git
cd floci-ui
pnpm install          # workspace installs all packages
Provide runtime configuration
cp .env.example .env  # edit as needed; currently only Docker ports are required
Start the full stack (API + UI) locally
docker compose up            # AWS‑only profile
docker compose --profile multicloud up   # include Azure & GCP adapters
Access the console
open http://localhost:4500

 Build the service matrix (required after adding a new adapter):  

cd packages/api && bun run scripts/service-matrix.ts

 The UI entry point is packages/frontend/index.html served by the API server at http://localhost:4500/api.  

 API routes are defined in packages/api/src/routes/*.ts; for example, GET /api/clouds/:cloud/services is implemented in packages/api/src/routes/clouds.ts.

Real‑World Use  
A CI pipeline runs a local Floci runtime (e.g., floci-runtime-aws) alongside the UI. After docker compose up, developers can:

In a test script
curl http://localhost:4500/api/clouds/aws/services | jq .
→ JSON list of available AWS services (EC2, EKS, S3, …)

The UI then displays live EC2 instances, EKS clusters, or S3 buckets without any placeholder data, letting engineers validate infrastructure code against their local emulator.

Code Health & Issues  
High – Runtime gaps – Azure Serverless adapter exists but the Azure runtime returns 501 (see packages/api/src/azure.test.ts & packages/api/src/azure.ts). UI will show “coming soon” rows, which may confuse users if not documented.  
Medium – Inconsistent Dockerfiles – Separate Dockerfile.package and per‑package Dockerfiles duplicate base image logic; a single multi‑stage Dockerfile could reduce image size and maintenance.  
Medium – Missing environment documentation – .env.example is present but does not list required variables for connecting to local runtimes (e.g., endpoint URLs). Consumers must infer these from code.  
Low – Linting scope – Frontend has eslint.config.js; the API package lacks an explicit ESLint config, potentially allowing style drift.  
Low – Test coverage uneven – 22 test files cover many adapters, but critical paths like packages/api/src/cloudProxy.ts have no dedicated unit tests.

Overall the repository includes a CI workflow (.github/workflows/ci.yml), a lockfile (pnpm-lock.yaml), and a reasonable test suite, indicating an active quality process.

The Bottom Line  
floci-ui provides a functional, container‑ready console that accurately reflects locally emulated cloud resources. It is well‑structured for a monorepo and ships with CI and tests, but teams should be aware of incomplete Azure Serverless support and the need to flesh out environment configuration documentation. Suitable for organizations that already run Floci runtimes and want a single pane of glass for multi‑cloud development.

forks.name: insights
forks.description: Open Source Business Intelligence Tool
forks.summary:
The Problem  
Frappe Insights was built to let non‑technical users create reports and dashboards without writing SQL, yet the underlying data‑access layer still requires knowledge of database schemas and join logic. Teams that already use the Frappe framework face a gap: extracting meaningful insights from existing apps typically means either learning SQL or building custom ETL pipelines, both of which slow down adoption.

What This Does  
Insights provides a visual query builder (frontend/src2/query/Query.vue) that walks users through table selection, joins, filters, and calculations, generating Ibis‑composed SQL behind the scenes. The chart builder (frontend/src2/charts/ChartBuilder.vue) auto‑suggests appropriate visualisations (BarChart, DonutChart, etc.) and renders them with eCharts. Dashboards are assembled via a drag‑and‑drop layout (frontend/src2/dashboard/VueGridLayout.vue) and can include shared filters (frontend/src2/dashboard/DashboardFilter.vue). Data can be pulled from MySQL, PostgreSQL, DuckDB, or BigQuery; connections are configured through UI dialogs (frontend/src2/datasource/Connect*Dialog.vue) or via Docker‑compose (docker/docker-compose.yml) for self‑hosted deployments.

How To Use It  
Setup: Run the provided easy‑install script to provision a production instance.  
  wget https://frappe.io/easy-install.py
  python3 ./easy-install.py deploy \
      --project=insightsprod_setup

  
  The script pulls the Docker compose file (docker/docker-compose.yml) and starts the required services (frontend, database connectors).  
Configuration: No secret files are checked in. Environment variables for database credentials are supplied through the compose file or at runtime via the UI connection dialogs.  
Running it: After the containers are up, open frontend/index.html in a browser. The app boots via frontend/src2/main.ts, which initialises the Vue router and loads the home workbook list (frontend/src2/home/HomeWorkbookList.vue).  

Real‑World Use  
A marketing analyst at a mid‑size firm can connect Insights to the company’s PostgreSQL sales and inventory databases. Using the query builder, they join orders → customers → products, apply a date‑range filter, and calculate year‑over‑year growth. The resulting table is visualised with a BarChart (frontend/src2/charts/components/BarChart.vue) and placed on a dashboard (frontend/src2/dashboard/Dashboard.vue) that the executive team accesses via a shared link. No SQL is written; the analyst only drags fields and sets conditions.

Code Health & Issues  
[Medium/SDLC] No LICENSE file – root directory lacks a license, so usage and redistribution rights are unclear.  
[Low/Risk] Dependencies declared without a lockfile – frontend/package.json lists npm packages but no package-lock.json or pnpm-lock.yaml, risking non‑reproducible builds.  
[Low/Risk] Sparse test coverage – only two test files are present; CI pipelines (frontend/.github/workflows/) run lint and build checks but lack unit or integration tests.  
[Medium] CI/CD maturity – GitHub Actions workflows exist (lint, frontend‑build, playwright) but no explicit security scanning or dependency‑audit steps are configured.  

The Bottom Line  
Insights delivers a low‑friction entry point for teams already invested in the Frappe ecosystem to add BI capabilities without SQL expertise. The Vue‑heavy frontend, Docker‑based deployment, and visual query builder are solid foundations. However, the absence of a license, lockfile, and meaningful test suite limits immediate adoption in regulated or mission‑critical environments. It is well‑suited for internal tooling, prototyping, or teams that can tolerate the current SDLC gaps while they establish proper licensing and dependency management.
