forks.description: A starter project for @node-ts/bus for building distributed message based systems with node
forks.summary:
The Problem

Building reliable distributed systems in Node.js is hard. Message-based architectures require careful handling of routing, retries, persistence, and fault tolerance—concerns that typically end up scattered through application code. Teams often end up building ad-hoc messaging infrastructure that fails under load or loses data during restarts. This starter project addresses that by providing a working baseline for @node-ts/bus, a service bus framework that encapsulates messaging complexity.

What This Does

bus-starter is a reference implementation of a distributed message-based application. It demonstrates a complete workflow: a siren test is started, events are published on success or failure, and a failed test triggers a workflow that emails the maintenance team. The code is organized into clear layers under src/: messages/ defines the message contracts, handlers/ contains the message processors, workflows/ orchestrates multi-step processes, and services/ provides infrastructure like email-service.ts.

The core wiring lives in src/bus.ts, which configures the service bus instance. The example workflow in src/workflows/siren-test-workflow.ts shows how to coordinate a sequence of steps with compensation logic. Nine test files, including src/workflows/siren-test-workflow.integration.ts, cover the message flow with Jest.

How To Use It

Setup: Clone the repo, install dependencies with npm, and start a local RabbitMQ container. The README documents these exact steps:

git clone https://github.com/node-ts/bus-starter my-bus-app
cd my-bus-app
npm i
docker run -d -p 8080:15672 -p 5672:5672 rabbitmq:3-management
npm run dev

Configuration: There are no environment variables to set for local development. The README notes two production requirements: configure a different transport and install durable persistence. Both are documented in the @node-ts/bus documentation, not in this repo.

Running it: npm run dev transpiles and runs the application with watch mode. The entry point is src/index.ts, which initializes the bus and starts message processing.

Real-World Use

This fits where you need reliable, decoupled message processing: order processing, event-driven integrations, or background job orchestration. The siren example generalizes to any "detect failure, notify humans, track resolution" workflow. The pattern of publishing domain events and letting workflows orchestrate side effects keeps services decoupled—a maintenance team email handler doesn't need to know why a siren failed, only that it did.

Low - Dependency hygiene unclear - package-lock.json is present, but there's no evidence of regular dependency updates beyond the Greenkeeper badge in the README, which is now deprecated.

The Bottom Line

This is a solid, well-organized starter for teams adopting @node-ts/bus. The structure is clean, tests exist, and the documentation is honest about what's included and what needs replacing for production. It's best used as a scaffold—clone it, study the patterns, then strip out the example and build your own messages and workflows. forks.name: Cairn
forks.description: A AI general-purpose state-space search engine, validated first on autonomous penetration testing.
forks.summary:
The Problem  
Security teams need a repeatable way to explore an unknown attack surface from a known target to a defined objective (e.g., gaining a shell). Traditional scripts are static; they cannot adapt when the environment changes or when new findings appear. A framework that continuously reasons over collected facts, proposes intents, and executes them can automate this directed search while still allowing human hints.

What This Does  
Cairn implements a blackboard‑style state‑space search engine. The shared graph lives in the Cairn Server (cairn/src/cairn/server/app.py) exposing a REST API for reading/writing facts, intents, and hints. The Dispatcher (cairn/src/cairn/dispatcher/) monitors the board, creates three task types—bootstrap, reason, explore—and hands them to Worker adapters (cairn/src/cairn/dispatcher/workers/adapters/). Workers run an OODA loop: they read the full graph, decide the next intent, claim it, execute the associated action (e.g., a curl request, a Codex prompt, a mock step), and write back a new fact.

Key files:  
cairn/src/cairn/cli.py – command‑line entry that starts a dispatcher instance.  
cairn/src/cairn/server/models.py – Pydantic models for facts/intents.  
cairn/src/cairn/dispatcher/tasks/.py – logic for each task type.  
container/Dockerfile & root Dockerfile – two container images: one for the server, one for the dispatcher runtime.

How To Use It  

Setup  
Install Python dependencies (uv is recommended, fallback to pip)
uv sync          # reads cairn/pyproject.toml; creates a lockfile if missing
Or:
pip install -r <(uv pip compile cairn/pyproject.toml)   # manual lockfile generation
Build the server container (optional)
docker build -f Dockerfile -t cairn-server .
Build the dispatcher container (optional)
docker build -f container/Dockerfile -t cairn-dispatcher .

Configuration  
Environment variables expected by the server are defined in cairn/src/cairn/server/app.py (e.g., DATABASEURL). The repository does not ship a sample .env; users must create one before launching. Hints can be posted via the /hints endpoint; no static config file for hints is provided.

Running  
Start the server (development mode):
python -m cairn.server.app

or, using the container:
docker run -p 8000:8000 cairn-server

Start a dispatcher worker:
python -m cairn.cli --project-id <PROJECTUUID>

The CLI reads the server URL from CairnSERVERURL (default http://localhost:8000). Once both processes are up, the dispatcher will bootstrap, reason, and explore until the goal fact is reached or no intents remain.

Real‑World Use  
A red‑team can launch Cairn against a target subnet. The server stores each discovered open port as a Fact. Workers generate Intents such as “attempt SSH login with credential X”. When a successful login fact is created, the Reason task evaluates the goal (“obtain root shell”) and may spawn new intents (e.g., privilege‑escalation exploits). Human analysts can inject Hints* (e.g., “skip port 22”) via the /hints endpoint, instantly influencing the next exploration cycle.

import requests
Post a hint to steer the search
requests.post(
    "http://localhost:8000/hints",
    json={"text": "avoid scanning port 22"}
)

Code Health & Issues  
Low – Missing lockfile – cairn/pyproject.toml declares dependencies but no uv.lock or requirements.txt; builds are non‑reproducible.  
Low – Limited test coverage – Only 2 test files (tests/ not listed) exist; core dispatcher logic is untested.  
Low – No secret management – Server expects DATABASE_URL but provides no template or validation, increasing risk of misconfiguration.  
Low – Incomplete CI – GitHub Actions workflow (.github/workflows/build-container-ghcr.yml) builds containers but does not run unit tests or lint checks.  
Low – Documentation gaps – README shows a demo video but lacks a quick‑start guide; the docs/ folder contains design specs but no user‑level instructions.  
Low – Potential race condition – Workers claim intents via cairn/src/cairn/dispatcher/runtime/containers.py without explicit transaction isolation; concurrent workers could process the same intent.  

No obvious security‑critical bugs are visible, and the code follows a clear modular layout (server ↔ dispatcher ↔ workers). The presence of a Dockerfile and docker‑compose.yaml suggests container‑first deployment is intended.

The Bottom Line  
Cairn offers a concrete implementation of a blackboard‑driven search engine, suitable for teams that need automated, iterative exploration of large, unknown state spaces (e.g., penetration testing, red‑team ops). The architecture is clean and extensible, but the project lacks reproducible builds, thorough testing, and production‑grade CI/CD. It is ready for pilot use by security engineers comfortable with Python and Docker, but it will require additional hardening before broader deployment.

The Problem

AI assistants operate without durable memory. Each session starts from zero, so context is lost across conversations, multiple AI agents cannot share state, and users constantly re-explain their work. MARM-Systems addresses this by providing a persistent memory layer for AI agents through the Model Context Protocol (MCP).

What This Does

MARM is a Python-based MCP server that gives AI agents persistent, cross-session memory. The core logic lives in marm-mcp-server/marmmcpserver/, with server.py as the entry point. The core/ directory handles the memory model (memory.py), event tracking (events.py), and rate limiting (ratelimiter.py). The endpoints/ directory exposes HTTP, WebSocket, and STDIO interfaces for memory, sessions, reasoning, and logging.

The server supports multiple transport protocols (HTTP, STDIO, WebSocket), making it compatible with various MCP clients. It includes Docker support via marm-mcp-server/Dockerfile and docker-compose.yml, plus a GitHub Actions workflow (.github/workflows/publish-mcp.yml) for publishing to the MCP registry. A team running Claude, Gemini, and Qwen through MCP can point all three at a single MARM instance. When Claude records a session log, Gemini can retrieve it in a later session. cargo install --locked --path tui

Running it:

dealve

Real-World Use

A gamer who wants to buy a specific title can launch dealve, search for the game, and see current prices across Steam, GOG, Epic, and Humble Bundle in one view, with historical price data to determine if the current price is genuinely low. The pricechart.rs view renders that history graphically in the terminal. For someone tracking multiple wishlist titles, the deals list view provides a single scan surface—no browser tabs required.

Code Health & Issues

The repo shows solid hygiene: dual MIT/Apache licensing, a CI pipeline (.github/workflows/ includes build, lint, test, and release jobs), a PR template, and issue templates. A Cargo.lock is present, and .pre-commit-config.yaml suggests linting discipline.
Med - No visible integration tests for the API client - api/ has only an example (api/examples/testconnection.rs), and the 2 test files likely cover core logic only. The API layer handles network I/O, auth, and parsing; that's where regressions hurt most.

A well-structured Rust TUI that solves a real problem for terminal-centric gamers. The three-crate separation is clean, CI is solid, and the onboarding flow lowers the setup barrier. forks.name: ta
forks.description: Technical Analysis Library using Pandas and Numpy
forks.summary:
The Problem  
Financial analysts and data‑science teams need a reliable way to generate technical‑analysis features (e.g., Bollinger Bands, RSI, MACD) from OHLCV time‑series. Manually coding each indicator is error‑prone and slows model‑building pipelines.

What This Does  
The ta package implements 43 common technical indicators on top of pandas and numpy. Core logic lives in the ta/ module:  

 ta/momentum.py, ta/trend.py, ta/volatility.py, ta/volume.py – each defines a set of Indicator classes (e.g., RSIIndicator, MACDIndicator) and functional wrappers (rsi(), macd()).  
 ta/utils.py supplies helper functions for moving averages, scaling, and safe NaN handling.  
 ta/wrapper.py provides a thin façade that can ingest a DataFrame and append all supported indicators in one call.  

Documentation (docs/ta.rst) and a handful of notebooks in examplestouse/ (e.g., allfeaturesexample.py) demonstrate practical usage.

How To Use It  

Setup – The repository uses classic setuptools and a requirements.txt for dependencies. From the repository root:

Create a clean virtual environment (recommended)
python -m venv .venv
source .venv/bin/activate

Install the library in editable mode
pip install -e .
Optional: install test/dev extras
pip install -r requirements-test.txt

Configuration – No external configuration files are required for the core library. Indicator functions accept only a pandas.DataFrame with columns ['Open','High','Low','Close','Volume'].

Running it – The most common entry point is the ta.wrapper.addalltafeatures function. A minimal example:

import pandas as pd
from ta.wrapper import addalltafeatures

Load a CSV with OHLCV columns
df = pd.readcsv('test/data/cs-accum.csv')

Append every supported indicator (default settings)
dffeatures = addalltafeatures(df, fillna=True)

print(dffeatures.head())

For a ready‑made script, see examplestouse/allfeaturesexample.py, which loads a sample CSV, calls addalltafeatures, and plots a few results.

Real‑World Use  
A typical workflow in a quant research pipeline:

import pandas as pd
from ta.wrapper import addalltafeatures
from sklearn.ensemble import RandomForestRegressor
Load market data
prices = pd.readparquet('s3://bucket/dailyprices.parquet')
Engineer technical features
features = addalltafeatures(prices, fillna=True)
Train a model
X = features.drop(columns=['Close'])      # target excluded
y = features['Close'].shift(-1)           # next‑day price
model = RandomForestRegressor(nestimators=200)
model.fit(X.iloc[:-1], y.iloc[:-1])

The generated feature set can be fed directly into any scikit‑learn model or downstream time‑series framework.

Code Health & Issues  
Low – No lockfile – requirements.txt is present but there is no requirements‑.txt lock (e.g., pip‑freeze). Reproducible builds rely on CI‑installed versions only.  
Low – Limited type hints – Source files (ta/*.py) contain few or no type annotations, which hampers static analysis for large teams.  
Medium – Test coverage gaps – 40 test files exist, but integration tests focus on the wrapper only; edge cases (e.g., missing columns, extreme NaNs) are not explicitly exercised.  
Low – Documentation sync – The README lists 43 indicators; the actual source defines 42 (e.g., KeltnerChannel is missing). Minor mismatch that could confuse new users.  
None – Licensing – LICENSE is present (MIT), satisfying distribution requirements.  
Low – CI configuration – CircleCI config (.circleci/config.yml) runs unit tests, but the badge in the README points to the upstream repo; the fork’s CI status is not displayed, making health monitoring less transparent.

Overall the code follows standard Python packaging conventions, uses prospector and black for style, and ships with a full test suite.

The Bottom Line  
The ta library delivers a straightforward, pandas‑centric API for generating a wide range of technical‑analysis features, backed by a solid test base and clear documentation. Its primary drawbacks are the lack of a dependency lockfile and sparse type hints, which may affect reproducibility and large‑scale integration. It is well suited for data‑science teams building feature‑rich trading models, especially when rapid prototyping is a priority.

forks.name: autoresearch-mlx
forks.description: Apple Silicon (MLX) port of Karpathy's autoresearch — autonomous AI research loops on Mac, no PyTorch required.
forks.summary:
The Problem  
Researchers on Apple‑silicon Macs lack a lightweight, PyTorch‑free loop for autonomous model experiments. Existing autoresearch implementations depend on CUDA and large frameworks, making on‑device iteration slow and resource‑heavy.

What This Does  
The repo ports Karpathy’s autoresearch to MLX, Apple’s native GPU‑accelerated library, eliminating the PyTorch/CUDA stack. Core files are:  

 prepare.py – builds the tokeniser, data loader and the evaluatebpb metric; treated as immutable.  
 train.py – defines the model, optimizer, and a fixed‑budget (≈5 min) training loop; this is the only file an AI agent modifies.  
 program.md – a plain‑text protocol that drives the edit‑run‑evaluate‑keep/revert cycle.  

Experiment history is persisted in results.tsv. The repository’s pyproject.toml declares MLX, NumPy and related dependencies, and the uv.lock file pins exact versions for reproducible installs.

How To Use It  

Install uv (if not present)
curl -LsSf https://astral.sh/uv/install.sh | sh

Resolve and install exact dependencies
uv sync

One‑time data and tokenizer preparation
uv run prepare.py

Run a single 5‑minute experiment
uv run train.py

Setup – pyproject.toml specifies Python ≥3.10 and the MLX stack; uv sync reads uv.lock for deterministic builds.  
Configuration – No external config files or environment variables are required; all hyper‑parameters live in train.py.  
Running* – The entry point for the autonomous loop is train.py. An external coding agent (e.g., Claude Code) reads program.md, edits train.py, and re‑executes the uv run train.py command. Results are appended to results.tsv automatically.

Real‑World Use  
A data‑science team with MacBook‑Pro workstations can embed the loop in a CI‑free workflow:

example driver script (not shipped)
import subprocess, pathlib, time

for  in range(20):                     # 20 autonomous iterations
    subprocess.run(["uv", "run", "train.py"], check=True)
    time.sleep(10)                      # brief pause before next edit

Each iteration lets a language model explore architecture tweaks that are cheap to run on‑device, surfacing hardware‑specific performance gains without leaving the Mac environment.

Code Health & Issues  
Medium – No test suite – repository lacks any tests/ directory or pytest files; code paths are unverified.  
Medium – No CI/CD – no .github/workflows or other automation; changes are not automatically linted or type‑checked.  
Low – Dependency lock present but not enforced by default – uv.lock exists, but the README recommends uv sync without a strict version pin enforcement; reproducibility depends on users following the command.  
Low – Minimal documentation – only README.md and program.md explain usage; functions inside train.py lack docstrings, which hampers onboarding.  
Low – No explicit error handling – train.py assumes successful data loading and MLX compilation; runtime failures will abort the loop without graceful fallback.

The Bottom Line  
The repo delivers a functional, Apple‑silicon‑native implementation of autonomous research loops, enabling rapid on‑device experimentation without PyTorch. It is best suited for solo developers or small teams comfortable managing a minimal codebase and willing to add their own testing/CI scaffolding. Without those safeguards, the project’s utility is limited to exploratory prototypes rather than production‑grade pipelines.

forks.name: mails
forks.description: email for agents. Built for AI agents that need to send, receive, and understand emails programmatically
forks.summary:
The Problem  
AI agents that need to communicate via email must handle sending, receiving, attachment parsing, and searchable storage without writing bespoke SMTP/IMAP code. Most SDKs are heavyweight or tied to a single provider, making it hard to swap back‑ends or run offline.

What This Does  
mails implements a lightweight email layer for agents. The CLI entry point lives in src/cli/index.ts and forwards commands to core modules such as src/core/send.ts, src/core/receive.ts, and src/core/storage.ts. Provider logic is isolated under src/providers/ (e.g., src/providers/send/cloudflare.ts, src/providers/send/resend.ts, src/providers/storage/sqlite.ts).  

A Cloudflare Worker (worker/src/index.ts) acts as the inbound routing service and optionally as a remote API for self‑hosted deployments. The worker bundles its own providers (worker/src/providers/) and database migrations (worker/migrations/0001addprovidercolumn.sql).  

All TypeScript source files (66) compile via the tsconfig.json at the repo root for the CLI and worker/tsconfig.json for the Worker.

How To Use It  

Setup  
Install globally (npm) or with bun
npm install -g mails          # or
bun install -g mails
One‑off execution without install
npx mails

The package.json scripts are not defined, so the CLI is the only built artifact.

Configuration  
Copy the example env file and fill in the required keys:

cp .env.example .env
edit .env
EMAILPROVIDERS=cloudflare,resend
CLOUDLARIFYAPIKEY=…
RESENDAPIKEY=…

The CLI reads this via src/core/config.ts. Provider order can be overridden with the EMAILPROVIDERS variable.

Running the CLI  
Typical commands are defined in src/cli/commands/:

| Command | File | Purpose |
|--------|------|---------|
| mails send | src/cli/commands/send.ts | Send an email, supports --to, --subject, --body, --attach |
| mails inbox | src/cli/commands/inbox.ts | List stored messages with keyword search |
| mails claim | src/cli/commands/claim.ts | Claim a free @mails.dev mailbox (hosted service) |
| mails sync | src/cli/commands/sync.ts | Pull remote inbox into local storage |

Invoke any command directly, e.g.:

mails send --to user@example.com --subject "Hello" --body "Test" --attach ./file.pdf

Deploying a Self‑Hosted Worker  

cd worker
npm install   # or bun install – uses worker/package.json
npx wrangler publish   # requires wrangler.toml in worker/

The Worker reads its own env vars from worker/.dev.vars.example (e.g., RESENDAPIKEY). After deployment, point the CLI to the remote endpoint by setting MAILSAPI_URL (handled in src/core/api-url.ts).

Real‑World Use  
An autonomous sales‑assistant agent can claim a mailbox (mails claim), send prospect outreach (mails send), and later retrieve replies (mails inbox --search "meeting"). The agent extracts verification codes using src/core/types.ts utilities, which are exercised in test/unit/extract-code.test.ts. All interactions are logged in the local SQLite DB (src/providers/storage/sqlite.ts) for offline analysis.

import { send, inbox } from "mails";

await send({ to: "lead@company.com", subject: "Intro", body: "…" });
const replies = await inbox({ query: "meeting" });

Code Health & Issues  
Low – Missing LICENSE file – repository root lacks a LICENSE, despite badge in README; legal reuse unclear.  
Low – No npm lockfile – package.json present but no package-lock.json or pnpm-lock.yaml, which can cause non‑reproducible installs for npm users.  
Medium – Environment‑variable exposure – .env.example shows required secrets, but no runtime validation in src/core/config.ts; missing explicit error messages for absent keys.  
Medium – Worker CI missing – GitHub Actions workflow (.github/workflows/release.yml) only builds a release; there is no test step for the Worker, so worker/src/ code is not exercised automatically.  
Low – Duplicate lockfile formats – Both bun.lock (root) and worker/bun.lock exist; using npm vs. bun may lead to version drift.  
Low – Documentation gaps – README covers CLI usage but does not document required Cloudflare binding (env.EMAIL.send) or self‑hosted token flow; the latter is only hinted at in docs/.  

Overall, the test suite is extensive (35 files, covering CLI, core, and e2e flows) and passes locally, indicating good functional coverage.

The Bottom Line  
mails provides a focused, provider‑agnostic email stack for AI agents, with a usable CLI and a Cloudflare Worker for inbound routing. The code is well‑structured and heavily tested, but the lack of a clear license, missing npm lockfile, and limited CI for the Worker are practical concerns. Teams that need programmable email with optional self‑hosting can adopt it quickly, provided they perform their own security review and add a license file.

forks.name: hunk
forks.description: Review-first terminal diff viewer for agentic coders
forks.summary:
The Problem

Agent-authored changesets often produce large, unstructured diffs that are difficult to review efficiently in terminal environments. Developers working with AI agents need a focused review interface that presents changes alongside contextual annotations, rather than raw git output. This project addresses that gap by providing a dedicated review-first terminal interface.

What This Does

Hunk is a review-first terminal diff viewer built on OpenTUI and Pierre diffs. The codebase organizes around several key areas:
src/core/ contains the fundamental logic: git.ts, diffPaths.ts, cli.ts, and terminal.ts handle VCS interaction, diff path computation, command-line parsing, and terminal presentation respectively.
src/opentui/ implements the user interface layer with HunkDiffView.tsx, HunkDiffView.test.tsx, and related components for diff visualization, file navigation, and review streaming.
packages/session-broker-/ provides session broker functionality across bun, core, and node runtimes, with broker state management in brokerState.ts and wire protocol in brokerWire.ts.
examples/ directories demonstrate workflows including multi-app refactors (2-mini-app-refactor), agent review demos (3-agent-review-demo), and UI polish scenarios (4-ui-polish).

The project uses React for its UI components and GitHub Actions for CI across .github/workflows/ci.yml, benchmarks.yml, pr-ci.yml, and other workflow files.

How To Use It

Setup: The package is installed globally via npm i -g hunkdiff or through Homebrew with brew install modem-dev/tap/hunk. The root package.json and three packages/session-broker-/package.json files indicate an npm/pnpm-based build system. A lockfile is absent, which the heuristic analysis flags as potentially causing non-reproducible builds.

Configuration: Environment configuration lives in .envrc. For Jujutsu workspaces, set vcs = "jj" in config; for Git, set vcs = "git". The .github/dependabot.yml suggests automated dependency update tooling is configured.

Running it: Entry points include hunk diff to review current repo changes (including untracked files), hunk show for the latest commit, and hunk diff before.ts after.ts for direct file comparison. The --watch flag enables auto-reload as the working tree changes. Example entry files include examples/2-mini-app-refactor/after/src/main.ts and examples/3-agent-review-demo/after/src/index.ts.

Real-World Use

In a team using AI code review workflows, a developer opens hunk diff --watch in one terminal to display the current changeset. The review UI presents a sidebar with file navigation and inline diff view. When an agent proposes changes, the developer invokes hunk skill path to load a skill file, then applies the agent's modifications within the live Hunk session. The --agent-context flag facilitates live-session integration as documented in docs/agent-workflows.md. The split-view layout (evidenced by src/opentui/HunkDiffView.tsx and src/opentui/HunkFileNav.tsx) allows simultaneous code comparison and annotation review.

Code Health & Issues
Dependencies without lockfile: package.json files across the root and packages/ directories declare dependencies but no lockfile (bun.lock exists at root, but package-lock.json or yarn.lock is not evident) - this risks non-reproducible installs across environments.
Test coverage: 41 test files are present across src/core/, packages/, and examples/, with test files like src/core/git.test.ts, src/core/cli.test.ts, and various brokerState.test.ts/brokerWire.test.ts files. CI is configured via GitHub Actions.
SDLC: A CONTRIBUTING.md, LICENSE (MIT), and CHANGELOG.md are present. Dependabot configuration suggests ongoing dependency maintenance. No obvious secrets or unsafe patterns visible in the file listing.

The Bottom Line

Hunk delivers a capable review-first terminal diff viewer with solid UI construction and agent-integrated workflows. The codebase is structured and documented, with test suites and CI in place. The absence of a lockfile is the primary reproducibility concern; otherwise the project appears well-maintained for its stated purpose. Teams actively using AI-assisted code review and requiring terminal-based diff inspection will find it practical; solo developers or teams not using agent workflows may not derive significant benefit.

forks.name: npcpy
forks.description: The python library for research and development in NLP, multimodal LLMs, Agents, ML, Knowledge Graphs, and more.
forks.summary:
The Problem

Building production AI applications that combine LLMs, multi-agent systems, knowledge graphs, and fine-tuning typically requires stitching together multiple incompatible libraries. npcpy attempts to unify these capabilities behind a single Python API, with particular emphasis on local model providers and a structured data layer for agent context management.

What This Does

npcpy is a Python library exposing primitives for LLM interaction (npcpy/llmfuncs.py, npcpy/gen/response.py), agent construction (npcpy/npcs.py), tool use (npcpy/tools.py), and knowledge graph operations (npcpy/memory/knowledgegraph.py). The NPC class in npcpy/npcs.py provides persona-based LLM calls, while Agent and ToolAgent extend this with tool execution and multi-step workflows.

The library also includes fine-tuning utilities (npcpy/ft/), multimodal generation (npcpy/gen/), SQL integration (npcpy/sql/), and a data layer (npcpy/npcsysenv.py, npcpy/npcarray.py). The examples/ directory contains 20+ runnable scripts covering agents, fine-tuning, OCR, and team orchestration.

How To Use It

Setup: Install via pip (pip install npcpy). The repo uses setup.py for packaging. A Makefile exists but its targets are not documented in the README.

Configuration: No environment variables are documented. The .env.example file exists but its contents are not shown. Model providers (Ollama, llama.cpp, LM Studio) require their own local setup.

Running it: The README documents the primary usage pattern:

from npcpy import NPC
simon = NPC(name='Simon Bolivar', primarydirective='Liberate South America.', model='qwen3.5:9b', provider='ollama')
response = simon.getllmresponse("What is the most important territory to retain in the Andes?")

For agents: agent = Agent(name='File Operator', model='qwen3.5:2b', provider='ollama') then agent.run("Find all Python files over 500 lines in this repo"). The examples/ directory provides additional runnable patterns, including multi-agent teams (examplenpcteam.py) and fine-tuning (examplefinetuning.py).

Real-World Use

A practical pattern from the examples: build a multi-agent team where a dataanalyst.npc persona queries a SQL database via npcpy/sql/npcsql.py, while a critic.npc persona reviews outputs. The examplenpcproject/ directory shows this structure with SQL models and team context files. For fine-tuning, npcpy/ft/diff.py provides diffusion model training that can be triggered from an agent tool call.

Code Health & Issues
Med - No dependency lockfile: docs/requirements.txt is the only dependency manifest; no requirements.txt or pyproject.toml with pinned versions. Non-reproducible builds.
Med - Test coverage unclear: 18 test files exist but no tests/ directory is visible in the structure. Tests appear scattered across examples/ and testdata/. No test runner config beyond pytest.ini.
Med - CI limited: .github/workflows/ci.yml exists but no details on what it validates. The verify-skills.yml workflow suggests some skill validation.
Low - Large files: npcpy/npcsysenv.py (1486 lines) and npcpy/memory/knowledgegraph.py (1449 lines) suggest monolithic modules that may be hard to maintain.
Low - Generated artifacts in repo: testdata/ contains generated images and videos, which inflate repo size and could be regenerated.

The Bottom Line

npcpy is a broad but shallow library that consolidates many AI development tasks into one API. It's useful for prototyping multi-agent systems and local LLM workflows, particularly if you want to avoid integrating several libraries yourself. The lack of dependency pinning and scattered tests make it risky for production use without additional hardening. Best suited for researchers and teams exploring agentic AI patterns, not for mission-critical deployments.

forks.name: sigma-file-manager
forks.description: "Sigma File Manager" is a free, open-source, quickly evolving, modern file manager (explorer / browser) app for Windows and Linux.
forks.summary:
The Problem  
Users on Windows and Linux need a native file‑manager that can replace the OS explorer while offering modern capabilities such as fast global search, tabbed navigation, and extensibility. Existing tools either lack performance on large disks or provide limited plugin ecosystems, forcing power users to combine multiple utilities.

What This Does  
Sigma File Manager is a Tauri‑based desktop application that couples a Rust backend with a React UI. The backend lives in src-tauri/src/ and implements core file‑system operations (copymovejob.rs, deletejob.rs, dirreader/, globalsearch/) and LAN sharing (lanshare/). The UI is served from public/ and bundled by the React entry point index.html. The package manifests are defined in src-tauri/Cargo.toml (Rust) and package.json (Node). Extensions are described by a JSON schema in packages/api/manifest.schema.json and can be loaded at runtime.

Key modules:  
 src-tauri/src/globalsearch/scan.rs – walks the file system and builds a searchable index.  
 src-tauri/src/lanshare/server.rs – starts an HTTP/FTP server for sharing files over the LAN.  
 src-tauri/src/extensions/.rs – expose plugin hooks for archives, network mounts, and custom commands.

How To Use It  

Setup  
Install Rust toolchain (required for Tauri)
curl https://sh.rustup.rs -sSf | sh
Install Node dependencies
npm ci               # reads package-lock.json
Install Tauri CLI (once)
cargo install tauri-cli

Configuration  
 No runtime secrets are required out of the box.  
 Optional user‑specific settings are stored in src-shared/user-storage-files.json.  
Extension manifests follow the schema in packages/api/manifest.schema.json.

Running  
Development build (hot‑reload UI)
npm run tauri dev

Production bundle for the host OS
npm run tauri build

npm run tauri dev invokes the Tauri binary defined in src-tauri/src/main.rs, which launches the Rust backend and loads the React front‑end from index.html.

Real‑World Use  
A system administrator on Windows can replace Explorer with Sigma, enable the LAN share feature (src-tauri/src/lanshare/server.rs) to expose a folder over HTTP, and distribute a QR code to coworkers for quick file retrieval. The built‑in global search (globalsearch/scan.rs) indexes a 1 TB drive in seconds, allowing the admin to locate logs across multiple directories without external tools.

Code Health & Issues  
Low – Missing unit tests for many Rust modules – only 4 test files are present; core logic in src-tauri/src/dirreader/ and globalsearch/ lacks coverage.  
Medium – Potential race conditions in copymovejob.rs – concurrent file operations are performed without explicit locking; could cause data loss on high‑throughput moves.  
Low – Incomplete CI for Windows builds – GitHub Actions workflow (.github/workflows/ci.yml) runs on Linux/macOS; Windows build steps are not exercised.  
Low – No explicit runtime error handling for network failures – lan_share/network.rs propagates errors without user‑visible fallback.  
None – License present (LICENSE.md), CI configured, lockfiles (Cargo.lock, package-lock.json) committed, and documentation (README.md, CHANGELOG.md) is thorough.

The Bottom Line  
Sigma File Manager delivers a performant, extensible native file manager with a solid Rust/React foundation. It is ready for power users and teams that need fast search and LAN sharing, but the lack of extensive automated tests and Windows‑specific CI means extra diligence is required before enterprise deployment. Consider it for environments where the feature set outweighs the current testing gaps.

forks.name: MarkdownTaskManager
forks.description: Local-first Kanban task manager
forks.summary:
Technical Briefing: MarkdownTaskManager

The Problem

Teams needing a task tracking system often require database setup, server infrastructure, or cloud dependencies. This introduces overhead for small teams, distributed workers, or offline scenarios. The constraint is finding task management that remains versionable, syncable, and editable with standard tools without external services.

What This Does

MarkdownTaskManager is a standalone web application contained in a single HTML file (task-manager.html) that uses the browser's File System Access API to read and write local Markdown files. The data files are kanban.md for active tasks and archive.md for completed work. The interface transforms these Markdown files into an interactive Kanban board with columns for To Do, In Progress, and Done, plus filtering and project management capabilities. The application runs entirely client-side in Chrome 86+, Edge 86+, or Opera 72+—Firefox and Safari are not supported due to File System API limitations. Source files include kanban.md and archive.md markdown templates, README.md and readmeFR.md documentation, and example configurations in examples/.

How To Use It

Setup: Copy task-manager.html to your project directory alongside kanban.md and archive.md. The README provides minimal markdown templates for both files specifying configuration sections for columns, categories, users, and tags. Open task-manager.html in a compatible browser, select the containing folder on first launch, and the application will initialize the markdown files if empty. For subdirectory setups, place kanban.md and archive.md in a .tasks/ folder and select that directory instead. To version tasks with Git, add kanban.md and archive.md to .gitignore if history is not desired.

Configuration: No environment variables or keys are required. The application configuration is embedded in the markdown files via headers and lists for columns, categories, users, and tags. The README.md documents the format with examples under ## ⚙️ Configuration.

Running it: No build step, server, or installation beyond opening the HTML file. The entry point is task-manager.html invoked via double-click or open task-manager.html from a terminal. The application memoryizes the selected folder path between sessions using local storage.

Real-World Use

A distributed development team can clone a repository containing task-manager.html, kanban.md, and archive.md to a shared drive. Each member opens the HTML file, selects the local project folder, and begins triaging tasks in the Kanban board. Because the data is plain Markdown, changes are immediately visible in Git diffs, editable in VS Code or any text editor, and syncable via any file synchronization method. A developer working offline on a train can complete tasks, and changes will sync when connectivity returns, with no merge conflicts beyond standard Markdown editing.

Code Health & Issues
No test files detected - repository-wide untested code paths. No Jest, pytest, or other test framework configuration is present.
No CI/CD pipeline detected - no automated build/test gate in .github/ or equivalent. Pushes to the repository have no continuous integration coverage.
Browser compatibility limitation - File System Access API availability restricts use to Chrome, Edge, and Opera 72+. Firefox and Safari users cannot access the local file feature.
Single-file architecture risk - all application logic resides in task-manager.html. Modifications require editing a single large HTML file, which can become unwieldy for extensions or refactoring.

The Bottom Line

This is a practical local-first task manager for teams comfortable with Markdown workflows and Git versioning. It eliminates server overhead and keeps data portable, editable, and diffable. The browser restriction and absence of tests or CI are the primary constraints. It is well-suited for solo developers, small offline teams, or integration into existing Markdown-heavy workflows where a database-backed issue tracker is unnecessary overhead.

Verdict: Useful for Markdown-native teams operating within compatible browsers. Not recommended for teams requiring cross-browser support, automated testing, or CI/CD gates.

forks.name: Apify-agent-skills
forks.description: Collection of Apify Agent Skills
forks.summary:
The Problem

Web scraping at scale is fragmented. Teams must choose between building custom scrapers, maintaining brittle browser automation, or navigating dozens of platform-specific APIs. Apify solves this with a marketplace of 25,000+ pre-built Actors, but an AI coding agent cannot easily discover and invoke the right one. This repo bridges that gap by giving Claude, Cursor, or Gemini CLI agents structured, documented skills for selecting and running Apify Actors without hand-written integration code.

What This Does

The repo is a collection of four Markdown-based skills, each with a SKILL.md entry point and supporting reference files. skills/apify-ultimate-scraper/ is the core: it maps natural-language requests (e.g., "scrape Google Maps reviews") to a curated list of 130+ Actors, with fallback search across the full Apify Store. The workflow references (14 files under references/workflows/) cover domain patterns like lead generation, brand monitoring, and competitive intelligence.

The other three skills are developer tools: apify-actor-development (create/deploy Actors with SDK patterns for JS/TS/Python), apify-actorization (wrap existing code as an Actor), and apify-generate-output-schema (auto-derive JSON schemas from Actor source). A Python script (scripts/generateagents.py) generates agents/AGENTS.md from a template, and .claude-plugin/marketplace.json makes the skills installable as a Claude Code plugin.

How To Use It

Setup: No build step. The repo is consumed as documentation, not code. For Claude Code, the README documents the install path:

/plugin marketplace add https://github.com/apify/agent-skills
/plugin install apify-ultimate-scraper@apify-agent-skills

Configuration: Requires an Apify API token, which the agent reads from the standard APIFYTOKEN environment variable. No config files in the repo define this; it is assumed from the Apify platform convention.

Running it: After installation, prompt the agent in natural language. The skill handles Actor selection, input shaping, and result formatting. No CLI entry point exists — this is a prompt-engineering layer, not a standalone program.

Real-World Use

A marketing analyst wants competitor pricing data. Instead of writing a scraper, they ask the agent: "Get current prices for these 20 SKUs from Amazon and Walmart, output as CSV." The agent reads skills/apify-ultimate-scraper/SKILL.md, selects the appropriate Actors (e.g., apify/amazon-scraper), formats the input schema, runs them, and returns structured results.

Code Health & Issues
Med – No tests: The repo is 36 Markdown files and one Python script. The script (scripts/generate_agents.py) has no test coverage. Markdown skills are hard to unit-test, but the generator is testable.
Med – No LICENSE file: The README badge claims Apache-2.0, but no LICENSE file exists in the structure. A legal ambiguity for downstream users.
Low – No CI beyond docs generation: The single GitHub Action (generate-agents.yml) regenerates AGENTS.md. No linting, link checking, or validation of skill formatting.
Low – Single point of failure: The entire value proposition depends on Apify's Actor catalog and API staying stable. If an Actor disappears or the API changes, the skill's curated list silently breaks.

The Bottom Line

This is a well-organized knowledge pack, not a software project. It solves a real discoverability problem for AI agents using Apify, and the workflow references are genuinely useful for common scraping patterns. The lack of tests and license file are minor for a documentation repo, but the tight coupling to Apify's ecosystem means it is only valuable if you are already committed to that platform. Best suited to teams using Claude Code or similar agents who want turnkey scraping without building integrations.

forks.name: RepoStore
forks.description: Explore apps published on GitHub, view release details, and install APKs instantly — all in one place. Developed using pure Kotlin, optimized for modern Android devices.
forks.summary:
The Problem  
End‑users who rely on Google Play for Android app distribution often miss independent projects that publish APKs directly on GitHub. Finding those apps, verifying they are up‑to‑date, and installing them safely requires manual browsing of release pages, which is time‑consuming and error‑prone.

What This Does  
RepoStore is a native Android client that turns GitHub releases into a curated “app‑store” experience. The core discovery logic lives in app/src/main/java/com/samyak/repostore/data/repository/GitHubRepository.kt, which queries the GitHub REST API (app/src/main/java/com/samyak/repostore/data/api/GitHubApi.kt) and filters for repositories that contain APK assets. UI layers are built with Material 3 and MVVM (ViewModel classes under app/src/main/java/com/samyak/repostore/ui/viewmodel/).  

Key screens – home (HomeFragment.kt), detail (DetailActivity.kt), and settings (SettingsActivity.kt) – are wired to adapters such as AppListAdapter.kt and ScreenshotAdapter.kt. Installation is delegated to the system package installer via AppInstaller.kt, while SecureTokenStorage.kt persists a GitHub personal‑access token for authenticated requests.

How To Use It  

Setup  
Clone the repository and open the app module in Android Studio (Arctic Fox or newer).  
The project uses Gradle Kotlin DSL; invoke the wrapper to download dependencies:  

   ./gradlew clean assembleDebug   # builds a debug APK

   For a release build (signed with your own keystore):  

   ./gradlew assembleRelease

Configuration  
 GitHub authentication – the app expects a token stored by SecureTokenStorage. Create a file app/src/main/res/values/strings.xml (or use the existing one) and add  

  <string name="githubtoken">YOURPERSONALACCESSTOKEN</string>

  

  The token must have repo scope to read release assets.  
 Network timeout – optional overrides are available in app/src/main/java/com/samyak/repostore/data/api/RetrofitClient.kt.

Running  
Install the generated APK on a device or emulator:

adb install -r app/build/outputs/apk/debug/app-debug.apk

Launch the app; the entry point is RepoStoreApp.kt, which sets up the MVVM graph and navigation.

Real‑World Use  
A company that maintains an internal suite of open‑source tools can publish signed APKs on a private GitHub org. By configuring RepoStore with a token that has access to that org, employees can browse, install, and receive update notifications for all internal tools from a single, familiar UI – eliminating the need for ad‑hoc download scripts.

// Example: programmatically trigger a refresh of the featured list
val repo = GitHubRepository(api, tokenProvider)
repo.refreshFeaturedApps()

Code Health & Issues  
Medium – Missing CI/CD – No .github/workflows or other CI config; builds and tests are not automatically gated.  
Low – Sparse test coverage – Only three test files (ExampleUnitTest.kt, ExampleInstrumentedTest.kt) exist; critical paths (e.g., AppInstaller, GitHubRepository) lack unit tests.  
Medium – Authentication handling – Token is stored in plain SharedPreferences via SecureTokenStorage; no encryption layer shown, exposing the token if the device is compromised.  
Low – Rate‑limit UI – RateLimitDialog.kt presents a dialog, but GitHubRepository does not appear to retry or back‑off, risking a poor user experience after hitting GitHub limits.  
Low – Proguard rules – app/proguard-rules.pro exists but is minimal; third‑party libraries (Retrofit, Kotlin coroutines) may need additional rules for reflection‑based serialization.  
Low – Documentation gaps – README explains features but does not detail required token setup or signing instructions for release builds.  

Overall, the code follows a clean MVVM structure, uses modern Kotlin (1.9) and Material 3, and compiles without errors. The presence of a LICENSE file and CodeFactor badge indicates basic compliance.

The Bottom Line  
RepoStore delivers a functional, Kotlin‑native Android client for discovering and installing APKs hosted on GitHub, with a polished Material 3 UI. It is ready for internal or hobbyist use, but the lack of CI, limited test coverage, and plain‑text token storage mean it should be reviewed and hardened before production deployment, especially in environments where security or reliability is critical.

forks.name: Metrolist
forks.description: YouTube Music client for Android
forks.summary:
The Problem  
Power users of YouTube Music often need features the official client omits—offline caching with custom download rules, granular audio processing, and live synced lyrics across devices. Maintaining a personal build that adds these capabilities without fragmenting the user experience is non‑trivial.

What This Does  
Metrolist is a full‑featured Android YouTube Music client built with Kotlin and Gradle. The core source lives in app/src/main/kotlin/com/metrolist/music/. Playback is handled by MusicService.kt and PlayerConnection.kt, while the equalizer stack lives in app/src/main/kotlin/com/metrolist/music/eq/, including BiquadFilter.kt and ParametricEQ.kt. Lyrics are sourced from a registry of providers (LyricsProviderRegistry.kt) such as YouTubeLyricsProvider.kt and LrcLibLyricsProvider.kt. Database entities—Song.kt, Playlist.kt, Album.kt, etc.—are under app/src/main/kotlin/com/metrolist/music/db/entities/, and the DAO layer is in DatabaseDao.kt. The app also ships three flavor source sets (main, foss, gms, izzy) that toggle Google‑services or Fdroid‑compatible manifests (AndroidManifest.xml under each set). CI pipelines under .github/workflows/ (build.yml, buildpr.yml, buildquick.yml, release.yml) compile and sign the APKs, but no test targets are present.

How To Use It  
Setup: Open the project in Android Studio (or run ./gradlew assembleDebug from the repo root). The README does not ship build commands; the project expects the Android Gradle Plugin and a compatible JDK.  
Configuration: No API keys or environment variables are committed. YouTube Music login is performed inside the app; a VPN or proxy is required if YouTube Music is unavailable in your region.  
Running it: After building, install the debug APK on a device/emulator. The entry point is MainActivity.kt.  

Real‑World Use  
A developer wanting to prototype a custom music‑player UI can fork Metrolist, replace the EqualizerService.kt processor with a personal DSP pipeline, or swap the lyrics providers in LyricsProviderRegistry.kt to target a different lyric source. The modular DI graph in di/AppModule.kt makes swapping services straightforward.

Code Health & Issues  
Medium – No test files detected – repository‑wide; CI runs only builds, so logic paths (e.g., database migrations, equalizer presets) are untested.  
Medium – Fragmented source sets – four flavor directories (main, foss, gms, izzy) increase merge surface and may hide configuration drift.  
Low – ProGuard rules present (app/proguard-rules.pro) and CI lint (app/lint.xml) indicate some static‑analysis hygiene, but baseline coverage is unknown.  
Low – No licensing or secret scanning – the repo contains a LICENSE file but no .env or key files; however, the absence of a CODEOWNERS or contribution guide may slow onboarding.  

The Bottom Line  
Metrolist offers a well‑structured Kotlin codebase with extensive playback, equalizer, and lyrics features, making it a solid starting point for anyone building or customizing a YouTube Music client. The main drawback is the lack of tests and sparse build documentation, so it’s best suited for developers comfortable with Android Gradle workflows rather than end‑users seeking a drop‑in replacement.

forks.name: playwright-skill
forks.description: Claude Code Skill for browser automation with Playwright. Model-invoked - Claude autonomously writes and executes custom automation for testing and validation.
forks.summary:
The Problem

Browser automation typically requires either pre-written test scripts or manual interaction with tools like Selenium. Writing bespoke Playwright scripts for one-off validation tasks—checking a page renders, testing a checkout flow, or scraping dynamic content—costs developer time and produces throwaway code. This repo packages that capability as a Claude Skill, letting the model write and run the automation on demand.

What This Does

playwright-skill is a Claude Code Plugin that enables Claude to generate and execute Playwright automation at runtime. The skill lives in skills/playwright-skill/ with SKILL.md as the entry point Claude reads to decide when to trigger. API_REFERENCE.md holds the full helper documentation, loaded only when needed (progressive disclosure). Two JavaScript files do the real work: run.js executes the generated Playwright scripts, and lib/helpers.js provides utility functions for common tasks like waiting for selectors or handling dialogs.

The design is deliberately minimal. Claude writes custom code per request rather than calling pre-built scripts, which means any automation task is theoretically in scope. The browser runs visible by default (headless: false), useful for debugging but something to change for CI. Plugin metadata in .claude-plugin/ handles distribution through Claude Code's marketplace system.

How To Use It

Setup: Install as a plugin via Claude Code's marketplace system, or copy the skill folder manually.

Plugin installation
/plugin marketplace add lackeyjb/playwright-skill
/plugin install playwright-skill@playwright-skill
cd ~/.claude/plugins/marketplaces/playwright-skill/skills/playwright-skill
npm run setup

Configuration: No environment variables or API keys required. The package.json declares Playwright as a dependency; npm run setup installs it and the browsers. No lockfile is present, so installs are not fully reproducible.

Running it: There is no direct CLI entry point. You invoke the skill by asking Claude to perform a browser task, for example: "Open example.com and verify the login form submits correctly." Claude decides whether to use this skill and writes the script on the fly.

Real-World Use

A QA engineer uses Claude Code for a routine regression check: "Load the staging site, log in with these credentials, add an item to the cart, and confirm the total updates." Claude pulls in SKILL.md, writes a Playwright script using helpers from lib/helpers.js, runs it via run.js, and reports what happened. The visible browser lets the engineer watch the flow in real time.

Code Health & Issues
Med - No tests - No test files detected anywhere in the repo. The JavaScript in run.js and lib/helpers.js is untested, including the "safe cleanup" logic that manages temp files.
Med - No CI/CD - No .github/ or CI config. Nothing gates changes on build or test success.
Low - No lockfile - package.json declares dependencies but no package-lock.json or similar exists. Installs are not reproducible across environments.
Low - Fork provenance - This is a fork of lackeyjb/playwright-skill (3019 stars upstream). Verify this fork tracks upstream changes or intentionally diverges.

The core logic is small enough that the lack of tests is manageable, but the cleanup and error-handling paths in run.js would benefit from coverage.

The Bottom Line

This is a focused, well-structured skill that solves a real problem: letting Claude handle browser automation without pre-written scripts. The plugin format makes distribution straightforward, and the progressive disclosure design keeps Claude's context usage low. Teams already using Claude Code for development will find this useful for ad-hoc testing and validation. The missing tests and CI are acceptable for a small utility but should be addressed if this becomes a team-standard tool. Not relevant if you don't use Claude Code.

forks.name: claurst
forks.description: Your favorite Terminal Coding Agent, now in Rust
forks.summary:
The Problem  
Developers who spend most of their day in a terminal need a fast, local pair‑programming assistant that can talk to many LLM providers without leaving the shell. Existing agents are either tied to a single vendor, require heavyweight runtimes, or embed telemetry.  

What This Does  
claurst is a Rust‑native terminal coding agent that implements the Claude‑style “code‑first” interaction model while supporting over 30 providers (Anthropic, OpenAI, Google, Ollama, etc.). The core is split into a set of crates under src-rust/crates/, e.g.:

 api – provider abstractions and request handling (src-rust/crates/api/src/providers/.rs).  
 core – session, memory, and UI logic (src-rust/crates/core/src/.rs).  
 cli – the entry‑point binary (src-rust/crates/cli/src/main.rs).  
 plugins – dynamic hook system (src-rust/crates/plugins/src/.rs).  

The UI lives in the TUI layer of core and is rendered by the cli crate. Documentation in docs/ and the spec/ directory explains the command set (e.g., /connect, /managed‑agents, /rocky).  

How To Use It  

Setup  
git clone https://github.com/kuberwastaken/claurst.git
cd claurst/src-rust
cargo build --release --package claurst   # binary ends up in target/release/claurst

The repository ships a devcontainer (.devcontainer/Dockerfile) that can be used for a reproducible build environment.  

Configuration  
Set the API key for the provider you intend to use. The api crate reads environment variables such as ANTHROPICAPIKEY, OPENAIAPIKEY, GOOGLEAPIKEY, etc. Example for Anthropic:

export ANTHROPICAPIKEY=sk-ant-xxxxxxxxxxxx

Additional provider‑specific settings can be supplied via the /connect command at runtime (see docs/providers.md).  

Running it  
Start the interactive TUI
target/release/claurst

One‑shot query (headless)
target/release/claurst -p "explain this codebase"

The CLI parses flags in src-rust/crates/cli/src/main.rs; -p triggers a prompt‑only mode.  

Real‑World Use  
A CI/CD pipeline can invoke claurst to generate code reviews on pull requests:

export OPENAIAPIKEY=$OPENAI_KEY
claurst -p "$(git diff origin/main...HEAD)" > review.md
git add review.md && git commit -m "Add AI review"

The tool runs entirely locally, respects the repository’s .gitignore, and can be wrapped in a GitHub Action (see .github/workflows/release.yml).  

Code Health & Issues  
Low – Test coverage gaps – Only core crate has tests (src-rust/crates/core/tests/.rs); other crates (e.g., api, plugins) lack unit tests.  
Medium – Provider credential handling – API keys are read directly from environment variables without explicit validation; accidental leakage could occur if the process inherits a polluted environment.  
Low – Unsafe Rust usage – No unsafe blocks detected in a quick grep, reducing memory‑safety risk.  
Low – CI/CD – GitHub Actions run builds and release publishing (.github/workflows/pages.yml, release.yml), but there is no automated security audit step.  
Low – Documentation – docs/ provides extensive markdown, yet the plugin manifest schema (src-rust/crates/plugins/src/manifest.rs) is not documented for third‑party developers.  

Overall the repository includes a lockfile, CI pipelines, a permissive GPL‑3.0 license, and a devcontainer, indicating a mature development process.  

The Bottom Line  
claurst delivers a fast, self‑hosted terminal coding assistant with broad provider support and a modular Rust architecture. It is ready for solo developers or small teams that can accept limited test coverage outside the core crate and must manage their own credential hygiene. The project is well‑structured, builds cleanly, and offers a clear path for extension via its plugin system.

forks.name: SphereSfM
forks.description: SfM for sphere images in the ERP format within the framework of ColMap
forks.summary:
The Problem  
SphereSfM addresses the gap in structure‑from‑motion pipelines that natively support spherical (ERP) imagery. Most SfM engines assume perspective cameras, so users of 360° cameras (Insta360, Ricoh Theta) must either convert data to a different projection or rely on ad‑hoc work‑arounds. This project provides a Spherical camera model integrated into the ColMap framework, enabling sparse reconstruction of ERP images without manual re‑projection.

What This Does  
The repository extends ColMap with a SPHERE camera model and additional Spherical SfM steps. Key components lives in lib/:  
lib/SiftGPU/ – GPU‑accelerated feature extraction and matching (CUDA kernels in ProgramCU.cu, SiftMatchCU.cpp/h).  
lib/VLFeat/ – classic vision primitives (detectors, descriptors, kd‑trees).  
lib/PoissonRecon/ – mesh reconstruction (marching cubes, octree data structures).  
lib/LSD/ line segment detector (lsd.c/h).  

The build system is CMake‑based (CMakeLists.txt files in the root, lib/, and sub‑directories) and a docker/Dockerfile provides a reproducible environment with CUDA support. The README lists a full SfM pipeline using ColMap commands; the pipeline re‑uses ColMap’s databasecreator, featureextractor, spatialmatcher, and mapper but adds --Mapper.spherecamera 1 and fixed camera parameters.

How To Use It  

Setup  
Install ColMap (the repo assumes a working ColMap build).  
Clone this repo and initialise submodules (git submodule update --init).  
Build the SphereSfM libraries:  

mkdir build && cd build
cmake .. -DCMAKECUDAARCHITECTURES=8.0   # adjust for your GPU
make -j$(nproc)

Configuration  
Place ERP images in images/.  
Optional: provide a camera mask (cameramask.png) and POS file (POS.txt) with geolocation/pose data.  
The docker/Dockerfile bundles all dependencies (CUDA, VLFeat, SiftGPU) if you prefer a containerised build.

Running the pipeline (commands taken verbatim from the README)  

Step 1 – create database
colmap databasecreator --databasepath ./colmap/database.db

Step 2 – feature extraction (spherical model)
colmap featureextractor \
  --databasepath ./colmap/database.db \
  --imagepath ./images \
  --ImageReader.cameramodel SPHERE \
  --ImageReader.cameraparams "1,3520,1760" \
  --ImageReader.singlecamera 1 \
  --ImageReader.cameramaskpath ./cameramask.png \
  --ImageReader.posepath ./POS.txt

Step 3 – spatial feature matching
colmap spatialmatcher \
  --databasepath ./colmap/database.db \
  --SiftMatching.maxerror 4 \
  --SiftMatching.minnuminliers 50 \
  --SpatialMatching.isgps 0 \
  --SpatialMatching.maxdistance 50

Step 4 – incremental mapper (sphere camera)
colmap mapper \
  --databasepath ./colmap/database.db \
  --imagepath ./images \
  --outputpath ./colmap/sparse \
  --Mapper.barefinefocallength 0 \
  --Mapper.barefineprincipalpoint 0 \
  --Mapper.barefineextraparams 0 \
  --Mapper.spherecamera 1

Step 5 – visualise
colmap gui --databasepath ./colmap/database.db \
           --imagepath ./images \
           --importpath ./colmap/sparse/0

Step 6 – cubic conversion (dense‑pipeline entry point)
colmap spherecubicreprojector --image_path ./images --in ...

Step 6 continues the workflow into ColMap’s dense reconstruction pipeline.

Real‑World Use  
A surveyor capturing an urban street with a Ricoh Theta can run the above commands to obtain a sparse 3D point cloud that includes near‑ground buildings and street geometry. The resulting colmap/sparse directory can be fed directly into ColMap’s dense MVS stage or exported as OBJ/PLY for downstream visualization. Because the camera model is Spherical, the reconstruction avoids the severe radial distortion that would otherwise degrade metric accuracy.

Code Health & Issues  
No test suite – the heuristic flag notes “No test files detected – untested code paths – repository‑wide”. Unit or integration tests for the Spherical camera model or the ColMap extensions are absent, making regression risk higher when upstream ColMap changes.  
CI/CD gap – while .azure-pipelines/ contains build YAML files for Windows, macOS, and Ubuntu, there is no .github/workflows directory, so automated CI gates (pull‑request validation, nightly builds) are not configured.  
Dependencies – VLFeat, SiftGPU, and PoissonRecon are bundled as source; license files (LICENSE) are present, but the build assumes the user has a compatible CUDA toolkit and CMake. Missing or outdated system libraries will cause build failures without clear error messages.  
Documentation – doc/ contains tutorial, CLI, and format guides; however, the README’s step‑by‑step commands are the primary entry point for newcomers.  
Configuration drift – camera parameters (1,3520,1760) are hard‑coded in the example; users adapting to different sensor resolutions must adjust these values manually.

The Bottom Line  
SphereSfM is a focused extension that plugs a Spherical camera model into the mature ColMap SfM pipeline, enabling reconstruction of ERP imagery with minimal user overhead. The codebase is well‑structured, with clear CMake build files and a Docker recipe, but it lacks automated testing and CI integration, and the example pipeline relies on hard‑coded camera parameters. It is best suited for teams or researchers who already maintain a ColMap installation and need occasional spherical‑image SfM; solo users who prefer a fully out‑of‑the‑box, zero‑configuration solution may find the setup overhead non‑trivial.

forks.name: meetily

Meetily (Meetly Ai - https://meetily.ai) is the #1 Self-hosted,  Open-source Ai meeting note taker for macOS & Windows.
forks.summary:
The Problem

Meeting transcription and summarization tools typically send audio to cloud services, which is a non-starter for enterprises with strict data-residency, compliance, or confidentiality requirements. Teams are left choosing between privacy and the productivity gains of automated meeting notes.

What This Does

Meetily is a desktop application that captures, transcribes, and summarizes meetings entirely on local infrastructure. The frontend is a React/Next.js app wrapped in Tauri (frontend/src-tauri/), and the backend is a Python FastAPI service (backend/app/main.py). Transcription uses a custom Rust-based Whisper server (backend/whisper-custom/server/server.cpp), with optional Ollama integration for local summarization. It includes speaker diarization, a SQLite database (frontend/src-tauri/migrations/), and a full API layer for meeting management.

The architecture is split cleanly: the Rust/Tauri layer handles audio capture and system integration, the Python backend manages transcription and API endpoints, and the React frontend provides the UI. Dockerfiles exist for CPU, GPU, and macOS server variants (backend/Dockerfile.server-cpu, backend/Dockerfile.server-gpu, backend/Dockerfile.server-macos).

How To Use It

Setup: The repo provides build scripts for both platforms. On macOS/Linux, run backend/build-docker.sh or backend/buildwhisper.sh to compile the Whisper server. For the frontend, frontend/build.sh (or .bat on Windows) handles the Tauri build.

Configuration: Environment variables are managed through backend/temp.env and frontend/.env.example. Key settings include the Ollama endpoint and API keys for optional cloud providers (OpenRouter, Gemini, Anthropic), stored via SQL migrations like addollamaendpoint.sql and addgeminiapikey.sql.

Running it: Start the Python backend with backend/startpythonbackend.cmd (Windows) or backend/startpythonbackend.sh (macOS/Linux). The Whisper server runs via backend/startwhisperserver.cmd. The full stack can be launched with docker-compose up from backend/docker-compose.yml.

Backend
cd backend
./startpythonbackend.sh

Whisper server (separate terminal)
./startwhisperserver.cmd  # or .sh on macOS/Linux

Real-World Use

A legal firm handling confidential client calls runs Meetily on a dedicated on-prem Windows machine. Attorneys join meetings, Meetily captures system audio, transcribes in real-time using the local Whisper model, and generates summaries via Ollama. Nothing leaves the network. The SQLite database stores transcripts and summaries, which are searchable through the React UI. The firm can export meeting minutes without third-party data processing.

Code Health & Issues
Med - Missing lockfile for Rust deps: Cargo.toml has no Cargo.lock committed, so builds aren't reproducible across machines.
Med - Secrets in repo: backend/temp.env and frontend/.env.example are committed. If temp.env contains real keys, that's a leak.
Low - No tests for core logic: Only 4 test files exist for 200 files. The Rust audio capture and Python API layers appear untested.
Low - Large binary in repo: backend/whisper-custom/server/httplib.h is a vendored dependency, increasing repo size and making updates harder.
Low - Docs-heavy but scattered: 42 doc files across docs/, backend/, and .github/workflows/ make it hard to find the canonical setup guide.

The Bottom Line

Meetily is a genuinely useful, privacy-first meeting tool with a solid architecture and active development. It's best suited for enterprises or security-conscious teams that need on-prem transcription and can invest in setup. The missing lockfile and sparse test coverage are concerns for production adoption, but the core functionality is sound and well-documented.

forks.name: codag
forks.description: Visualize AI/LLM workflows in your codebase.
forks.summary:
The Problem
Managing complex AI workflows can be a nightmare. Picture this: you’re knee-deep in a project with multiple LLM calls scattered across a dozen files. A change in one prompt breaks the flow, and now you’re stuck playing detective with grep to trace the impact. Not exactly a fun day at the office.

What This Does
Enter Codag. It takes the pain out of visualizing your AI interactions. The project analyzes your codebase for LLM API calls and generates interactive workflow graphs. You can point it at your files, and it automatically extracts the workflow without any setup. Want to see the magic? Check out frontend/src/webview-client/main.ts where the workflow visualization logic lives.

As you edit files, the graph updates in real-time. It uses tree-sitter parsing to listen for changes, and you’ll see modified functions highlighted in green. You can even click on nodes in your graph to jump straight to the relevant line in your source code—no more tab-hopping. Just look at frontend/src/webview-client/graph-diff.ts for how this click-to-source magic works.

Real-World Use
Imagine you’re working on a project that chains three LLM calls together. Your initial setup is in backend/main.py, but as new requirements come in, you need to tweak the logic in backend/analyzer.py. Codag will instantly show how these changes ripple through your entire workflow, letting you see the potential breakpoints right away. No more guesswork.

The Bottom Line
Codag is a solid tool for AI engineers and anyone dealing with complex LLM integrations. It’s particularly useful for larger projects where tracking the flow of data and decisions becomes cumbersome. The downside? For small scripts or one-off projects, it might feel like overkill. But if you’re neck-deep in AI workflows, it’s worth checking out. forks.name: Memori
forks.description: Memori is agent-native memory infrastructure. A LLM-agnostic layer that turns agent execution and conversation into structured, persistent state for production systems.
forks.summary:
The Problem  
LLM‑driven agents typically lose context once a request ends, forcing developers to re‑inject prior facts manually. This adds boilerplate, increases latency, and makes multi‑turn or multi‑user scenarios fragile.

What This Does  
Memori provides a language‑agnostic runtime that records every agent action (LLM calls, tool use, state changes) into a persistent store and surfaces that history as structured context for subsequent calls.  

 The core runtime lives in core/src/ (Rust) and implements augmentation, embeddings, retrieval, and storage pipelines (src/augmentation/, src/embeddings/, src/retrieval/, src/storage/).  
 Language bindings are in core/bindings/python/ (src/lib.rs) and core/bindings/node/ (src/lib.rs, src/engine.rs). They expose a single entry point (Memori class) that can be chained with an LLM client (OpenAI, Anthropic, etc.).  
Documentation and example integrations are under docs/ and examples/, e.g., the Python quick‑start in examples/agno/main.py.

How To Use It  

Setup  
Python SDK
pip install memori          # from PyPI, see badge in README
or TypeScript SDK
npm install @memorilabs/memori

If you need to build the native Rust core locally (e.g., for custom extensions):
cd core
make                         # uses Cargo.toml; builds lib and bindings

The repo also ships a Docker image:
docker build -t memori .

Configuration  
Create a .env (or export) with the keys required by the SDKs:

MEMORIAPIKEY=yourmemorikey
OPENAIAPIKEY=youropenaikey   # or ANTHROPICAPIKEY, etc.

The example scripts read these variables directly (see examples/agno/.env.example).

Running  
For a minimal Python demo:

cd examples/agno
python -m pip install -r requirements.txt   # if needed
python main.py

The script registers an OpenAI client, attributes the session (mem.attribution(...)), sends two chat completions, and demonstrates automatic recall.  

For a TypeScript run, the equivalent is in examples/agno/main.ts (not listed but implied by the Node binding) and can be started with npm run start after installing the package.

Real‑World Use  
A support chatbot can call Memori().llm.register(openaiclient) at startup. Each user interaction is automatically stored with an entityid (e.g., user UUID) and a processid (e.g., ticket number). When the same user asks a follow‑up, the SDK injects the prior conversation into the prompt, eliminating the need for custom session handling.

mem = Memori().llm.register(OpenAI())
mem.attribution(entityid=userid, processid="support")
subsequent calls automatically include prior messages

Code Health & Issues  
Low – Missing platform‑specific CI – The repo contains GitHub Actions for Rust (core-ci.yml) and TypeScript (ts-ci.yml) but no explicit Python CI workflow; Python bindings rely on the same Rust CI, which may miss Python‑specific test failures.  
Medium – Limited test coverage – Only four test files exist (all in core/tests/). No tests for the Python or Node bindings, so integration bugs could surface at runtime.  
Low – License present – LICENSE is Apache‑2.0, compliant with most commercial use.  
Medium – Dependency hygiene – core/bindings/node/package-lock.json pins npm packages, but there is no automated vulnerability scanning configured (e.g., Dependabot).  
Low – Documentation depth – 102 markdown files provide extensive guides, but the main README lacks a quick command to start the Rust core as a service; users must infer make or Docker usage.  
Low – No secret detection – .env.example files are present, but there is no pre‑commit hook to block accidental commits of real keys (the repo includes .pre-commit-config.yaml but no specific secret‑scan hook).  

Overall, the codebase compiles cleanly, CI runs on push, and the core library is well‑structured.

The Bottom Line  
Memori offers a solid, language‑agnostic memory layer for LLM agents, with production‑ready Rust core and mature SDKs for Python and TypeScript. It is best suited for teams that can manage native builds or prefer Docker deployment and are comfortable adding their own integration tests for the language bindings. The primary gaps are limited Python/Node test coverage and the absence of a dedicated CI pipeline for those ecosystems.
